body.text:
kāmaśūtrasya viṣayānukramaḥ
1. sādhāraṇam
  1. 1. (1) śāstra^saṃgrahaḥ
  1. 2. (2) trivargapratipattiḥ
  1. 3. (3) vidyāsamuddeśaḥ
  1. 4. (4) nāgarakavṛttam
  1. 5. (5) nāyakasahāyadūtīkarmavimarśaḥ
body.translated_text:
Table of contents of the <s>Kāmasūtra</s>:
1. General (<s>sādhāraṇa</s>)
  1.1. (1) Summary of the treatise
  1.2. (2) Pursuit of the three aims of life
  1.3. (3) Enumeration of the arts
  1.4. (4) The life of a man-about-town
  1.5. (5) Discussion of the hero's companions and the work of female messengers

body.text:
2. sāṃprayogikaṃ
  2. 1. (6) pramāṇa^kāla^bhāvebhyo rata^avasthāpanam
  2. 2. (7) āliṅganavicārā
  2. 3. (8) cumbana^vikalpās
  2. 4. (9) nakharadanajātayaḥ
  2. 5.(10) daśana^cchedyavihayo
  2. 6.(11) saṃveśanaprakārāś citraratāni
  2. 7.(12) prahaṇanaprayogās tadyuktāś ca sītkṛta^upakramāḥ
  2. 8.(13) puruṣopasṛptāni puruṣāyitaṃ
  2. 9.(14) aupariṣṭakaṃ
  2.10.(15) rata^arambha^avasānikaṃ rata^viśeṣāḥ praṇayakalahaś ca
body.translated_text:
2. On sexual union (<s>sāṃprayogika</s>)
  2.1. (6) Classification of sexual union according to size, duration, and temperament
  2.2. (7) Varieties of embraces
  2.3. (8) Types of kisses
  2.4. (9) Types of nail-marks and biting
  2.5. (10) Methods of biting
  2.6. (11) Modes of lying down and unusual positions
  2.7. (12) Methods of striking, with accompanying sighing and moaning
  2.8. (13) Woman acting the man's part
  2.9. (14) Oral congress
  2.10. (15) Beginning and end of congress, special types, and lovers' quarrels

body.text:
3. kanyāsaṃprayuktakaṃ
  3. 1.() varaṇasaṃvidhānam saṃbandhaniścayaḥ ca
  3. 2.() kanyāvisrambhaṇam
  3. 3.() bālāyām upakramāḥ iṅgitākārasūcanam ca
  3. 4.() ekapuruṣābhiyogāḥ
  3. 5.() vivāhayoga
body.translated_text:
3. On virgins (<s>kanyāsaṃprayuktaka</s>)
  3.1. Arrangement of betrothal and determination of marriage
  3.2. Winning the girl's confidence
  3.3. Approaches to a young girl, and the interpretation of gestures and expressions
  3.4. Pursuit by a single man
  3.5. Union through marriage

4. On the wife (<s>bhāryādhikārika</s>)
  4.1. Conduct of the sole wife, and behavior during the husband's absence
  4.2. Conduct of the senior wife and others

body.text:
5. pāradārikaṃ
  5.2.() paricayakāraṇāny abhiyogā
  5.3.() bhāvaparīkṣā
  5.4.() dūtīkarmāṇi
  5.5.() īśvarakāmitaṃ
  5.6.() āntaḥpurikaṃ dārarakṣitakaṃ
body.translated_text:
5. On other men's wives (<s>pāradārika</s>)
  5.2. Reasons for acquaintance and approaches
  5.3. Examination of feelings
  5.4. Tasks of the female messenger
  5.5. The love-life of a ruler
  5.6. Life in the harem, and guarding of wives

body.text:
6. vaiśikaṃ
  6.2.() kāntānuvṛttaṃ
  6.3.() arthāgamopāyā viraktaliṅgāni viraktapratipattir niṣkāsanakramās
  6.4.() viśīrṇapratisaṃdhānaṃ
  6.5.() lābhaviśeṣāḥ
  6.6.() arthānarthanubandhasaṃśayavicārā veśyāviśeṣāś ca
body.translated_text:
6. On courtesans (<s>vaiśika</s>)
  6.2. Following the beloved
  6.3. Means of acquiring wealth, signs of disaffection, treatment of the disaffected, and methods of dismissal
  6.4. Reunion after separation
  6.5. Special types of profit
  6.6. Consideration of gains, losses, attendant consequences, and doubts; and special types of courtesans

body.text:
7. aupaniṣadikaṃ
  7.1.() subhagaṃkaraṇaṃ vaśīkaraṇaṃ vṛṣyāś ca yogāḥ
  7.2.() naṣṭarāgapratyānayanaṃ vṛddhividhayaś citrāś ca yogā
...............................................................
body.translated_text:
7. On esoteric practices (<s>aupaniṣadika</s>)
  7.1. Making oneself attractive, subjugation, and virility-enhancing practices
  7.2. Restoring lost passion, methods of augmentation, and unusual recipes
...............................................................
1. General (<s>sādhāraṇa</s>)
1.1. (1) Summary of the treatise
1.1.1. Salutation to <s>Dharma</s>, <s>Artha</s>, and <s>Kāma</s>.
1.1.2. Because it is the subject of the treatise.
1.1.3. And to the teachers who make known its conventions.
1.1.4. Because of its connection with them.

body.text: 1.1.5/.prajāpatir hi prajāḥ sṛṣṭvā tāṣāṃ sthiti^nibandhanaṃ trivargasya sādhanam adhyāyānāṃ śatasahasreṇa^agre provāca//(p.3)
body.translated_text: 1.1.5. <s>Prajāpati</s>, having created beings, first proclaimed the means of accomplishing the three aims of life (<s>trivarga</s>) — the foundation for their maintenance — in a hundred thousand chapters.
1.1.6. From that, <s>Manu Svāyaṃbhuva</s> separately extracted the portion pertaining to <s>dharma</s>.
1.1.7. <s>Bṛhaspati</s> [extracted] the portion pertaining to <s>artha</s> (material prosperity).

body.text: 1.1.8/.mahādeva^anucaraś ca nandī sahasreṇa^adhyāyānāṃ pṛthak kāmasūtraṃ provāca//(p.4)
body.translated_text: 1.1.8. And <s>Nandī</s>, the attendant of <s>Mahādeva</s>, separately proclaimed the <s>Kāmasūtra</s> in a thousand chapters.

body.text: 1.1.9/.tad eva tu pañcabhir adhyāyaśatair auddālakiḥ śvetaketuḥ saṃcikṣepa//(p.4)
body.translated_text: 1.1.9. <s>Śvetaketu Auddālaki</s> then abridged that same [work] into five hundred chapters.

body.text: 1.1.10/.tad eva tu punar adhyardhena^adhyāyaśatena sādhāraṇa^sāṃprayogika^kanyā^saṃprayuktaka^bhāryā^adhikārika^pāradārika^vaiśi ka^aupaniṣadikaḥ saptabhir adhikaraṇair bābhravyaḥ pāñcālaḥ saṃcikṣepa//(p.5)
body.translated_text: 1.1.10. Then <s>Bābhravya</s> the <s>Pāñcāla</s> further abridged that same [work] into one hundred and fifty chapters, in seven sections: general, on sexual union, on virgins, on the wife, on other men's wives, on courtesans, and on esoteric practices.

body.text: 1.1.11/.tasya ṣaṣṭhaṃ vaiśikam adhikaraṇaṃ pāṭaliputrikāṇāṃ gaṇikānāṃ niyogād dattakaḥ pṛthak cakāra//(p.5)
body.translated_text: 1.1.11. From that, <s>Dattaka</s> separately extracted the sixth section on courtesans, at the request of the courtesans of <s>Pāṭaliputra</s>.

body.text: 1.1.12/.tat^prasaṅgāc cārāyaṇaḥ sādhāraṇam adhikaraṇaṃ pṛthak provāca/ suvarṇanābhaḥ sāṃprayogikam/ ghoṭakamukhaḥ kanyā^saṃprayuktakam/ gonardīyo bhāryā^adhikārikam/ goṇikāputraḥ pāradārikam/ kucumāra aupaniṣadikam iti/
body.translated_text: 1.1.12. In connection with that, <s>Cārāyaṇa</s> separately taught the general section; <s>Suvarṇanābha</s> the section on sexual union; <s>Ghoṭakamukha</s> the section on virgins; <s>Gonardīya</s> the section on the wife; <s>Goṇikāputra</s> the section on other men's wives; and <s>Kucumāra</s> the section on esoteric practices.

body.text: 1.1.13/.evaṃ bahubhir ācāryais tacchāstraṃ khaṇḍaśaḥ praṇītam utsannakalpam abhūt/
body.translated_text: 1.1.13. Thus, the treatise, composed piecemeal by many teachers, became nearly extinct.

body.text: 1.1.14/.tatra dattaka^ādibhiḥ praṇītānāṃ śāstra^avayavānām ekadeśatvāt, mahad iti ca bābhravīyasya duradhyeyatvāt, saṃkṣipya sarvam artham alpena granthena kāmasūtram idaṃ praṇītam//(p.6)
body.translated_text: 1.1.14. Since the portions of the treatise composed by <s>Dattaka</s> and others were each only partial, and since the work of <s>Bābhravya</s>, being extensive, was difficult to study, this <s>Kāmasūtra</s> was composed, summarizing all the content in a concise text.
1.1.15. Here is the enumeration of its sections, topics, and chapters:

body.text: 1.1.16/.śāstra^saṃgrahaḥ/ trivarga^pratipattiḥ/ vidyā^samuddeśaḥ/ nāgarika^vṛttam/ nāyaka^sahāya^dūtīkarma^vimarśaḥ/ iti sādhāraṇaṃ prathamam adhikaraṇam/ adhyāyāḥ pañca/ prakaraṇāni pañca/(p.7)
body.translated_text: 1.1.16. Summary of the treatise; pursuit of the three aims of life; enumeration of the arts; the life of a man-about-town; discussion of the hero's companions and the work of female messengers — this is the first section, 'General,' with five chapters and five sub-topics.

body.text:
1.1.17/.pramāṇa^kāla^bhāvebhyo rata^avasthāpanam/ prīti^viśeṣāḥ/ āliṅgana^vicārāḥ/ cumbana^vikalpāḥ/ nakha^radana^jātayaḥ/ daśana^cchedya^vidhayaḥ/ deśyā upacārāḥ/ saṃveśana^prakārāḥ/ citra^ratāni/ prahaṇana^yogāḥ/ tadyuktāś ca sītkṛta^upakramāḥ/ puruṣāyitam/ puruṣopasṛptāni/ aupariṣṭakam/ rata^ārambha^avasānikam/ rata^viśeṣāḥ/ praṇayakalahaḥ/ iti sāṃprayogikaṃ
dvitīyam adhikaraṇam/ adhyāyā daśa/ prakaraṇāni saptadaśa/(p.7)
body.translated_text: 1.1.17. Classification of sexual union according to size, duration, and temperament; special types of affection; varieties of embraces; types of kisses; types of nail-marks and biting; methods of biting; regional customs; modes of lying down; unusual positions; methods of striking; with accompanying sighing and moaning; woman acting the man's part; oral congress; beginning and end of congress; special types; lovers' quarrels — this is the second section, 'On Sexual Union,' with ten chapters and seventeen sub-topics.

body.text: 1.1.18/.varaṇa^vidhānam/ saṃbandha^nirṇayaḥ/ kanyā^visrambhaṇam/ *bālāyā[ch:bālāyāḥ] upakramāḥ/ iṅgita^ākāra^sūcanam/ eka^puruṣa^abhiyogaḥ/ prayojyasya^upāvartanam/ abhiyogataś ca kanyāyāḥ pratipattiḥ/ vivāha^yogaḥ/ iti kanyā^saṃprayuktakaṃ tṛtīyam adhikaraṇam/ adhyāyāḥ pañca/ prakaraṇāni nava/(p.7)
body.translated_text: 1.1.18. Arrangement of betrothal; determination of marriage; winning the girl's confidence; approaches to a young girl; interpretation of gestures and expressions; pursuit by a single man; manipulating an intermediary; and the girl's response to advances; union through marriage — this is the third section, 'On Virgins,' with five chapters and nine sub-topics.

body.text: 1.1.19/.eka^cāriṇī^vṛttam/ pravāsa^caryā/ sapatnīṣu jyeṣṭhā^vṛttam/ kaniṣṭhā^vṛttam/ punarbhū^vṛttam/ durbhagā^vṛttam/ *āntaḥpurikam[ch:antaḥpurikam]/ puruṣasya (p.8) bahvīṣu pratipattiḥ/ iti bhāryā^adhikārikaṃ caturtham adhikaraṇam/ adhyāyau dvau/ prakaraṇāny aṣṭau/(p.8)
body.translated_text: 1.1.19. Conduct of the sole wife; behavior during the husband's absence; conduct of the senior co-wife; conduct of the junior [co-wife]; conduct of a remarried woman; conduct of an unlucky wife; life in the harem; and the husband's conduct with many [wives] — this is the fourth section, 'On the Wife,' with two chapters and eight sub-topics.

body.text: 1.1.20/.strī^puruṣa^śīla^avasthāpanam/ vyāvartana^kāraṇāni/ strīṣu siddhāḥ puruṣāḥ/ ayatna^sādhyā yoṣitaḥ/ paricaya^kāraṇāni/ abhiyogāḥ/ bhāva^parīkṣā/ dūtī^karmāṇi/ īśvara^kāmitam/ āntaḥpurikaṃ dāra^rakṣitakam/ iti pāra^dārikaṃ pañcamam adhikaraṇam/ adhyāyāḥ ṣaṭ/ prakaraṇāni daśa/(p.8)
body.translated_text: 1.1.20. Assessment of the characters of women and men; reasons for acquaintance; men who succeed with women; women easily won; reasons for acquaintance; approaches; examination of feelings; tasks of the female messenger; the love-life of a ruler; life in the harem and guarding of wives — this is the fifth section, 'On Other Men's Wives,' with six chapters and ten sub-topics.

body.text: 1.1.21/.gamya^cintā/ gamana^kāraṇāni/ upāvartana^vidhiḥ/ kānta^anuvartanam/ artha^āgama^upāyāḥ/ virakta^liṅgāni/ virakta^pratipattiḥ/ niṣkāsana^prakārāḥ/ viśīrṇa^pratisaṃdhānam/ lābha^viśeṣaḥ/ artha^anartha^anubandha^saṃśaya^vicāraḥ/ veśyā^viśeṣāś ca/ iti vaiśikaṃ ṣaṣṭham adhikaraṇam/ adhyāyāḥ ṣaṭ/ prakaraṇāni dvādaśa/(p.8)
body.translated_text: 1.1.21. Reflection on suitable clients; reasons for going [to a client]; method of attachment; following the beloved; means of acquiring wealth; signs of disaffection; treatment of the disaffected; methods of dismissal; reunion after separation; special types of profit; consideration of gains, losses, attendant consequences, and doubts; and special types of courtesans — this is the sixth section, 'On Courtesans,' with six chapters and twelve sub-topics.

body.text: 1.1.22/.subhagaṃ^karaṇam/ vaśīkaraṇam/ vṛṣyāś ca yogāḥ/ naṣṭa^rāga^pratyānayanam/ vṛddhi^vidhayaḥ/ citrāś ca yogāḥ/ ity aupaniṣadikaṃ saptamam adhikaraṇam/ adhyāyau dvau/ prakaraṇāni ṣaṭ/ (p.8)
body.translated_text: 1.1.22. Making oneself attractive; subjugation; and virility-enhancing practices; restoring lost passion; methods of augmentation; and unusual recipes — this is the seventh section, 'On Esoteric Practices,' with two chapters and six sub-topics.

body.text: 1.1.23/.evaṃ ṣaṭtriṃśad adhyāyāḥ/ catuḥṣaṣṭiḥ prakaraṇāni/ adhikaraṇāni sapta/ sapādaṃ ślokasahasram/ iti śāstrasya saṃgrahaḥ//(p.8)
body.translated_text: 1.1.23. Thus there are thirty-six chapters, sixty-four sub-topics, seven sections, and slightly over a thousand verses. This is the summary of the treatise.
1.1.24a. Having stated this summary, the detailed exposition will now be set forth.
1.1.24b. For the learned in the world prefer both concise and detailed exposition.
1.2. (2) Pursuit of the three aims of life (<s>trivargapratipattiḥ</s>).

body.text: 1.2.1/.śata^āyur vai puruṣo vibhajya kālam anyonya^anubaddhaṃ parasparasya^anupaghātakaṃ trivargaṃ seveta//(p.10)
body.translated_text: 1.2.1. A man's lifespan being a hundred years, dividing his time, he should pursue the three aims of life (<s>trivarga</s>) — which are interconnected and do not obstruct one another.
1.2.2. In childhood, [he should pursue] the acquisition of learning and other goals pertaining to <s>artha</s> (material prosperity).
1.2.3. And <s>kāma</s> (pleasure) in youth.
1.2.4. In old age, <s>dharma</s> (righteousness) and <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation).
1.2.5. Or, since life is uncertain, one should pursue them as occasion arises.
1.2.6. But one should observe celibacy (<s>brahmacarya</s>) until the completion of education.

body.text: 1.2.7/.alaukikatvād adṛṣṭa^arthatvād apravṛttānāṃ yajñā^ādīnāṃ śāstrāt pravartanam, *laukikatvād[ch:laukitvād] dṛṣṭa^arthatvāc ca pravṛttebhyaś ca māṃsa^bhakṣaṇa^ādibhyaḥ śāstrād eva nivāraṇaṃ dharmaḥ//(p.12)
body.translated_text: 1.2.7. <s>Dharma</s> is: the performance through [Vedic] teaching of acts such as sacrifices and the like that are not of this world and whose results are unseen, since they are not naturally undertaken; and the prohibition through [Vedic] teaching of acts such as eating meat and the like that are worldly and whose results are seen, even though naturally practiced.
1.2.8. One should understand it from the <s>Śruti</s> (Vedic revelation) and from the company of those learned in <s>dharma</s>.
1.2.9. <s>Artha</s> (material prosperity) is: the acquisition of learning, land, gold, cattle, grain, household goods, implements, friends, and the like, and the increase of what has been acquired.
1.2.10. One should understand it from the practice of superintendents and from merchants versed in commerce and convention.

body.text: 1.2.11/.srotra^tvak^cakṣur^jihvā^ghrāṇānām ātma^saṃyuktena manasā^adhiṣṭhitānāṃ sveṣu sveṣu viṣayeṣv ānukūlyataḥ pravṛttiḥ kāmaḥ//(p.13)
body.translated_text: 1.2.11. <s>Kāma</s> (pleasure) is: the engagement of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose — directed by the mind connected with the self — in their respective objects, in a manner that is agreeable.

body.text: 1.2.12/.sparśa^viśeṣa^viṣayāt tv asya^abhimānika^sukha^anuviddhā phalavaty artha^pratītiḥ prādhānyāt kāmaḥ//(p.14)
body.translated_text: 1.2.12. But <s>kāma</s>, principally, is the fruitful experience — accompanied by the pleasure of self-consciousness — that arises from the object of touch in particular.
1.2.13. One should understand it from the <s>Kāmasūtra</s> and from the company of men-about-town.
1.2.14. When these [three aims] come together, each preceding one is more important.

body.text: 1.2.15/.arthaś ca rājñaḥ/ tan^mūlatvāl lokayātrāyāḥ/ veśyāyāś ca^iti trivarga^pratipattiḥ//(p.15)
body.translated_text: 1.2.15. But <s>artha</s> [is more important] for a king, since worldly affairs are rooted in it; and for a courtesan as well. This is the pursuit of the three aims of life.

body.text: 1.2.16/.dharmasya^alaukikatvāt tadabhidhāyakaṃ śāstraṃ yuktam/ upāya^pūrvakatvād artha^siddheḥ/ upāya^pratipattiḥ śāstrāt//(p.16)
body.translated_text: 1.2.16. Since <s>dharma</s> is not of this world, a treatise that expounds it is appropriate. Since the accomplishment of <s>artha</s> requires prior means, the understanding of those means comes from a treatise.

body.text: 1.2.17/.tiryag^yoniṣv api tu svayaṃ pravṛttatvāt kāmasya nityatvāc ca na śāstreṇa kṛtyam asti^ity ācāryāḥ//(p.16)
body.translated_text: 1.2.17. But the teachers say: since <s>kāma</s> operates spontaneously even among animals, and since it is constant, there is no need for a treatise.
1.2.18. Since [the act of] sexual union depends on both man and woman, it requires a method.
1.2.19. And the understanding of that method comes from the <s>Kāmasūtra</s> — says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.

body.text: 1.2.20/.triyag^yoniṣu punar anāvṛtatvāt strījāteś ca, ṛtau yāvad arthaṃ pravṛtter abuddhi^pūrvakatvāc ca pravṛttīnām anupāyaḥ pratyayaḥ//(p.17)
body.translated_text: 1.2.20. Among animals, since the female sex is unrestricted, since they engage [in mating] only during the season and only as much as needed, and since their activities are not preceded by deliberation — [their] mating requires no method.
1.2.21. One should not practice <s>dharma</s> — since its results are in the future and uncertain.
1.2.22. For what fool would transfer what is in hand to another?
1.2.23. Better a pigeon today than a peacock tomorrow.
1.2.24. Better a certain copper coin than an uncertain gold coin — so say the <s>Lokāyatikas</s> (materialists).

body.text: 1.2.25/.śāstrasya^anabhiśaṅkyatvād abhicāra^anuvyāhārayoś ca kvacit phala^darśanān nakṣatra^candra^sūrya^tārā^graha^cakrasya loka^arthaṃ buddhi^pūrvakam iva pravṛtter darśanād varṇa^āśrama^ācāra^sthiti^lakṣaṇatvāc ca lokayātrāyā hastagatasya ca bījasya bhaviṣyataḥ sasya^arthe tyāga^darśanāc cared dharmān iti vātsyāyanaḥ//(p.19)
body.translated_text: 1.2.25. [Reply:] Since the <s>śāstra</s> (sacred teaching) is not to be doubted; since the results of imprecation and counter-assertion are sometimes seen; since the movement of the circle of constellations, moon, sun, stars, and planets appears as if purposefully directed for the sake of the world; since the conduct of the world is characterized by the rules of class (<s>varṇa</s>) and life-stage (<s>āśrama</s>); and since one observes the casting of seed in hand for the sake of future harvest — therefore one should practice <s>dharma</s> — says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.

body.text: 1.2.26/.na^arthāṃś caret/ prayatnato +api hy ete +anuṣṭhīyamānā na^eva kadācit syuḥ// ananuṣṭhīyamānā api yadṛcchayā bhaveyuḥ//(p.21)
body.translated_text: 1.2.26. One should not pursue <s>artha</s> — for even when undertaken with effort, [results] may never come about, while even without effort, they may come about by chance.
1.2.27. All that is caused by time, they say.

body.text: 1.2.28/.kāla eva hi puruṣān artha^anarthayor jaya^parājayayoḥ sukha^duḥkhayoś ca sthāpayati//(p.21)
body.translated_text: 1.2.28. For it is time alone that places men in prosperity and adversity, victory and defeat, happiness and sorrow.

body.text: 1.2.29/.kālena balir indraḥ kṛtaḥ/ kālena *vyavaropitaḥ[ch:vyaparopitaḥ]/ kāla eva punar apy enaṃ kartā^iti kāla^kāraṇikāḥ//(p.22)
body.translated_text: 1.2.29. 'By time, <s>Bali</s> was made <s>Indra</s>; by time, he was deposed; time alone will make him [<s>Indra</s>] again' — thus [argue] those who attribute everything to time.
1.2.30. Since all undertakings are preceded by human effort, effort is the [true] means and cause.

body.text: 1.2.31/.avaśyaṃ bhāvino +apy arthasya^upāya^pūrvakatvād eva/ na niṣkarmaṇo bhadram asti^iti vātsyāyanaḥ//(p.23)
body.translated_text: 1.2.31. Even for what is destined to happen, since it is preceded by means — there is no good fortune for the inactive. Thus says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.

body.text: 1.2.32/.na kāmāṃś caret/ dharma^arthayoḥ pradhānayor evam anyeṣāṃ ca satāṃ pratyanīkatvāt/ anartha^jana^saṃsargam asad^vyavasāyam aśaucam anāyatiṃ ca^ete puruṣasya janayanti//(p.23)
body.translated_text: 1.2.32. One should not indulge in pleasures (<s>kāma</s>) [to excess]. Because of their antagonism to <s>dharma</s> and <s>artha</s>, which are primary, and to [the conduct of] other virtuous people; because of the association with unworthy persons [that results from it]; [because of its leading to] evil —
1.2.33. And likewise, heedlessness, levity, untrustworthiness, and unacceptability.

body.text: 1.2.34/.bahavaś ca kāmavaśagāḥ sagaṇā eva vinaṣṭāḥ śrūyante//(p.24)
body.translated_text: 1.2.34. And many who were enslaved by pleasure are heard to have perished together with their retinues.

body.text: 1.2.35/.yathā dāṇḍakyo nāma bhojaḥ kāmād brāhmaṇa^kanyām abhimanyamānaḥ sabandhu^rāṣṭro vinanāśa//(p.24)
body.translated_text: 1.2.35. For example, the <s>Bhoja</s> king named <s>Dāṇḍakya</s>, lusting after a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> girl, was destroyed together with his kinsmen and kingdom.

body.text: 1.2.36/.devarājaś ca^ahalyām atibalaś ca kīcako draupadīṃ rāvaṇaś ca sītām apare ca^anye ca bahavo dṛśyante kāmavaśagā vinaṣṭā ity artha^cintakāḥ//(p.24)
body.translated_text: 1.2.36. And <s>Indra</s> the king of gods with <s>Ahalyā</s>, the mighty <s>Kīcaka</s> with <s>Draupadī</s>, <s>Rāvaṇa</s> with <s>Sītā</s> — and many others are seen to have been destroyed, enslaved by pleasure.

body.text: 1.2.37/.śarīra^sthiti^hetutvād āhāra^sadharmāṇo hi kāmāḥ/ phala^bhūtāś ca dharma^arthayoḥ//(p.25)
body.translated_text: 1.2.37. For pleasures are like food, being the cause of sustaining the body; and they are the fruit of <s>dharma</s> and <s>artha</s>.

body.text: 1.2.38/.boddhavyaṃ tu doṣeṣv iva/ na hi bhikṣukāḥ santi^iti sthālyo na^adhiśrīyante/ na hi mṛgāḥ santi^iti yavā na^upayanta iti vātsyāyanaḥ//(p.25) bhavanti ca^atra ślokāḥ: ---(p.25)
body.translated_text: 1.2.38. But one should be aware of their dangers. For it is not the case that because there are mendicants, cooking pots should not be placed on the fire; nor that because there are deer, barley should not be sown.

body.text: 1.2.39ab/.evam arthaṃ ca kāmaṃ ca dharmaṃ ca^upācaran naraḥ/(p.25)
body.translated_text: 1.2.39. Therefore, a man should pursue <s>dharma</s>, <s>artha</s>, and <s>kāma</s>, and also liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>), in such a way that none causes harm to another. //
1.3. On the study of the arts (<s>kalā</s>):

body.text: 1.2.40ab/.kiṃ syāt paratra^ity āśaṅkā kārye yasmin na jāyate/(p.26)
body.translated_text: 1.3.1. A man should study the <s>Kāmasūtra</s> and the arts and sciences subsidiary to it, along with <s>dharma</s> and <s>artha</s>.

body.text: 1.2.40cd/.na ca^arthaghnaṃ sukhaṃ ca^iti śiṣṭās tatra vyavasthitāḥ//(p.26)
body.translated_text: 1.3.2. Girls too, before marriage, should study this [science] along with its arts and sciences, privately. And after marriage, [they should do so] with the husband's consent.

body.text: 1.2.41ab/.trivarga^sādhakaṃ yat syād dvayor ekasya vā punaḥ/(p.26)
body.translated_text: 1.3.3. Some teachers say: Since women cannot understand the <s>śāstras</s>, it is useless for them to study.

body.text: 1.2.41cd/.kāryaṃ tad api kurvīta na tv eka^arthaṃ dvi^bādhakam//(p.26)
body.translated_text: 1.3.4. <s>Vātsyāyana</s> [replies]: But women understand the practice, and the practice is grounded in the <s>śāstra</s>.

1.3.5. And this is not limited to this [science] alone; for in the world, even those who know the <s>śāstra</s> slightly are governed by the practice, and the practice has its origin in the <s>śāstra</s>.
1.3.6. And therefore <s>Jyotiṣa</s> (astronomy), though far beyond [common understanding], is practiced along with its observances.
1.3.7. Likewise, culinary science and others.

body.text: 1.3.3/.yoṣitāṃ śāstra^grahaṇasya^abhāvād anarthakam iha śāstre strī^śāsanam ity ācāryāḥ//(p.27)
body.translated_text: 1.3.8. Therefore, a woman who knows the <s>śāstra</s> is worthy of more reverence.

body.text: 1.3.4/.prayoga^grahaṇaṃ tv āsām/ prayogasya ca śāstra^pūrvakatvād iti vātsyāyanaḥ//(p.28)
body.translated_text: 1.3.9. Indeed, even mere knowledge of the science's practice is a cause of respect for a woman. //

body.text: 1.3.5/.tan na kevalam iha^eva/ sarvatra hi loke kati cid eva śāstrajñāḥ/ sarvajana^viṣayaś ca prayogaḥ//(p.28)
body.translated_text: 1.3.10. A girl, therefore, should learn the sixty-four arts from a woman preceptress with whom she is confident, or from a female companion already versed in them,

body.text: 1.3.6/.prayogasya ca dūrastham api śāstram eva hetuḥ//(p.28)
body.translated_text: 1.3.11. or from her mother's sister, or from an old female attendant who is trustworthy, or from a female friend, or from a female mendicant.

body.text: 1.3.7/.asti vyākaraṇam ity avaiyākaraṇā api yājñikā ūhaṃ kratuṣu prayuñjate//(p.29)
body.translated_text: 1.3.12. The sixty-four arts are [listed as follows]:

1.3.13-15. Singing, playing instruments, dancing, painting, cutting <s>tilaka</s> marks on the forehead, making designs with rice and flowers, flower-arranging, dyeing the teeth, limbs, and hair, inlaying gems in floors, bed-making, making music with water [in jars], splashing with water, secret arts, garland-making,

body.text: 1.3.9/.tathā^aśva^ārohā gaja^ārohāś ca^aśvān gajāṃś ca^anadhigata^śāstrā api vinayante//(p.29)
body.translated_text: wearing ornaments on the head, dressing, decorating the ears with ornaments, preparing perfumes, adorning with jewelry, conjuring, <s>Kucumāra</s>'s [aphrodisiac] recipes, sleight of hand, preparing various foods, drinks, and intoxicating beverages,

body.text: 1.3.10/.tathā^asti rājā^iti dūrasthā api janapadā na maryādām ativartante tadvad etat//(p.29)
body.translated_text: needlework and weaving, playing the <s>vīṇā</s> and drum, riddles and puzzles, the game of completing verses, reciting difficult passages, reading books and plays,

body.text: 1.3.11/.santy api khalu śāstra^prahata^buddhayo gaṇikā rājaputryo mahāmātra^duhitaraś ca//(p.30)
body.translated_text: completing passages from plays and stories, weaving cane and bamboo mats, woodwork, carpentry, knowledge of architecture and house-building, testing of precious stones and metals,

body.text: 1.3.12/.tasmād vaiśvāsikāj janād rahasi prayogāñ chāstram ekadeśaṃ vā strī gṛhṇīyāt//(p.30)
body.translated_text: metallurgy, knowledge of the color and origin of gems, skill in horticulture, cock-fighting, quail-fighting and ram-fighting, training parrots and mynahs to speak, skill in applying unguents, massage, and hairdressing,

body.text: 1.3.13/.abhyāsa^prayojyāṃś ca cātuḥṣaṣṭikān yogān kanyā rahasy ekākiny abhyaset//(p.30)
body.translated_text: reading signs and gestures, understanding foreign languages, knowledge of regional dialects, making flower-chariots, [reading] omens and portents, making mechanical devices,

body.text: 1.3.14/.ācāryās tu kanyānāṃ pravṛtta^puruṣa^saṃprayogā saha^saṃpravṛddhā dhātreyikā/ tathā^bhūtā vā niratyaya^saṃbhāṣaṇā sakhī/ savayāś ca mātṛṣvasā/ visrabdhā tat^sthānīyā vṛddha^dāsī/ pūrva^saṃsṛṣṭā vā bhikṣukī/ svasā ca viśvāsa^prayogāt//(p.30)
body.translated_text: training the memory, reciting in concert, making verse improvisations, knowledge of dictionaries and encyclopedias, knowledge of prosody,

body.text:
1.3.15/.gītaṃ, vādyaṃ, nṛtyaṃ, ālekhyaṃ, viśeṣakacchedyaṃ, taṇḍula^kusuma^vali^vikārāḥ, puṣpa^āstaraṇaṃ, daśana^vasana^aṅga^rāgaḥ, maṇi^bhūmikā^karma, śayana^racanam, udaka^vādyam, udaka^āghātaḥ, citrāś ca yogāḥ, mālya^grathana^vikalpāḥ, śekharakā^pīḍa^yojanaṃ, nepathya^prayogāḥ, karṇa^pattra^bhaṅgāḥ, gandha^yuktiḥ, bhūṣaṇa^yojanam,(p.32) aindrajālāḥ, kaucumārāś
ca yogāḥ, hasta^lāghavaṃ, vicitra^śāka^yūṣa^bhakṣya^vikāra^kriyā, pānaka^rasa^rāga^āsava^yojanaṃ, sūcīvāna^karmāṇi, sūtra^krīḍā, vīṇā^ḍamaruka^vādyāni, prahelikā, pratimālā, durvācakayogāḥ, pustaka^vācanaṃ, nāṭaka^ākhyāyikā^darśanaṃ, kāvya^samasyā^pūraṇaṃ, paṭṭikā^*vetra^vāna[ch:vāna.vetra]^vikalpāḥ, takṣa^karmāṇi, takṣaṇaṃ, vāstu^vidyā, rūpya^*ratna[ch
omits]^parīkṣā, dhātu^vādaḥ, maṇi^rāga^ākara^jñānaṃ, vṛkṣāyurveda^yogāḥ, meṣa^kukkuṭa^lāvaka^yuddha^vidhiḥ, śuka^sārikā^pralāpanam, utsādane saṃvāhane keśa^mardane ca kauśalyaṃ[ch:kauśalaṃ], akṣara^muṣṭikā^kathanaṃ, mlecchita^vikalpāḥ, deśa^bhāṣā^vijñānaṃ, puṣpa^śakaṭikā, nimitta^jñānaṃ, yantra^mātṛkā, dhāraṇa^mātṛkā, saṃpāthyaṃ, mānasī, kāvya^kriyā,
abhidhāna^*koṣaḥ[ch:kāṣaḥ], chando^jñānaṃ, kriyā^kalpaḥ, chalitaka^yogāḥ, vastra^gopanāni, *dyūti^viśeṣāḥ[ch:dyūta^viśeṣaḥ], ākarṣa^krīḍā, bāla^krīḍanakāni, vainayikīnāṃ (p.33) vaijayikīnāṃ vyāyāmikīnāṃ ca vidyānāṃ jñānam, iti catuḥṣaṣṭir aṅgavidyāḥ kāmasūtrasya^avayavinyaḥ//(p.34)
body.translated_text: knowledge of poetic figures, knowledge of literary arts, knowledge of the art of disguise, knowledge of artful dressing,

body.text: 1.3.16/.pāñcālikī ca catuḥṣaṣṭir aparā/ tasyāḥ prayogān anvavetya sāṃprayogike vakṣyāmaḥ/ kāmasya tad^ātmakatvāt//(p.41)
body.translated_text: games of chance, the game of <s>ākarṣa</s>, children's games, knowledge of etiquette, the science of victory — these are the sixty-four arts.
1.3.16. Along with these, the [eighteen] arts of <s>Pāñcāla</s> are also mentioned. //

1.3.17. A woman who is endowed with a good disposition and the knowledge of these arts, whether she is a wife, a <s>gaṇikā</s> (courtesan), or a widow, obtains a distinguished position in the assembly of men.

body.text: 1.3.18a/.pūjitā sā sadā rājñā guṇavadbhiś ca saṃstutā/(p.42)
body.translated_text: 1.3.18. A king's daughter and a minister's daughter, by these arts, gain the hearts of their husbands even though the latter may have thousands of women.
1.3.19. And if separated [from her husband] and fallen into misfortune, a woman can live happily even in a foreign land by means of these arts alone.
1.3.20. A man who knows these arts, who is eloquent and skilled in flirtation, quickly wins the hearts of women even by mere acquaintance.
1.3.21. The attainment of these arts depends on one's circumstances, but the man-about-town (<s>nāgaraka</s>) should know them all. //
1.4. The life of the man-about-town (<s>nāgaraka</s>):

1.4.1. Having obtained wealth by gift, conquest, trade, or service, or by inheritance, or by both [inheritance and acquisition], a man should become a householder and lead the life of a man-about-town.
1.4.2. He should settle in a city, a market-town, or wherever good people dwell, near water.
1.4.3. There he should make a dwelling having [an outer room], an inner room, and a bedroom.

1.4.4. In the outer room, a bed, low in the middle and soft, with pillows on both sides and a white coverlet; at its head, a couch; and upon it, ointments for the night, garlands, a pot of beeswax, bark of the <s>citron</s> tree, betel-leaves;

body.text: 1.3.22b/.deśa^kālau tv apekṣya^āsāṃ prayogaḥ saṃbhaven na vā//(p.42)
body.translated_text: 1.4.5. on the floor, a spittoon; a <s>vīṇā</s> hanging from an ivory peg on the wall; a drawing board; a case of brushes; some book or other; and garlands of the yellow <s>amaranth</s>.
1.4.6. Not far [from the bed], on the ground, a round seat; a box for dice and other games; and outside, a cage for birds. Separately, a seat for woodwork and other mechanical arts.

body.text: 1.4.1/.gṛhītavidyaḥ pratigraha^jaya^kraya^nirveśa^adhigatair arthair anvaya^āgatair ubhayair vā gārhasthyam adhigamya nāgaraka^vṛttaṃ varteta//(p.43)
body.translated_text: 1.4.7. In the garden, a well-shaded swing-seat and a bench of baked clay strewn with flowers.

body.text: 1.4.2/.nagare pattane kharvaṭe mahati vā sajjana^āśraye sthānam/ yātrā^vaśād vā//(p.44)
body.translated_text: 1.4.8. Such is the arrangement of the dwelling. //

body.text: 1.4.3/.tatra bhavanam āsanna^udakaṃ vṛkṣa^vāṭikāvad vibhakta^karma^kakṣaṃ dvi^vāsa^gṛhaṃ kārayet//(p.44)
body.translated_text: 1.4.9. Now, the daily routine: Rising in the morning, he attends to his bodily needs; then cleans his teeth; applies a moderate amount of ointment and fragrance to his body; puts on a garland and a <s>tilaka</s> mark of collyrium; looks at his face in a mirror; takes betel-leaves; and then attends to his work.

body.text:
1.4.4/.bāhye ca vāsa^gṛhe suślakṣṇam ubhaya^upadhānaṃ madhye vinataṃ śukla^uttara^cchadaṃ śayanīyaṃ syāt/ pratiśayyikā ca/ tasya śiro^bhāge kūrca^sthānam, vedikā ca/ tatra rātri^śeṣam anulepanaṃ mālyaṃ siktha^karaṇḍakaṃ saugandhika^puṭikā mātuluṅga^tvacas tāmbūlāni ca syuḥ/ bhūmau patad^grahaḥ/ nāga^danta^avasaktā vīṇā/citraphalakam/ vartikāsamudgakaḥ/
yaḥ kaścit pustakaḥ/ kuraṇṭakamālāś ca/ nātidūre bhūmau vṛtta^āstaraṇaṃ samastakam/ ākarṣa^phalakaṃ dyūta^phalakaṃ ca/ tasya bahiḥ krīḍā^śakuni^pañjarāṇi/ ekānte ca takṣa^takṣaṇa^sthānam anyāsāṃ ca krīḍānām/ svāstīrṇā preṅkhādolā vṛkṣavāṭikāyāṃ sapracchāyā/ sthaṇḍila^pīṭhikā ca sakusumeti bhavana^vinyāsaḥ//(p.45)
body.translated_text: 1.4.10. Every day, bathing; every other day, anointing the body; every three days, applying <s>phenaka</s> (soap); every four days, shaving the face; every five or ten days, removing body hair. All this without fail.

body.text: 1.4.5/.sa prātar utthāya kṛta^niyata^kṛtyaḥ, gṛhīta^danta^dhāvanaḥ, mātrayā^anulepanaṃ dhūpaṃ srajam iti ca gṛhītvā, dattvā sikthakam alaktakaṃ ca, dṛṣṭvā^ādarśe mukham, gṛhīta^mukha^vāsa^tāmbūlaḥ, kāryāṇy anutiṣṭhet//(p.47)
body.translated_text: 1.4.11. And the sweat [from the armpits] should be continuously wiped away. After food, in the afternoon — [the routine continues]:

body.text: 1.4.6/.nityaṃ snānam/ dvitīyakam utsādanam/ tṛtīyakaḥ phenakaḥ/ caturthakam āyuṣyam/ pañcamakaṃ daśamakaṃ vā pratyāyuṣyam ity ahīnam/ sātatyāc ca saṃvṛta^kakṣā^sveda^apanodaḥ/
body.translated_text: 1.4.12. Teaching parrots and mynahs to talk; attending cock-fights, quail-fights, and ram-fights; various arts and conversation with jesters, confidence-men, and bards; the afternoon nap.
1.4.13. In the evening, beautifully dressed, [he goes out for] entertainment.

body.text: 1.4.8/.bhojana^anantaraṃ śuka^sārikā^pralāpana^vyāpārāḥ/ lāvaka^*kukkaṭa[ch:kukkuṭa]^meṣa^yuddhāni/ tās tāś ca kalā^krīḍāḥ/ pīṭhamarda^viṭa^vidūṣaka^āyattā vyāpārāḥ/ divā^śayyā ca/
body.translated_text: 1.4.14. He should arrange gatherings around musical performances, meetings in assembly, drinking parties, excursions to gardens, and verse-completion games and amusements.
1.4.15. On a known day of the fortnight or month, there should always be an assembly in the temple of <s>Sarasvatī</s> for those appointed.

body.text: 1.4.10/.pradoṣe ca saṃgītakāni/ tad ante ca prasādhite vāsa^gṛhe saṃcārita^surabhi^dhūpe sasahāyasya śayyāyām abhisārikāṇāṃ pratīkṣaṇam,
body.translated_text: 1.4.16. Visiting performers should give a show for them; on the second day, they should certainly receive honors in return; and thereafter, according to their merit —
1.4.17. And the honoring and welcoming of visitors who have joined the assembly. This is the custom of the guild (<s>gaṇa-dharma</s>).

body.text: 1.4.12/.āgatānāṃ ca manoharair ālāpair upacāraiś ca sasahāyasya^upakramāḥ/
body.translated_text: 1.4.18. By this, the gatherings (<s>ghaṭā</s>) established in honor of various deities are explained. //

body.text: 1.4.13/.varṣa^pramṛṣṭane pathyānāṃ durdinā^abhisārikāṇāṃ svayam eva punar maṇḍanam, mitra^janena vā paricaraṇam ity āhorātrikam//(p.48)
body.translated_text: 1.4.19. In the house of a courtesan, or in a hall, or at someone's residence, those of equal learning, intellect, character, wealth, and age, together with courtesans, should engage in suitable conversation and seating —

body.text: 1.4.14/.ghaṭā^nibandhanam, goṣṭhī^samavāyaḥ, samāpānakam, udyāna^gamanam, samasyāḥ krīḍāś ca pravartayet/
body.translated_text: 1.4.20. And there, [they should enjoy] verse-completion games of poetry or arts.

body.text: 1.4.15/.pakṣasya māsasya vā prajñāte (p.50) +ahani sarasvatyā bhavane niyuktānāṃ nityaṃ samājaḥ/
body.translated_text: 1.4.21. Therein, those who are brilliant and charming to the world should be honored; and those who are equal in affection should be welcomed.

body.text: 1.4.16/.kuśīlavāś ca^āgantavaḥ prekṣaṇakam eṣāṃ dadyuḥ/ dvitīye +ahani tebhyaḥ pūjā niyataṃ labheran/ tato yathāśraddham eṣāṃ darśanam utsargo vā/ vyasana^utsaveṣu ca^eṣāṃ parasparasya^ekakāryatā/
body.translated_text: 1.4.22. And drinking parties at each other's houses.

body.text: 1.4.17/.āgantūnāṃ ca kṛta^samavāyānāṃ pūjanam abhyupapattiś ca/ iti gaṇa^dharmaḥ/
body.translated_text: 1.4.23. There, courtesans should serve and also drink various [beverages]: honey-wine, <s>maireya</s>, spirits, and fermented liquors, together with various salty, fruity, green-vegetable, bitter, pungent, and sour relishes.

body.text: 1.4.18/.etena taṃ taṃ devatā^viśeṣam uddiśya saṃbhāvita^sthitayo ghaṭā vyākhyātāḥ//(p.51)
body.translated_text: 1.4.24. By this, excursions to gardens are explained.

body.text: 1.4.19/.veśyā^bhavane sabhāyām anyatamasya^*udavasite[ch:udvasite] vā samāna^vidyā^buddhi^śīla^vitta^vayasāṃ saha veśyābhir anurūpair ālāpair āsana^bandho goṣṭhī/
body.translated_text: 1.4.19. In the house of a courtesan, in an assembly hall, or at the residence of any one [of the group], those of equal learning, intellect, character, wealth, and age, together with courtesans, engage in suitable conversation—this seated gathering is called a <s>goṣṭhī</s> (social assembly).
1.4.20. And there [they engage in] poetic riddles (<s>kāvya-samasyā</s>) or artistic riddles (<s>kalā-samasyā</s>).
1.4.21. In that [assembly], those who are brilliant and charming to the world are to be honored; and those equal in affection are to be invited.
1.4.22. And drinking parties (<s>āpānaka</s>) [take place] at one another's houses.

1.4.23. There, the courtesans should serve and also drink [themselves] honey-wine (<s>madhu</s>), <s>maireya</s>, <s>surā</s>, and fruit-liquors, with various salty, fruity, green-vegetable, bitter, pungent, and sour relishes.
1.4.24. By this, the excursion to gardens is [also] explained.

body.text: 1.4.25/.pūrvāhṇa eva svalaṃkṛtās turaga^adhirūḍhā veśyābhiḥ saha paricāraka^anugatā gaccheyuḥ/ daivasikīṃ ca yātrāṃ tatra^anubhūya kukkuṭa^yuddha^dyūtaiḥ prekṣābhir anukūlaiś ca ceṣṭitaiḥ kālaṃ gamayitvā aparāhṇe gṛhīta^tad^udyāna^upabhoga^cihnās tathā^eva pratyāvrajeyuḥ/
body.translated_text: 1.4.25. In the forenoon itself, well-adorned, mounted on horses, together with courtesans and followed by attendants, they should go forth. And having enjoyed the daily festival there, having passed the time with cock-fights, gambling, shows, and agreeable activities, in the afternoon, bearing the marks of having enjoyed that garden, they should return in the same manner.
1.4.26. By this, the excursion for water-sports in summer to [places with] artificially constructed reservoirs of water is [also] explained.
1.4.27. The <s>Yakṣa</s>-night; the <s>Kaumudī</s> vigil; [the festival of] <s>Suvasantaka</s> (the Beautiful Spring).

body.text: 1.4.28/.sahakāra^bhañjikā, abhyūṣakhādikā, visakhādikā, navapatrikā, udakakṣveḍikā, pāñcāla^anuyānam, eka^śālmalī, kadambayuddhāni, tās tāś ca māhimānyo deśyāś ca krīḍā janebhyo viśiṣṭam ācareyuḥ/ iti saṃbhūya krīḍāḥ//(p.56)
body.translated_text: 1.4.28. The breaking of mango branches (<s>sahakāra-bhañjikā</s>), roasted-grain eating (<s>abhyūṣakhādikā</s>), the <s>Viśākha</s> festival, the nine-plants ceremony (<s>navapatrikā</s>), water-splashing sport (<s>udakakṣveḍikā</s>), the <s>Pāñcāla</s> procession, the single <s>śālmalī</s> [game], <s>kadamba</s>-battles, and other such great festivals and regional games—they should observe these in a manner distinguished from [that of] common people. Thus [ends the section on] group amusements.
1.4.29. And for one who moves about alone, according to the capacity of his resources—

body.text: 1.4.30/.gaṇikāyā nāyikāyāś ca sakhībhir nāgarakaiś ca saha caritam etena vyākhyātam//(p.57)
body.translated_text: 1.4.30. the conduct of the courtesan (<s>gaṇikā</s>) and the leading lady (<s>nāyikā</s>) together with female friends and urbane men is explained by this.

body.text: 1.4.31/.avibhavas tu śarīra^mātro mallikā^phenaka^kaṣāya^mātra^paricchadaḥ pūjyād (p.57)deśād āgataḥ kalāsu vicakṣaṇas tad^upadeśena goṣṭhyāṃ veśa^ucite ca vṛtte sādhayed ātmānam iti pīṭha^mardaḥ//(p.58)
body.translated_text: 1.4.31. But one without resources, possessing only his body, with only jasmine-soap and astringent as his accoutrements, having come from a respected region, skilled in the arts, should by instructing in those [arts] establish himself in assemblies and in conduct befitting the urbane life—this is the <s>pīṭhamarda</s> (parasite/companion).

body.text: 1.4.32/.bhukta^vibhavas tu guṇavān sakalatro veśe goṣṭhyāṃ ca bahumatas tad upajīvī ca viṭaḥ//(p.58)
body.translated_text: 1.4.32. But one whose resources have been enjoyed [and spent], who is virtuous, who has a wife, who is respected in urbane society and assemblies, and who subsists on that [respect]—this is the <s>viṭa</s> (libertine/courtier).

body.text: 1.4.33/.ekadeśa^vidyas tu krīḍanako viśvāsyaś ca vidūṣakaḥ/ vaihāsiko vā/
body.translated_text: 1.4.33. But one who has partial knowledge, who is playful and trusted—this is the <s>vidūṣaka</s> (jester). Or the <s>vaihāsika</s> (buffoon).
1.4.34. These are the counselors of courtesans and urbane men, appointed for alliances and conflicts.

body.text: 1.4.35/.tair bhikṣukyaḥ kalā^vidagdhā muṇḍā vṛṣalyo vṛddha^gaṇikāś ca vyākhyātāḥ//(p.59)
body.translated_text: 1.4.35. By them are explained [the roles of] female mendicants, women skilled in the arts, shaven-headed women, low-caste women, and aged courtesans.

body.text: 1.4.36/.grāma^vāsī ca sajātān vicakṣaṇān kautūhalikān protsāhya nāgarakajanasya vṛttaṃ varṇayañ śraddhāṃ ca janayaṃs tad eva^anukurvīta/ goṣṭhīś ca pravartayet/ saṃgatyā janam anurañjayet/ karmasu ca sāhāyyena ca^anugṛhṇīyāt/ upakārayec ca/ iti nāgaraka^vṛttam//(p.59)
body.translated_text: 1.4.36. And one living in a village, having encouraged discerning and curious persons of his own community, describing the conduct of urbane people, generating faith [in it], should imitate that very [conduct]; and should organize assemblies; should delight people through sociability; and should assist them through cooperation and favors. Thus [ends the section on] urbane conduct.
1.4.37a. Not exclusively in Sanskrit, nor exclusively in the regional language—
1.4.37b. one who tells stories in assemblies [in a mixed manner] becomes highly regarded in society.
1.4.38a. An assembly that is hateful to the people, or one that spreads unrestrained [rumor],

body.text: 1.4.38b/.parahiṃsā^ātmikā yā ca na tām avatared budhaḥ//(p.60)
body.translated_text: 1.4.38b. or one whose nature is harming others—a wise man should not enter it.
1.4.39a. With an assembly that follows the people's minds, whose sole purpose is play,
1.4.39b. a learned man, keeping company [with it], achieves success in society.
1.5. (Chapter 5): Deliberation on the work of the hero's companions and messengers

body.text: 1.5.1/.kāmaś caturṣu varṇeṣu savarṇataḥ śāstrataś ca^ananya^pūrvāyāṃ prayujyamānaḥ putrīyo yaśasyo laukikaś ca bhavati//(p.61)
body.translated_text: 1.5.1. <s>Kāma</s> (love), when practiced among the four <s>varṇas</s> (classes) with one of the same class, according to the scriptures, and with a woman not previously [married to another], results in offspring, fame, and worldly [acceptance].

body.text: 1.5.2/.tad^viparīta uttama^varṇāsu para^parigṛhītāsu ca/ pratiṣiddho +avara^varṇāsv aniravasitāsu/ veśyāsu punarbhūṣu ca na śiṣṭo na pratiṣiddhaḥ/ sukha^arthatvāt//(p.61)
body.translated_text: 1.5.2. The opposite of that—with women of higher classes and with those possessed by others—is forbidden. With women of lower classes who are not secluded [from society], and with courtesans and remarried women—it is neither prescribed nor forbidden, since it is for the sake of pleasure alone.

body.text: 1.5.3/.tatra nāyikās tisraḥ kanyā punarbhūr veśyā ca/ iti//(p.62)
body.translated_text: 1.5.3. There, the heroines (<s>nāyikā</s>) are of three kinds: the maiden (<s>kanyā</s>), the remarried woman (<s>punarbhū</s>), and the courtesan (<s>veśyā</s>).
1.5.4. A woman possessed by another, [approached] due to some other reason, is a fourth [type], called <s>pākṣikī</s> (occasional)—so says <s>Goṇikāputra</s>.
1.5.5. He [considers her so] when he thinks: 'This one is a <s>svairiṇī</s> (a woman of independent conduct).'

body.text: 1.5.6/.anyato +api bahuśo vyavasita^cāritrā tasyāṃ veśyāyām iva gamanam uttama^varṇinyām api na dharma^pīḍāṃ kariṣyati/ punarbhūr iyam//(p.63)
body.translated_text: 1.5.6. [Thinking:] 'Even otherwise, one whose conduct is extensively determined [by experience]—going to such a woman, even if of the highest class, will not cause injury to <s>dharma</s>, as with a courtesan. She is a remarried woman (<s>punarbhū</s>).'
1.5.7. [If she is] previously [wedded to] another [but now] confined [by a new husband]—there is no doubt regarding this [classification].

body.text: 1.5.8/.patiṃ vā mahāntam īśvaram asmad^amitra^saṃsṛṣṭam iyam avagṛhya prabhutvena carati/ sā mayā saṃsṛṣṭā snehād enaṃ vyāvartayiṣyati//(p.64)
body.translated_text: 1.5.8. [Thinking:] 'Or she, having seized a great and powerful husband who is allied with my enemy, dominates [him] with authority. She, when united with me out of affection, will turn him away [from my enemy].'

body.text: 1.5.9/.virasaṃ vā mayi śaktam apakartukāmaṃ ca prakṛtim āpādayiṣyati//(p.64)
body.translated_text: 1.5.9. [Or:] 'She will bring back to a favorable disposition [my] hostile [adversary] who is hostile toward me, capable [of harm], and desirous of harming [me].'

body.text: 1.5.10/.tayā vā mitrī^kṛtena mitra^kāryam amitra^pratīghātam anyad vā duṣpratipādakaṃ kāryaṃ sādhayiṣyāmi//(p.65)
body.translated_text: 1.5.10. [Or:] 'Through him who has been befriended by her, I shall accomplish a friendly purpose, the repelling of an enemy, or some other task difficult to accomplish.'

body.text: 1.5.11/.saṃsṛṣṭo vā^anayā hatvā^asyāḥ patim asmadbhāvyaṃ tad aiśvaryam evam adhigamiṣyāmi//(p.65)
body.translated_text: 1.5.11. [Or:] 'Being united with her, having killed her husband, I shall obtain that sovereignty which is destined to be mine.'

body.text: 1.5.12/.niratyayaṃ vā^asyā gamanam artha^anubaddham/ ahaṃ ca niḥsāratvāt kṣīṇa^vṛtty^upāyaḥ/ so +aham anena^upāyena taddhanam atimahad akṛcchrād adhigamiṣyāmi/
body.translated_text: 1.5.12. [Or:] 'Going to her is without danger and connected with profit. And I, being without resources, have exhausted my means of livelihood. By this means I shall easily obtain that exceedingly great wealth of hers.'

body.text: 1.5.13/.marmajñā vā mayi dṛdham abhikāmā sā mām anicchantaṃ doṣa^vikhyāpānena dūṣayiṣyati//(p.65)
body.translated_text: 1.5.13. [Or:] 'She, knowing my vulnerabilities and being intensely desirous of me, will ruin me—unwilling [though I am]—by publicizing [my] faults.'

body.text: 1.5.14/.asad^bhūtaṃ vā doṣaṃ śraddheyaṃ duṣparihāraṃ mayi kṣepsyati yena me vināśaḥ syāt//(p.66)
body.translated_text: 1.5.14. [Or:] 'She will cast upon me a false but credible and hard-to-refute fault, by which my destruction would come about.'

body.text: 1.5.15/.āyatimantaṃ vā vaśyaṃ patiṃ matto vibhidya dviṣataḥ saṃgrāhayiṣyati//(p.66)
body.translated_text: 1.5.15. [Or:] 'She will separate her husband, who is prosperous and under her control, from me and attach him to my enemies.'

body.text: 1.5.16/.svayaṃ vā taiḥ saha saṃsṛjyeta/ madavarodhānāṃ vā dūṣayitā patir asyās tad asyāham api dārān eva dūṣayan pratikariṣyāmi//(p.66)
body.translated_text: 1.5.16. [Or:] 'She herself will unite with them [my enemies]. Or her husband is a corrupter of my women—so I too shall retaliate by corrupting his wife.'
1.5.17. [Or:] 'By royal command, I shall kill through her his enemy who is within [his household].'

body.text: 1.5.18/.yāmanyāṃ kāmayiṣye sāsyā vaśagā/ tām anena saṃkrameṇa^adhigamiṣyāmi/
body.translated_text: 1.5.18. [Or:] 'The other woman whom I desire is under her control—through this connection I shall obtain her.'
1.5.19. [Or:] 'She will transfer to me a maiden—unobtainable [otherwise]—who is under her authority, and who is beautiful and wealthy.'

body.text: 1.5.20/.mama^amitro vāsyāḥ patyā sahaikībhāvam upagatas tam anayā rasena yojayiṣyāmi^ity evam ādibhiḥ kāraṇaiḥ parastriyam api prakurvīta//(p.67)
body.translated_text: 1.5.20. [Or:] 'My enemy has become united with her husband—through her, I shall administer poison to him.' For such reasons as these, one may approach even the wife of another.

body.text: 1.5.21/.iti sāhasikyaṃ na kevalaṃ rāgād eva/ iti para^parigraha^gamana^kāraṇāni/
body.translated_text: 1.5.21. Thus [the approach to] the adventurous type (<s>sāhasikī</s>) is not merely out of passion alone. These are the reasons for approaching another's wife.

body.text: 1.5.22/.etair eva kāraṇair mahāmātra^saṃbaddhā rāja^saṃbaddhā vā tatra^eka^deśa^cāriṇī kā cid anyā vā kārya^saṃpādinī vidhavā pañcamī^iti cārāyaṇaḥ/
body.translated_text: 1.5.22. For these very reasons, one connected with a high official or connected with the king, one who moves about in a certain region for such purposes, or any other woman who accomplishes tasks—a widow [is considered] the fifth [type]—so says <s>Cārāyaṇa</s>.
1.5.23. That same one, when she has become a female ascetic, is the sixth—so says <s>Suvarṇanābha</s>.
1.5.24. The daughter of a courtesan, or a female attendant not previously [wedded to another], is the seventh—so says <s>Ghoṭakamukha</s>.
1.5.25. A young woman of good family who has passed beyond childhood, [considered separately] due to the difference in approach, is the eighth—so says <s>Gonardīya</s>.

body.text: 1.5.26/.kārya^antara^abhāvād etāsām api pūrvāsv eva^upalakṣaṇam, tasmāc catasra eva nāyikā iti vātsyāyanaḥ/
body.translated_text: 1.5.26. Since there is no distinct purpose [for these additional types], they are merely indicated within the earlier [categories]; therefore there are only four heroines—so says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.
1.5.27. The third type [i.e., the courtesan] is a separate category, and the fifth [i.e., the widow] [is also separate]—so say some.

body.text: 1.5.28/.eka eva tu sārva^laukiko nāyakaḥ/ pracchannas tu dvitīyaḥ/ viśeṣā^lābhāt/ uttama^adhama^madhyamatāṃ tu guṇa^aguṇato vidyāt/ tāṃs tu^ubhayor api guṇa^aguṇān vaiśike vakṣyāmaḥ//(p.69)
body.translated_text: 1.5.28. But there is only one universal hero. A second [type is] the clandestine one, due to [his] not attaining distinction. One should know the superior, inferior, and middling [types] by their merits and demerits. And those merits and demerits of both [hero and heroine] we shall discuss in the section on courtesans.

body.text: 1.5.29/.agamyās tv eva^etāḥ ---kuṣṭhiny unmattā patitā bhinnarahasyā prakāśaprārthinī gataprāyayauvanā^atiśvetā^atikṛṣṇā durgandhā saṃbandhinī sakhī pravrajitā saṃbandhi^sakhi^śrotriya^rājadārāś ca//(p.69)
body.translated_text: 1.5.29. But these are the unapproachable ones: a leper, a madwoman, an outcaste, one whose secrets are disclosed, one who openly solicits, one whose youth is past, one excessively fair, one excessively dark, one foul-smelling, a kinswoman, a female friend, a female ascetic, and the wives of kinsmen, friends, Vedic scholars, and kings.
1.5.30. One who has been observed [to have been enjoyed] by five men—there is no unapproachable woman—so say the followers of <s>Bābhravya</s>.
1.5.31. Except for the wives of kinsmen, friends, Vedic scholars, and kings—so says <s>Goṇikāputra</s>.

body.text: 1.5.32/.saha pāṃsu^krīḍitam upakāra^saṃbaddhaṃ samāna^śīla^vyasanaṃ saha^adhyāyinaṃ yaś ca^asya marmāṇi rahasyāni ca vidyāt, yasya ca^ayaṃ vidyād vā dhātrapatyaṃ sahasaṃvṛddhaṃ mitram//(p.71)
body.translated_text: 1.5.32. One with whom one has played in the dust [as children], one connected by mutual favors, one of similar character and habits, a fellow-student, one who knows one's vulnerabilities and secrets, and one whose [vulnerabilities and secrets] one also knows, a foster-sibling, and one who has grown up together—[these are the types of] friends.

body.text: 1.5.33/.pitṛ^paitāmaham avisaṃvādakam adṛṣṭa^vaikṛtaṃ vaśyaṃ dhruvam alobha^śīlam aparihāryam amantra^visrāvi^iti mitrasaṃpat//(p.71)
body.translated_text: 1.5.33. The qualities of a [good] friend: inherited from father and grandfather, not deceitful, of unseen changefulness, compliant, steadfast, not covetous in disposition, indispensable, and not divulging counsel.

body.text: 1.5.34/.rajaka^nāpita^mālākāra^gāndhika^saurika^bhikṣuka^gopālaka^tāmbūlika^s auvarṇika^pīṭhamarda^viṭa^vidūṣakādayo mitrāṇi/ tad^yoṣin^mitrāś ca nāgarakāḥ syur iti vātsyāyanaḥ//(p.72)
body.translated_text: 1.5.34. Washermen, barbers, garland-makers, perfumers, liquor-sellers, mendicants, cowherds, betel-sellers, goldsmiths, <s>pīṭhamardas</s>, <s>viṭas</s>, <s>vidūṣakas</s>, and the like are [the typical] friends. And the female friends of their wives [are also friends]—the urbane men should have [such connections]—so says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.

body.text: 1.5.35/.yad ubhayoḥ sādhāraṇam ubhayatrodāraṃ viśeṣato nāyikāyāḥ suvisrabdhaṃ tatra dūtakarma//(p.72)
body.translated_text: 1.5.35. That which is common to both [parties], noble on both sides, and especially trusted by the heroine—there the work of the messenger [is employed].

body.text: 1.5.36/.paṭutā dhārṣṭyam iṅgitākārajñatā pratāraṇa^kālajñatā viṣahya^buddhitvaṃ laghvī pratipattiḥ sa^upāyā ca^iti dūtaguṇāḥ//(p.72) bhavati ca^atra ślokaḥ ---(p.73)
body.translated_text: 1.5.36. Cleverness, boldness, understanding of gestures and expressions, knowledge of the right time for deception, steady-mindedness, and quick and resourceful response—these are the qualities of a messenger. And here there is a verse:
1.5.37ab. Self-possessed, having friends, resourceful, understanding emotions, knowing place and time—
1.5.37cd. such a man can win even an unobtainable woman without effort.
Book Two: The Section on Sexual Union (<s>Sāṃprayogika</s>), the Second Book
2.1. (Chapter 6): Classification of the states of union according to measure, time, and temperament

body.text: 2.1.1/.śaśo vṛṣo +aśva iti liṅgato nāyaka^viśeṣāḥ/ nāyikā punarmṛgī vaḍavā hastinī ca^iti//(p.74)
body.translated_text: 2.1.1. The hare, the bull, and the horse—these are the types of heroes according to [size of the] sexual organ. And the heroines are the doe (<s>mṛgī</s>), the mare (<s>vaḍavā</s>), and the elephant-cow (<s>hastinī</s>).
2.1.2. In a union of equal [types], there are three equal unions.

body.text: 2.1.3/.viparyayeṇa viṣamāṇi ṣaṭ/ viṣameṣv api puruṣa^ādhikyaṃ ced anantara^saṃprayoge dve ucca^rate/ vyavahitam ekam uccatararatam/ viparyaye punar dve nīca^rate/ vyavahitam ekaṃ nīcatara^rataṃ ca/ teṣu samāni śreṣṭhāni/ tara^śabda^aṅkite dve kaniṣṭhe/ śeṣāṇi madhyamāni//(p.75)
body.translated_text: 2.1.3. In the reverse [combinations], there are six unequal unions. Even among the unequal, if there is excess on the man's side, in the immediately adjacent pairing there are two 'high unions'; the one that skips [a type] is the 'highest union.' In the reverse case, there are two 'low unions'; the one that skips [a type] is the 'lowest union.' Among these, the equal [unions] are the best; the two marked by the suffix '-tara' (highest/lowest) are the worst; the rest are middling.

body.text: 2.1.4/.sāmye +apy ucca^aṅkaṃ nīca^aṅkāj jyāyaḥ/ iti pramāṇato nava^ratāni//(p.76)
body.translated_text: 2.1.4. Even among the equal, the 'high-marked' [union] is better than the 'low-marked.' Thus according to measure there are nine types of union.

body.text: 2.1.5/.yasya saṃprayoga^kāle prītir udāsīnā vīryam alpaṃ kṣatāni ca na sahate sa manda^vegaḥ//(p.76)
body.translated_text: 2.1.5. One whose pleasure is indifferent at the time of union, whose vigor is slight, and who cannot endure scratches—he is of mild passion (<s>manda-vega</s>).
2.1.6. The opposite of that produces the middling and intense passions; and likewise for the heroine.
2.1.7. And in this [classification] too, just as with measure, there are nine types of union.
2.1.8. Likewise, according to duration also, heroes are of quick, middling, and prolonged [types].
2.1.9. Regarding [duration in] the woman, there is a dispute.
2.1.10. A woman does not experience pleasure (<s>bhāva</s>) in the same manner as a man.
2.1.11. But through continuous [effort], her itch (<s>kaṇḍūti</s>) is removed by the man.

body.text: 2.1.12/.sā punar ābhimānikena sukhena saṃsṛṣṭā rasa^antaraṃ janayati/ tasmin sukha^buddhir asyāḥ/
body.translated_text: 2.1.12. That [sensation], being mixed with an ego-based pleasure, produces a different flavor (<s>rasa</s>). In that lies her sense of pleasure.

body.text: 2.1.13/.puruṣa^*pratīteś[ch:prīteś] ca^anabhijñatvāt kathaṃ te sukham iti praṣṭum aśakyatvāt/
body.translated_text: 2.1.13. And because of the inability to know the man's experience, [and] the impossibility of asking 'What is your pleasure?'—

body.text: 2.1.14/.katham etad upalabhyata iti cet puruṣo hi ratim adhigamya svecchayā viramati, na striyam apekṣate, na tv evaṃ strī^ity auddālakiḥ//(p.78)
body.translated_text: 2.1.14. 'How is this perceived?' — If [asked]: A man, having attained satisfaction, ceases of his own will; he does not depend on the woman. But a woman is not like that—so says <s>Auddālaki</s>.

body.text: 2.1.15/.tatra^etat syāt/ cira^vege nāyake striyo +anurajyante śīghra^vegasya bhāvam anāsādya^avasāne +abhyasūyinyo *bhavati[ch:bhavanti]/ tat sarvaṃ bhāva^prāpter aprāpteś ca lakṣaṇam//(p.79)
body.translated_text: 2.1.15. Here one might say: women become attached to a man of slow vigor; not having reached the state of a man of quick vigor, they are dissatisfied at the end. All that is a sign of the attainment or non-attainment of <s>bhāva</s> (sexual climax).

body.text: 2.1.16/.tac ca na/ kaṇḍūti^pratīkāro +api hi dīrgha^kālaṃ priya iti/ etad upapadyata eva/ tasmāt saṃdigdhatvād alakṣaṇam iti//(p.80)
body.translated_text: 2.1.16. But that is not so; for even the scratching of an itch is pleasant for a long time. This is perfectly reasonable. Therefore, because it is doubtful, it is not a [definitive] characteristic.
2.1.17a. In sexual union, the itching of the woman is relieved by the man;
2.1.17b. and that [relief], mixed with a sense of pride, is called pleasure.

body.text: 2.1.18/.sātatyād yuvatir ārambhāt prabhṛti bhāvam adhigacchati/ puruṣaḥ punar anta eva/ etad upapannataram/ na hy asatyāṃ bhāva^prāptau garbha^saṃbhava iti bābhravīyāḥ//(p.80)
body.translated_text: 2.1.18. Through continuity, the young woman reaches <s>bhāva</s> (climax) from the very beginning; the man, however, only at the end. This is more reasonable. For without the attainment of <s>bhāva</s>, conception would not occur — so say the <s>Bābhravīyas</s>.
2.1.19. Even here, the same doubt and the same refutation [apply] again.

body.text: 2.1.20/.tatra^etat syāt --- sātatyena rasa^prāptāv ārambha^kāle madhyastha^cittatā na^atisahiṣṇutā ca/ tataḥ krameṇa^adhiko rāga^yogaḥ śarīre nirapekṣatvam/ ante ca virāma^abhīpsā^ity etad upapannam iti//(p.82)
body.translated_text: 2.1.20. Here one might say: when the experience [of pleasure] is attained through continuity, at the beginning there is indifference of mind and an inability to endure [much]. Then gradually there is an increase in the union of passion with the body, and indifference toward it. And at the end, a desire for cessation — this is reasonable.

body.text: 2.1.21/.tac ca na/ sāmānye +api bhrānti^saṃskāre kulālacakrasya bhramarakasya vā bhrāntāv eva vartamānasya prārambhe manda^vegatā tataś ca krameṇa pūraṇam vegasyā^ity upapadyate/ dhātu^kṣayāc ca virāma^abhīpsā^iti/ tasmād anākṣepaḥ//(p.82)
body.translated_text: 2.1.21. But that is not so. Even in the general case of a rotational momentum — such as the rotation of a potter's wheel or a spinning top — when it is already in the process of spinning, at the beginning the velocity is slow, and then there is a gradual filling up of the velocity — this is reasonable. And the desire for cessation is due to the depletion of the bodily constituents (<s>dhātu</s>). Therefore, this is not a [valid] objection.

body.text: 2.1.22a/.suratā^ante sukhaṃ puṃsāṃ strīṇāṃ tu satataṃ sukham/(p.83)
body.translated_text: 2.1.22a. At the end of lovemaking, pleasure [comes] for men; but for women, pleasure is continuous.
2.1.22b. And the desire for cessation arises due to the depletion of the bodily constituents.
2.1.23. Therefore, the manifestation of pleasure (<s>rasa</s>) of women too should be regarded as the same as that of men.

body.text: 2.1.24/.kathaṃ hi samānāyām eva^ākṛtāv eka^artham abhiprapannayoḥ kārya^vailakṣaṇyaṃ syād
body.translated_text: 2.1.24. For how could there be a difference in the effect for two who have engaged in the same act, when the form [of their pleasure] is the same?
2.1.25. Because of the difference in the means and the difference in the sense of self.

body.text: 2.1.26/.katham upāya^vailakṣaṇyaṃ tu sargāt/ kartā hi puruṣo +adhikaraṇaṃ yuvatiḥ/ anyathā hi kartā kriyāṃ pratipadyate +anyathā ca^ādhāraḥ/ tasmāc ca^upāya^vailakṣaṇyāt sargād abhimāna^vailakṣaṇyam api bhavati/ abhiyoktā^aham iti puruṣo +anurajyate/ abhiyuktā^aham anena^iti yuvatir iti vātsyāyanaḥ//(p.84)
body.translated_text: 2.1.26. How is the difference in means? By nature. For the man is the agent and the woman is the receptacle. The agent engages in the act in one way, and the receptacle in another. And from this difference in means, which is natural, there arises also a difference in the sense of self. The man takes pride [thinking] 'I am the aggressor'; the woman [thinking] 'I am aggressed upon by him' — so says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.

body.text: 2.1.27/.tatra^etat syād upāya^vailakṣaṇyavad eva hi kārya^vailakṣaṇyam api kasmān na syād iti/ tac ca na/ hetumad upāya^vailakṣaṇyam/ tatra kartrādhārayor bhinna^lakṣaṇatvād ahetumat kārya^vailakṣaṇyam anyāyyaṃ syāt/ ākṛter abhedād iti/ (p.85)
body.translated_text: 2.1.27. Here one might say: just as there is a difference in means, why should there not also be a difference in the effect? But that is not so. The difference in means has a cause — namely, the distinct characteristics of agent and receptacle. But a difference in effect without a cause would be unjustified — because of the non-difference of form.

body.text: 2.1.28/.tatra^etat syāt/ saṃhatya kārakair eko +artho +abhinirvartyate/ pṛthak pṛthak svārtha^sādhakau punar imau tad ayuktam iti//(p.85)
body.translated_text: 2.1.28. Here one might say: a single result is accomplished by the factors acting together. But these two each accomplish their own purpose separately — that is not justified.

body.text: 2.1.29/.tac ca na/ yugapad aneka^artha^siddhir api dṛśyate/ yathā meṣayor abhighāte kapitthayor bhede mallayor yuddha iti/ na tatra kāraka^bheda iti ced iha^api na vastu^bheda iti/ upāya^vailakṣaṇyaṃ tu sargād iti tad abhihitaṃ purastāt/ tena^ubhayor api sadṛśī sukha^pratipattir iti//(p.86)
body.translated_text: 2.1.29. But that is not so. Even the accomplishment of multiple results simultaneously is observed — as in the collision of two rams, the splitting of two wood-apples, the fight of two wrestlers. If [one says] there is no difference of factors there — then here too there is no difference of substance. But the difference in means is natural — that has been stated previously. Therefore, the experience of pleasure is similar for both.
2.1.30a. Because of the non-difference of the species, equal pleasure for husband and wife is accepted.
2.1.30b. Therefore, the woman should be treated in such a way that she attains pleasure first.

body.text: 2.1.31/.sadṛśatvasya siddhatvāt, kāla^yoginy api bhāvato +api kālataḥ pramāṇavad eva nava ratāni//(p.87)
body.translated_text: 2.1.31. Since similarity [of pleasure] has been established, even considering the compatibility of time, both by disposition and by time, there are nine types of sexual unions, just as with size.

body.text: 2.1.32/.raso ratiḥ prītir bhāvo rāgo vegaḥ samāptir iti rati^paryāyāḥ/ saṃprayogo rataṃ rahaḥ śayanaṃ mohanaṃ surata^paryāyāḥ//(p.88)
body.translated_text: 2.1.32. <s>Rasa</s> (passion), <s>rati</s> (pleasure), <s>prīti</s> (delight), <s>bhāva</s> (feeling), <s>rāga</s> (desire), <s>vega</s> (intensity), <s>samāpti</s> (consummation) — these are synonyms of <s>rati</s> (sexual pleasure). <s>Saṃprayoga</s> (union), <s>rata</s> (lovemaking), <s>rahas</s> (intimacy), <s>śayana</s> (lying together), <s>mohana</s> (enchantment) — these are synonyms of <s>surata</s> (sexual intercourse).

body.text: 2.1.33/.pramāṇa^kāla^bhāvajānāṃ saṃprayogāṇām ekaikasya navavidhatvāt teṣāṃ vyatikare surata^saṃkhyā na śakyate kartum/ atibahutvāt//(p.88)
body.translated_text: 2.1.33. Since each of the unions based on size, time, and disposition is ninefold, the number of types of sexual intercourse, in their permutations, cannot be enumerated — because of their excessive multiplicity.
2.1.34. In those [unions], one should employ the appropriate techniques based on reasoning — so says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.

body.text: 2.1.35/.prathama^rate caṇḍa^vegatā śīghra^kālatā ca puruṣasya, tad viparītam uttareṣu/ yoṣitaḥ punar etad eva viparītam/ ā dhātu^kṣayāt/
body.translated_text: 2.1.35. In the first bout of lovemaking, the man has fierce intensity and quick timing; in subsequent [bouts], the reverse. For the woman, it is the very opposite — until the depletion of the bodily constituents.
2.1.36. And the depletion of the man's constituents [occurs] before the depletion of the woman's — this is the general statement.
2.1.37a. Because of softness, because of being easily aroused, and by the very nature of women,

body.text: 2.1.37b/.prāpnuvanty āśu tāḥ prītim ity ācāryā vyavasthitāḥ//(p.91)
body.translated_text: 2.1.37b. they quickly attain delight — so the teachers have determined.
2.1.38a. This much has been explained regarding sexual union for those who are skilled.
2.1.38b. For the understanding of the less skilled, a detailed exposition will now be given.
2.1.39a. From practice, from self-regard (<s>abhimāna</s>), from conviction,
2.1.39b. and from the sense objects — the experts in the science declare pleasure to be fourfold.
2.1.40a. That which arises from the practice of actions involving external [objects] such as sound and the like,
2.1.40b. that pleasure, characterized by habitual practice, should be known in activities such as hunting and the like.
2.1.41a. Even in actions not previously practiced, that which is not of the nature of a sense-object,

body.text: 2.1.41b/.saṃkalpāj jāyate prītir yā sā syād ābhimānikī//(p.92)
body.translated_text: 2.1.41b. the pleasure that arises from imagination — that is called the pleasure of self-regard (<s>ābhimānikī</s>).
2.1.42a. That which belongs to the third nature (<s>tṛtīyā prakṛti</s>) and to the woman in the superior position (<s>upariṣṭaka</s>),
2.1.42b. and should be known in various activities such as kissing and the like.
2.1.43a. Where, in another cause of pleasure, [one thinks] 'this is no different [from my beloved]' —
2.1.43b. that too is called by the experts in the science the pleasure of conviction (<s>saṃpratyayātmikā</s>).
2.1.44a. The pleasure that is of the nature of a sense-object, directly perceptible and established in common experience —
2.1.44b. since it has the primary result, and the others too serve that purpose.
2.1.45a. Having considered these [types of] pleasure according to the treatise, with the characteristics taught by the treatise,

body.text: 2.1.45b/.yo yathā vartate bhāvas taṃ tathā^eva prayojayet//(p.94)
body.translated_text: 2.1.45b. whatever disposition (<s>bhāva</s>) one finds [in the partner], one should employ it accordingly.
2.2. (7) Types of embraces (<s>āliṅgana</s>)
2.2.1. [Some] teachers say that the sixty-four (<s>catuḥṣaṣṭi</s>) are an auxiliary of sexual union, because there are sixty-four topics.
2.2.2. According to the teachers, this very science is the sixty-four.

body.text: 2.2.3/.kalānāṃ catuḥṣaṣṭitvāt tāsāṃ ca saṃprayoga^aṅga^bhūtatvāt kalā^samūho vā catuḥṣaṣṭir iti/ ṛcāṃ daśatayīnāṃ ca saṃjñitatvāt/ iha^api tad^artha^saṃbandhāt/ pañcāla^saṃbandhāc ca bahv^ṛcair eṣā pūjā^arthaṃ saṃjñā pravartitā ity eke//(p.95)
body.translated_text: 2.2.3. Because the arts (<s>kalā</s>) are sixty-four in number, and because they are auxiliaries of sexual union, the collection of arts may also be called the sixty-four. Because of the convention regarding the 'groups of ten' of the <s>Ṛk</s> [verses]. Here too, because of the connection with that meaning. And because of the connection with <s>Pañcāla</s>, some say this designation was introduced by the <s>Bahvṛcas</s> (followers of many <s>Ṛk</s> verses) for the purpose of reverence.

body.text: 2.2.4/.āliṅgana^cumbana^nakha^cchedya^daśana^cchedya^saṃveśana^sītkṛta^puru ṣa^āyita^aupariṣṭakānām aṣṭānām aṣṭadhā vikalpa^bhedād aṣṭāv aṣṭakāś catuḥṣaṣṭir iti bābhravīyāḥ//(p.96)
body.translated_text: 2.2.4. Embracing, kissing, scratching, biting, positions of lying together, moaning (<s>sītkṛta</s>), the woman acting the man's part (<s>puruṣāyita</s>), and oral congress (<s>aupariṣṭaka</s>) — these eight, each having eight variations, make eight groups of eight, [totaling] sixty-four — so say the <s>Bābhravīyas</s>.

body.text: 2.2.5/.vikalpa^vargāṇām aṣṭānāṃ nyūna^adhikatva^darśanāt prahaṇana^viruta^puruṣopasṛpta^citrarata^ādīnām anyeṣām api vargāṇām iha praveśanāt prāyovādo +ayam/ yathā sapta^parṇo vṛkṣaḥ pañca^varṇo balir iti vātsyāyanaḥ//(p.96)
body.translated_text: 2.2.5. Since the eight categories of variations are seen to have more or fewer [subdivisions], and since other categories too — such as striking, sounds, the man's approach, and various positions — are also included here, this is merely an approximate statement. Like [saying] 'the seven-leafed tree' or 'the five-colored offering' — so says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.

body.text: 2.2.6/.tatra^asamāgatayoḥ prīti^liṅga^dyotana^artham āliṅgana^catuṣṭayam ---spṛṣṭakam, viddhakam, uddhṛṣṭakam, pīḍitakam, iti//(p.97)
body.translated_text: 2.2.6. There are four embraces for those who have not yet come together, for the purpose of indicating the signs of affection: <s>spṛṣṭaka</s> (the touching), <s>viddhaka</s> (the piercing), <s>uddhṛṣṭaka</s> (the rubbing), and <s>pīḍitaka</s> (the pressing).
2.2.7. In all cases, the extension of the [term for the] action is by means of the conventional designation.

body.text: 2.2.8/.saṃmukha^āgatāyāṃ prayojyāyām anya^apadeśena gacchato gātreṇa gātrasya sparśanaṃ spṛṣṭakam//(p.97)
body.translated_text: 2.2.8. When [the woman] approaches from the front, the touching of body against body under some pretext while he passes by — that is <s>spṛṣṭaka</s> (the touching).

body.text: 2.2.9/.prayojyaṃ sthitam upaviṣṭaṃ vā vijane kiṃcid gṛhṇatī payodhareṇa *vidhyet[ch:viddhyet]/ nāyako +api tām avapīḍya gṛhṇīyād iti viddhakam//(p.98)
body.translated_text: 2.2.9. When the woman, standing or seated in a solitary place, reaches for something and pierces [him] with her breast — and the man too should grasp her, pressing against her — that is <s>viddhaka</s> (the piercing).
2.2.10. Both of these [are performed] by those whose conversation has not yet become intimate.

body.text: 2.2.11/.tamasi jana^saṃbādhe vijane vā^atha śanakair gacchator na^atihrasva^kālam uddharṣaṇaṃ parasparasya gātrāṇām uddhṛṣṭakam//(p.98)
body.translated_text: 2.2.11. In the dark, in a crowd, or in a solitary place, when walking slowly, the mutual rubbing of each other's limbs for not too short a time — that is <s>uddhṛṣṭaka</s> (the rubbing).

body.text: 2.2.12/.tad eva kuḍya^saṃdaṃśena stambha^saṃdaṃśena vā sphuṭakam avapīḍayed iti pīḍitakam//(p.99)
body.translated_text: 2.2.12. That very [rubbing], when one presses firmly against a wall or a pillar — that is <s>pīḍitaka</s> (the pressing).
2.2.13. Both of these [are performed] by those who have understood each other's intentions.

body.text: 2.2.14/.latā^veṣṭitakaṃ vṛkṣa^adhirūḍhakaṃ tila^taṇḍulakaṃ kṣīra^nīrakam iti catvāri saṃprayoga^kāle//(p.99)
body.translated_text: 2.2.14. <s>Latāveṣṭitaka</s> (the twining of a creeper), <s>vṛkṣādhirūḍhaka</s> (the climbing of a tree), <s>tilataṇḍulaka</s> (the sesame-and-rice), <s>kṣīranīraka</s> (the milk-and-water) — these four [are performed] at the time of union.

body.text: 2.2.15/.latā^iva śālam āveṣṭayantī cumbana^arthaṃ mukham avanamayet/ uddhṛtya manda^sītkṛtā tam āśritā vā kiṃcid rāmaṇīyakaṃ paśyet tal^latā^āveṣṭitakam//(p.99)
body.translated_text: 2.2.15. Twining around [her lover] like a creeper around a <s>śāla</s> tree, she bends [his] face down for the purpose of kissing; or, lifting herself up, giving a soft moan, leaning on him, she gazes at something charming — that is <s>latāveṣṭitaka</s> (the twining of a creeper).

body.text: 2.2.16/.caraṇena caraṇam ākramya dvitīyena^ūru^deśam ākramantī veṣṭayantī vā tat^pṛṣṭha^sakta^ekabāhur dvitīyena^aṃsam avanamayantī īṣan^manda^sītkṛta^kūjitā cumbana^artham eva^adhiroḍhum icched iti vṛkṣa^adhirūḍhakam//(p.100)
body.translated_text: 2.2.16. Stepping on his foot with one foot, pressing or entwining his thigh-region with the other, one arm clasped to his back, bending his shoulder with the other, moaning softly and cooing, she desires to climb up for the purpose of kissing — that is <s>vṛkṣādhirūḍhaka</s> (the climbing of a tree).
2.2.17. Both of these are performed while standing.

body.text: 2.2.18/.śayana^gatāv eva^ūrū^vyatyāsaṃ bhuja^vyatyāsaṃ ca sasaṃgharṣam iva ghanaṃ saṃsvajete tat^tila^taṇḍulakam//(p.100)
body.translated_text: 2.2.18. While lying down, intertwining thighs and intertwining arms, pressing together tightly as if rubbing against each other — that is <s>tilataṇḍulaka</s> (the sesame-and-rice).

body.text: 2.2.19/.rāga^andhāv anapekṣita^atyayau parasparam anuviśata iva^utsaṅga^gatāyām abhimukha^upaviṣṭāyāṃ śayane vā^iti kṣīra^jalakam//(p.101)
body.translated_text: 2.2.19. Blinded by passion, heedless of any transgression, they enter into each other as it were — whether she is on his lap facing him, or on the bed — that is <s>kṣīranīraka</s> (the milk-and-water).
2.2.20. Both of these [are performed] at the time of passion.
2.2.21. These are the embraces [described] according to the <s>Bābhravīyas</s>.
2.2.22. <s>Suvarṇanābha</s>, however, [gives] four additional single-limb embraces.

body.text: 2.2.23/.tatra^ūru^saṃdaṃśena^ekam ūrum ūrudvayaṃ vā sarva^prāṇaṃ pīḍayet ity ūru^upagūhanam//(p.102)
body.translated_text: 2.2.23. Therein, pressing one thigh or both thighs with the grip of the thighs, with all one's force — that is the thigh-embrace.

body.text: 2.2.24/.jaghanena jaghanam avapīḍya prakīryamāṇa^keśa^hastā nakha^daśana^prahaṇana^cumbana^prayojanāya tadupari laṅghayet taj^jaghana^upagūhanam//(p.102)
body.translated_text: 2.2.24. Pressing the loins against the loins, with disheveled hair in hand, leaping upon [the partner] for the purpose of scratching, biting, striking, and kissing — that is the loin-embrace.

body.text: 2.2.25/.stanābhyām uraḥ praviśya tatra^eva bhāram āropayed iti stana^āliṅganam//(p.102)
body.translated_text: 2.2.25. Pressing the chest with the breasts, placing one's weight there — that is the breast-embrace.

body.text: 2.2.26/.mukhe mukham āsajya^akṣiṇī akṣṇor lalāṭena lalāṭam āhanyāt sā lalāṭikā//(p.102)
body.translated_text: 2.2.26. Pressing mouth against mouth, striking eyes against eyes, forehead against forehead — that is the forehead-kiss (<s>lalāṭikā</s>).

body.text: 2.2.27/.saṃvāhanam apy upagūhana^prakāram ity eke manyante/ saṃsparśatvāt//(p.103)
body.translated_text: 2.2.27. Some consider massage (<s>saṃvāhana</s>) also a type of embrace, because it involves touching.
2.2.28. [But] it is not, because it has a different time, a different purpose, and is not shared [between the two] — so says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.
2.2.29a. Even for those who are asking, listening,
2.2.29b. or speaking about the entire method of embracing, desire arises in people.

body.text: 2.2.30a/.ye +api hy aśāstritāḥ ke cit saṃyogā rāga^vardhanāḥ/(p.103)
body.translated_text: 2.2.30a. Even those unions that increase passion and are not prescribed in the treatise,
2.2.30b. they too should be employed with care in sexual union.
2.2.31a. The scope of treatises extends only so long as people's passion is mild.

body.text: 2.2.31b/.rati^cakre pravṛtte tu na^eva śāstraṃ na ca kramaḥ//(p.104)
body.translated_text: 2.2.31b. Once the wheel of passion has begun turning, there is neither treatise nor sequence.
2.3. (8) Types of kisses (<s>cumbana</s>)

body.text: 2.3.1/.cumbana^nakha^daśana^cchedyānāṃ na paurva^aparyam asti/ rāga^yogāt/ prāk^saṃyogād eṣāṃ prādhānyena prayogaḥ/ prahaṇana^sītkṛtayoś ca saṃprayoge//(p.104)
body.translated_text: 2.3.1. There is no fixed sequence for kissing, nail-marks, and bites — because they arise from passion. Before union, these are primarily employed; striking and sighing [are employed] during intercourse.
2.3.2. Everything [may be done] everywhere — since passion is not to be restricted. Thus says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.

body.text: 2.3.3/.tāni prathama^rate na^ativyaktāni viśrabdhikāyāṃ vikalpena ca prayuñjīta/ tathābhūtatvād rāgasya/ tataḥ param atitvarayā viśeṣavatsam uccayena rāga^saṃdhu^kṣaṇa^artham//(p.105)
body.translated_text: 2.3.3. In the first act of love, these should not be too pronounced, and should be employed discriminately, on one who is at ease — since passion is of such a nature. Thereafter, with great haste and with special [attention to] the accumulation [of pleasure], for the purpose of kindling passion.
2.3.4. Kissing [is applied to] the forehead, the locks of hair, the cheeks, the eyes, the chest, the breasts, the lips, and the interior of the mouth.
2.3.5. [Additionally,] the junction of the thighs, the arms, and the navel region — [according to the practice] of the <s>Lāṭas</s> (people of Lāṭa).

body.text: 2.3.6/.rāga^vaśād deśa^pravṛtteś ca santi tāni tāni sthānāni, na tu sarva^jana^prayojyāni^iti vātsyāyanaḥ//(p.106)
body.translated_text: 2.3.6. Due to the influence of passion and regional customs, there are various other places [for kissing]; but they are not [to be considered] applicable to all people — thus says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.

body.text: 2.3.7/.tad yathā --- nimitakaṃ sphuritakaṃ ghaṭṭitakam iti trīṇi kanyā^cumbanāni//(p.106)
body.translated_text: 2.3.7. Namely — <s>nimitaka</s> (the nominal kiss), <s>sphuritaka</s> (the throbbing kiss), and <s>ghaṭṭitaka</s> (the touching kiss) — these are three kisses [appropriate for] a maiden.

body.text: 2.3.8/.balāt kāreṇa niyuktā mukhe mukham ādhatte na tu viceṣṭata iti nimitakam//(p.107)
body.translated_text: 2.3.8. When compelled by force, she places her mouth upon his mouth but does not move — this is <s>nimitaka</s> (the nominal kiss).

body.text: 2.3.9/.vadane praveśitaṃ ca^oṣṭhaṃ manāga^patra^pāvagrahītum icchantī *syandayati[ch:spandayati] svam oṣṭhaṃ na^uttaram utsahata iti sphuritakam//(p.107)
body.translated_text: 2.3.9. When, wishing to take hold of the lip placed in her mouth with a slight, bashful grasp, she moves her own lip but does not venture further — this is <s>sphuritaka</s> (the throbbing kiss).

body.text: 2.3.10/.īṣat^parigṛhya vinimīlita^nayanā kareṇa ca tasya nayane avacchādayantī jihvā^agreṇa ghaṭṭayati iti ghaṭṭitakam//(p.107)
body.translated_text: 2.3.10. When, slightly grasping [his lip], with eyes closed, covering his eyes with her hand, she touches [his mouth] with the tip of her tongue — this is <s>ghaṭṭitaka</s> (the touching kiss).

body.text: 2.3.11/.samaṃ tiryag udbhrāntam avapīḍitakam iti caturvidham apare//(p.107)
body.translated_text: 2.3.11. Others [enumerate] four kinds: <s>sama</s> (the straight kiss), <s>tiryak</s> (the oblique kiss), <s>udbhrānta</s> (the turned kiss), and <s>avapīḍitaka</s> (the pressed kiss).

body.text: 2.3.12/.aṅguli^saṃpuṭena piṇḍīkṛtya nirdaśanam oṣṭha^puṭena^avapīḍayed ity avapīḍitakaṃ pañcamam api karaṇam//(p.108)
body.translated_text: 2.3.12. Gathering [the lips] into a ball with the cup of the fingers and pressing [them] down to bite, pressing with the lip — this is <s>avapīḍitaka</s> (the pressed kiss), a fifth technique.
2.3.13. And one should engage in a game (<s>dyūta</s>) regarding this [kissing].
2.3.14. The one who first seizes the lower lip is the winner.
