body.text: 2.3.15/.tatra jitā sa^ardha^ruditaṃ karaṃ vidhunuyāt praṇuded daśet parivartayed balād āhṛtā vivadet punar apy astu paṇa iti brūyāt/ tatra^api jitā dviguṇam āyasyet//(p.109)
body.translated_text: 2.3.15. The one who loses therein should, with half-crying, shake off the hand, push away, bite, twist about, and being seized by force, should quarrel and say 'let there be another wager.' If defeated again therein, she should show double vexation.

body.text: 2.3.16/.viśrabdhasya pramattasya vā^adharam avagṛhya daśana^antargatam anirgamaṃ kṛtvā hased utkrośet tarjayed valged *āhvayen[ch:āhlayen] nṛtyet pranartita^bhruṇā ca vicala^nayanena mukhena vihasantī tāni tāni ca brūyāt/ iti cumbana^dyūta^kalahaḥ//(p.109)
body.translated_text: 2.3.16. Seizing the lower lip of one who is relaxed or distracted, placing it between the teeth so that it cannot escape, she should laugh, cry out, threaten, leap about, challenge, dance, and with dancing eyebrows and rolling eyes, laughing, she should say various things. Thus is the quarrel-game of kissing.
2.3.17. By this, the quarrel-games of nail-marks, bites, and striking are explained.
2.3.18. These techniques are employed only by those of intense passion — from habituation to that [intensity].

body.text: 2.3.19/.tasyāṃ cubanty āmayam apy uttaraṃ gṛhṇīyāt/ ity uttara^cumbitam//(p.111)
body.translated_text: 2.3.19. When she kisses, she should also take the upper [lip] in return — this is <s>uttaracumbitam</s> (the return kiss).

body.text: 2.3.20/.oṣṭha^saṃdaṃśena^avagṛhya^oṣṭha^dvayam api cumbeta/ iti saṃpuṭakaṃ striyāḥ, puṃso vā +ajātavyañ janasya//(p.111)
body.translated_text: 2.3.20. Seizing both lips with a lip-clasp, she kisses — this is <s>saṃpuṭaka</s> (the box kiss), [done by] the woman, or by a man who has not yet grown facial hair.

body.text: 2.3.21/.tasminn itaro +api jihvayā^āsyā daśanān ghaṭṭayet tālu jihvāṃ ca^iti jihvā^yuddham//(p.112)
body.translated_text: 2.3.21. In that [box kiss], the other too touches with the tongue the teeth and palate and tongue of the mouth — this is <s>jihvāyuddha</s> (the tongue-combat).
2.3.22. By this, the forceful seizing of the face, teeth, and giving [of kisses] is explained.

body.text: 2.3.23/.samaṃ pīḍitam añcitaṃ mṛdu śeṣa^aṅgeṣu cumbanaṃ sthāna^viśeṣa^yogāt/ iti cumbana^viśeṣāḥ//(p.112)
body.translated_text: 2.3.23. Kissing that is even, pressed, curved, and soft — on the remaining limbs, according to the particular place. Thus are the special kinds of kissing.
2.3.24. Looking at the face of one who is sleeping, kissing according to one's own desire — this is the passion-kindling [kiss].

body.text: 2.3.25/.pramattasya vivadamānasya vā +anyato +abhimukhasya supta^abhimukhasya vā nidrā^vyāghāta^arthaṃ calitakam//(p.113)
body.translated_text: 2.3.25. [Kissing] one who is distracted, or quarreling, or facing another direction, or facing sleep, for the purpose of disturbing slumber — this is <s>calitaka</s> (the disturbing kiss).
2.3.26. When one has returned late at night, kissing [the woman] who is sleeping on the bed according to one's own desire — this is <s>prātibodhika</s> (the awakening kiss).

body.text: 2.3.27/.sāpi tu bhāva^jijñāsa^arthinī nāyakasya^agamana^kālaṃ saṃlakṣya vyājena suptā syāt//(p.113)
body.translated_text: 2.3.27. She too, wishing to know his feelings, noting the time of the lover's arrival, should pretend to be asleep.

body.text: 2.3.28/.ādarśe kuḍye salile vā prayojyāyāś chāyā^cumbanam ākāra^pradarśana^artham eva kāryam//(p.114)
body.translated_text: 2.3.28. Kissing the shadow [of the beloved] in a mirror, on a wall, or in water — this should be done for the purpose of showing one's feelings.

body.text: 2.3.29/.bālasya citra^karmaṇaḥ pratimāyāś ca cumbanaṃ saṃkrāntakam āliṅganaṃ ca//(p.114)
body.translated_text: 2.3.29. Kissing a child, a painting, or an image — this is <s>saṃkrāntaka</s> (the transferred kiss), and likewise an embrace.

body.text: 2.3.30/.tathā niśi prekṣaṇake svajana^samāje vā samīpe gatasya prayojyāyā hasta^aṅguli^cumbanaṃ saṃviṣṭasya vā pāda^aṅguli^cumbanam//(p.114)
body.translated_text: 2.3.30. Similarly, at night, at a spectacle, or at a gathering of one's own people, when one has come near — kissing the hand or fingers of the beloved; and when reclining, kissing the toes.

body.text: 2.3.31/.saṃvāhikāyās tu nāyakam ākāra^yantyā nidrā^vaśād akāmāyā iva tasya^ūrvor vadanasya nidhānam ūru^cumbanaṃ pāda^aṅguṣṭha^*cumbanaṃ[ch:omits] ca^ity ābhiyogikāni//(p.115) bhavati ca^atra ślokaḥ ---(p.115)
body.translated_text: 2.3.31. As for the masseuse, when she is making her feelings known to the lover, as if unwillingly due to sleep, she places her face on his thighs — kissing the thighs, and kissing the big toe — these are the preliminary [kisses]. And here is a verse:
2.3.32ab. One should return what is done: a counter-blow for a blow,
2.3.32cd. and in the same manner, a return kiss for a kiss.
2.4 [Chapter on nail-marks]:
2.4.1. When passion increases, scratching with the nails, which has the nature of friction [is employed].

body.text: 2.4.2/.tasya prathama^samāgame pravāsa^pratyāgamane pravāsa^gamane kruddha^prasannāyāṃ mattāyāṃ ca prayogaḥ/ na nityam acaṇḍa^vegayoḥ//(p.116)
body.translated_text: 2.4.2. Its employment is at the first union, on return from a journey, on departure for a journey, with one who is angry and then pleased, and with one who is intoxicated — but not habitually, and not with those who are not of intense passion.
2.4.3. The same applies to bites — or according to habituation.

body.text: 2.4.4/.tad^ācchuritakam ardhacandro maṇḍalaṃ rekhā vyāghra^nakhaṃ mayūra^padakaṃ śaśa^plutakam utpala^patrakam iti rūpato +aṣṭa^vikalpam//(p.117)
body.translated_text: 2.4.4. Those [nail-marks] have eight varieties by form: <s>ācchuritaka</s> (the sounding mark), <s>ardhacandra</s> (the half-moon), <s>maṇḍala</s> (the circle), <s>rekhā</s> (the line), <s>vyāghranakha</s> (the tiger's claw), <s>mayūrapadaka</s> (the peacock's foot), <s>śaśaplutaka</s> (the hare's leap), and <s>utpalapatraka</s> (the lotus-petal).

body.text: 2.4.5/.kakṣau stanau galaḥ pṛṣṭhaṃ jaghanam ūrū ca sthānāni//(p.117)
body.translated_text: 2.4.5. The places [for nail-marks are]: the armpits, the breasts, the throat, the back, the buttocks, and the thighs.

body.text: 2.4.6/.pravṛtta^rati^cakrāṇāṃ na sthānam asthānaṃ vā vidyata iti suvarṇanābhaḥ//(p.117)
body.translated_text: 2.4.6. For those engaged in the wheel of passion, there is no [distinction of] proper and improper place — thus says <s>Suvarṇanābha</s>.

body.text: 2.4.7/.tatra savya^hastāni pratyagra^śikharāṇi dvi^tri^śikharāṇi caṇḍa^vegayor nakhāni syuḥ//(p.117)
body.translated_text: 2.4.7. Therein, for those of intense passion, the nails of the left hand should be freshly pointed, with two or three points.

body.text: 2.4.8/.anugatarāji samam ujjvalam amalinam avipāṭitaṃ vivardhiṣṇu mṛdu^snigdha^darśanam iti nakha^guṇāḥ//(p.118)
body.translated_text: 2.4.8. The qualities of nails: [they should be] with even lines, smooth, lustrous, clean, unbroken, growing, and soft and oily in appearance.

body.text: 2.4.9/.dīrghāṇi hasta^śobhīny āloke ca yoṣitāṃ citta^grāhīṇi gauḍānāṃ nakhāni syuḥ//(p.118)
body.translated_text: 2.4.9. The nails of the <s>Gauḍas</s> (people of Gauḍa) should be long, beautiful on the hand, and captivating to women's minds when seen.
2.4.10. Those of the <s>Dākṣiṇātyas</s> (Southerners) should be short, enduring of work, and suited to one's wish in applying the various techniques.
2.4.11. Those of the <s>Mahārāṣṭrakas</s> (people of Mahārāṣṭra) should be medium, partaking of both [qualities].

body.text: 2.4.12/.taiḥ suniyamitair hanu^deśe stanayor adhare vā laghu^karaṇam anudgata^lekhaṃ sparśa^mātra^jananād romāñ cakaramante saṃnipāta^vardhamāna^śabdam ācchuritakam//(p.119)
body.translated_text: 2.4.12. With those [nails], well-controlled, a light application on the cheek, the breasts, or the lower lip — not leaving a raised mark, causing only the sensation of touch and thereby producing horripilation, with a sound that increases at the point of contact — this is <s>ācchuritaka</s> (the sounding mark).

body.text: 2.4.13/.prayojyāyāṃ ca tasya^aṅga^saṃvāhane śirasaḥ kaṇḍūyane piṭaka^bhedane vyākulīkaraṇe bhīṣaṇena prayogaḥ//(p.119)
body.translated_text: 2.4.13. On the beloved, its application is in the massage of the limbs, scratching of the head, bursting of pimples, creating agitation, and in frightening.
2.4.14. A curved nail-mark impression on the throat, the breast, and the back is <s>ardhacandra</s> (the half-moon).
2.4.15. Those very two, facing each other, [form] <s>maṇḍala</s> (the circle).
2.4.16. Its application is on the navel region, the small of the back, and the groin.
2.4.17. A not-too-long line [is applied] on all places.
2.4.18. That very [line], curved, like a tiger's claw — on the breast.
2.4.19. A line directed toward the nipple, made with five [nails] facing [toward it] — this is <s>mayūrapadaka</s> (the peacock's foot).
2.4.20. Five nail-marks placed close together on the nipple of the breast, in praise of that union — this is <s>śaśaplutaka</s> (the hare's leap).
2.4.21. A mark in the shape of a lotus petal on the breast and back, and on the girdle-path — this is <s>utpalapatraka</s> (the lotus-petal).

body.text: 2.4.22/.ūrvoḥ stana^pṛṣṭhe ca pravāsaṃ gacchataḥ smāraṇīyakaṃ saṃhatāś catasras tisro vā lekhāḥ/ iti nakha^karmāṇi//(p.121)
body.translated_text: 2.4.22. On the thighs and the back, when one is departing on a journey — four or three lines pressed together as a memento. Thus are the nail-techniques.
2.4.23. And one should also make others with various fanciful designs.

body.text: 2.4.24/.vikalpānām anantatvād ānantyāc ca kauśala^vidher abhyāsasya ca sarva^gāmitvād rāga^ātmakatvāc chedyasya prakārān ko +abhisamīkṣitum arhati^ity ācāryāḥ//(p.122)
body.translated_text: 2.4.24. Since the varieties are endless, since the rules of skill are also endless, since practice is all-pervading, and since the [art of] marking is of the nature of passion — who is able to enumerate [all] the kinds? — thus say the teachers.

body.text: 2.4.25/.bhavati hi rāge +api citra^apekṣā/ vaicitryāc ca parasparaṃ rāgo janayitavyaḥ/ vaicakṣaṇya^yuktāś ca gaṇikās tat^kāminaś ca parasparaṃ prārthanīyā bhavanti/ dhanur^vedād iṣv api hi śastra^karma^śāstreṣu vaicitryam eva^apekṣyate kiṃ punar iha^iti vātsyāyanaḥ//(p.122)
body.translated_text: 2.4.25. For even in passion, there is an appreciation for artistry. And from variety, mutual passion is to be generated. And courtesans endowed with skill, and men who desire them, become mutually sought after. For even in archery, in the science of weapons and combat, variety alone is valued — how much more so here! — thus says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.

body.text: 2.4.26/.na tu paraparigṛhītāsv evaṃ *kurthāt[ch:kuryāt]/ pracchanneṣu pradeśeṣu tāsām anusmaraṇa^arthaṃ rāga^vardhanāc ca viśeṣān darśayet//(p.123)
body.translated_text: 2.4.26. But one should not do thus with women belonging to others. On concealed parts of their [bodies], one should show special marks for the purpose of recollection and for increasing passion.
2.4.27a. When a woman sees nail-marks on hidden places,
2.4.27b. even if long-abandoned, a fresh and delicate affection arises.
2.4.28a. In long-abandoned passions, affection would meet with destruction,
2.4.28b. were it not for nail-marks that remind one of the abode of passion.
2.4.29a. Seeing from afar a young woman whose breasts bear the traces of nails,
2.4.29b. even in another, respect and the arousal of passion arise.
2.4.30a. And a man marked with nail-marks on [various] parts of his body

body.text: 2.4.30b/.cittaṃ sthiram api prāyaś calayaty eva yoṣitaḥ//(p.124)
body.translated_text: 2.4.30b. generally agitates even the steadfast mind of a woman.
2.4.31a. There is nothing else sharper for increasing passion
2.4.31b. than the effects of the acts produced by nails and teeth.
2.5 [Chapter on bites]:

body.text: 2.5.1./.uttarauṣṭham antarmukhaṃ nayanam iti muktvā cumbanavad daśana^radana^sthānāni//(p.125)
body.translated_text: 2.5.1. Except for the upper lip, the interior of the mouth, and the eyes, the places for bites are the same as for kisses.

body.text: 2.5.2/.samāḥ snigdha^cchāyā rāga^grāhiṇo yukta^pramāṇā niśchidrās tīkṣṇa^agrā iti daśana^guṇāḥ//(p.125)
body.translated_text: 2.5.2. The qualities of teeth: even, glossy in appearance, capable of being colored [by betel], of proper proportion, without gaps, and with sharp points.

body.text: 2.5.3/.kuṇṭhā rājy^udgatāḥ paruṣāḥ viṣamāḥ ślakṣṇāḥ pṛthavo viralā iti ca doṣāḥ//(p.125)
body.translated_text: 2.5.3. And the defects: blunt, ridged-and-protruding, rough, uneven, soft, wide, and spaced apart.

body.text: 2.5.4/.gūḍhakam ucchūnakaṃ bindur bindumālā *pravāsa[ch:pravāla]^maṇir maṇi^mālā khaṇḍa^abhrakaṃ varāha^carvitakam iti daśana^cchedana^vikalpāḥ//(p.126)
body.translated_text: 2.5.4. <s>Gūḍhaka</s> (the hidden bite), <s>ucchūnaka</s> (the swollen bite), <s>bindu</s> (the point), <s>bindumālā</s> (the line of points), <s>pravālamaṇi</s> (the coral jewel), <s>maṇimālā</s> (the jewel-garland), <s>khaṇḍābhraka</s> (the broken cloud), and <s>varāhacarvitaka</s> (the boar's bite) — these are the varieties of bites.
2.5.5. A <s>gūḍhaka</s> (hidden bite) is to be discerned by a mere redness, not too red.
2.5.6. That same, swollen from pressing, is <s>ucchūnaka</s> (the swollen bite).
2.5.7. Both of those, [forming] a point, on the middle of the lower lip.
2.5.8. The swollen bite and the coral jewel — [are applied] on the cheek.
2.5.9. The ear-ornament kiss, and the nail-and-bite mark — these are the adornments of the left cheek.
2.5.10. The <s>pravālamaṇi</s> (coral jewel) is achieved by the practice of the combination of teeth and lip.
2.5.11. This applies to everything, including the jewel-garland.
2.5.12. The <s>bindu</s> (point) is achieved by the gripping of a small area of skin with two teeth.
2.5.13. [When made] with all [teeth], the <s>bindumālā</s> (line of points) [is achieved].
2.5.14. Therefore, the two garlands [are made] on the regions of the throat, the armpit, and the groin.
2.5.15. And a line of points on the forehead and the thighs.
2.5.16. Like a circle with uneven peaks — <s>khaṇḍābhraka</s> (the broken cloud) is [made] on the breast and back alone.

body.text: 2.5.17/.saṃhatāḥ pradīrghā bahvyo daśana^pada^rājayas tāmra^antarālā varāha^carvitakam/ stana^pṛṣṭha eva//(p.128)
body.translated_text: 2.5.17. Compact, elongated, and numerous rows of tooth-marks with reddish intervals is the 'boar's bite' (<s>varāhacarvitaka</s>) — on the breasts and back only.
2.5.18. Both of these [nail-marks and bite-marks] are for those of intense passion. Thus [ends the section on] bite-marks.

body.text: 2.5.19/.viśeṣake karṇa^pūre puṣpa^āpīḍe tāmbūla^palāśe tamāla^pattre ca^iti prayojya^āgāmiṣu nakha^daśana^cchedya^ādīny ābhiyogikāni//(p.128)
body.translated_text: 2.5.19. On a forehead ornament, an ear ornament, a flower garland, a betel leaf, or a <s>tamāla</s> leaf — these are among the love-tokens to be employed; [they serve] on objects intended for the beloved.
2.5.20. And one should treat women according to regional custom.
2.5.21. Women of the central region (<s>Madhyadeśa</s>) are mostly refined, accustomed to clean practices, and averse to kissing, nail-marks, and tooth-marks.
2.5.22. As are women of <s>Bāhlīka</s> and <s>Avantī</s>.
2.5.23. But they have a predilection for unusual positions.
2.5.24. Women of <s>Mālava</s> and <s>Ābhīra</s> are primarily fond of embracing, kissing, nail-marks, tooth-marks, and sucking; they avoid wounds but are amenable to striking.
2.5.25. Women of the regions between the rivers <s>Sindhu</s> and <s>Ṣaṣṭha</s> are accustomed to oral congress.
2.5.26. Women of <s>Aparānta</s> and <s>Lāṭa</s> are of intense passion but mild in their sighing and moaning.

body.text: 2.5.27/.dṛḍha^prahaṇana^yoginyaḥ khara^vegā eva, apadravya^pradhānāḥ strīrājye kośalāyāṃ ca//(p.130)
body.translated_text: 2.5.27. Those fond of vigorous striking and rough passion, and primarily using artificial devices, are found in the kingdom of women and in <s>Kośala</s>.
2.5.28. Women of <s>Āndhra</s> are naturally soft, fond of lovemaking, with a taste for impurity, and without [strict] rules of conduct.
2.5.29. Women of <s>Mahārāṣṭra</s> are passionate about the practice of all sixty-four arts, fond of vulgar and harsh speech, and impetuous in their approaches in bed.
2.5.30. Women of the city (<s>nāgarika</s>) display similar behavior only in private.
2.5.31. Women of <s>Drāviḍa</s>, when pressed, gradually release their passion during lovemaking.
2.5.32. Women of <s>Vānavāsī</s> are of moderate passion, tolerant of everything, who cover their own bodies but laugh at others' bodies, and who avoid obscene, vulgar, and harsh [speech].
2.5.33. Women of <s>Gauḍa</s> are soft-spoken, affectionate, and with tender limbs.

body.text: 2.5.34/.deśa^sātmyāt prakṛti^sātmyaṃ balīya iti suvarṇanābhaḥ/ na tatra deśyā upacārāḥ//(p.132)
body.translated_text: 2.5.34. Natural temperament is stronger than regional custom — says <s>Suvarṇanābha</s>. Therefore, regional customs do not [always] apply.

body.text: 2.5.35/.kāla^yogāc ca deśād deśa^antaram upacāra^veṣa^līlāś ca^*anugacchanti[ch:anucchanti]/ tac ca vidyāt//(p.132)
body.translated_text: 2.5.35. And through the association of time, customs, dress, and mannerisms pass from one region to another — this too one should know.

body.text: 2.5.36/.upagūhana^ādiṣu ca rāga^vardhanaṃ pūrvaṃ pūrvaṃ vicitram uttaram uttaraṃ ca//(p.132)
body.translated_text: 2.5.36. And in embracing and the like, each successive [technique] is more varied and intensifies passion.

body.text: 2.5.37a/.vāryamāṇaś ca puruṣo yat kuryāt tad anu kṣatam/(p.133)
body.translated_text: 2.5.37a. And when a man makes a mark despite being resisted, subsequently a wound [results].
2.5.37b. The woman, not tolerating it, retaliates with the same in double measure.
2.5.38a. The retaliation for a dot (<s>bindu</s>) is a garland (<s>mālā</s>), and for a garland, a cloud-fragment (<s>abhrakhaṇḍaka</s>).
2.5.38b. Thus, seized by anger and the like, she retaliates with quarrels.
2.5.39a. Grasping his hair, raising his face, she should then drink [his lips],
2.5.39b. and hiding, she should bite here and there, excited by passion.
2.5.40a. Raising [herself] to the neck of her beloved, resting on the surface of his chest,
2.5.40b. she should apply a 'jewel necklace' [of bite-marks], and whatever else is noted.
2.5.41a. Even during the day, in a crowd, [she should examine] what was displayed by the hero,
2.5.41b. and pointing to her own marks, she should laugh, unnoticed by others.
2.5.42a. As if wrinkling her face, as if reproaching the hero,
2.5.42b. she should display the marks on her own body, as if with jealousy.
2.5.43a. Through such mutual harmony, for both who are modest,
2.5.43b. love does not diminish even in a hundred years.
2.6. (11) Modes of lying down and unusual positions (<s>citraratāni</s>).

body.text: 2.6.1/.rāga^kāle viśālayanty eva jaghanaṃ mṛgī saṃviśed ucca^rate//(p.135)
body.translated_text: 2.6.1. At the time of passion, a 'doe' (<s>mṛgī</s>) woman should lie down expanding her hips in the high congress.
2.6.2. An 'elephant' (<s>hastinī</s>) woman, as if contracting [her body], should [lie down] in low congress.
2.6.3. Where equal union is proper, [she should lie] with back flat.
2.6.4. By these two [the 'mare' (<s>vaḍavā</s>) congress] is explained.
2.6.5. There she should receive the hero with her hips.
2.6.6. And artificial devices are especially [used] in low congress.

body.text: 2.6.7/.utphullakaṃ vijṛmbhitakam indrāṇikaṃ ca^iti tritayaṃ mṛgyāḥ prāyeṇa//(p.136)
body.translated_text: 2.6.7. The 'wide-open' (<s>utphullaka</s>), the 'yawning' (<s>vijṛmbhitaka</s>), and the '<s>Indrāṇī</s>' — these three are mostly for the 'doe' woman.
2.6.8. Lowering the head and raising the hips upward is the 'wide-open' position.
2.6.9. There one should allow room for movement.

body.text: 2.6.10/.anīce sakthinī tiryag avasajya pratīcched iti vijṛmbhitakam//(p.137)
body.translated_text: 2.6.10. Raising the thighs crosswise not low and receiving — this is the 'yawning' position.

body.text: 2.6.11/.pārśvayoḥ samam ūrū vinyasya pārśvayor jānunī nidadhyād ity abhyāsa^yogād indrāṇī//(p.137)
body.translated_text: 2.6.11. Placing both thighs equally at the sides and placing the knees at the sides — through practice, this is the '<s>Indrāṇī</s>' position.
2.6.12. By this [position], even one suited for high congress can be accommodated.
2.6.13. Reception with the 'closed' position (<s>saṃpuṭa</s>) is for low congress.
2.6.14. By this, even lower congress of the 'elephant' woman [is accommodated].
2.6.15. The 'closed' (<s>saṃpuṭaka</s>), the 'pressed' (<s>pīḍitaka</s>), the 'entwined' (<s>veṣṭitaka</s>), and the 'mare' (<s>vāḍavaka</s>) —

body.text: 2.6.16/.ṛju^prasāritāv ubhāv apy ubhayoś caraṇāv iti saṃpuṭaḥ//(p.138)
body.translated_text: 2.6.16. When both partners' legs are both stretched straight — this is the 'closed' position.

body.text: 2.6.17/.sa dvividhaḥ --- pārśva^saṃpuṭa uttāna^saṃpuṭaś ca/ tathā karma^yogāt/
body.translated_text: 2.6.17. It is of two kinds: the side-closed and the supine-closed, according to the manner of execution.

body.text: 2.6.18/.pārśveṇa tu śayāno dakṣiṇena nārīm adhiśayīteti sārva^trikam etat//(p.138)
body.translated_text: 2.6.18. Lying on the side, one should lie over the woman on the right — this is universal.
2.6.19. Pressing the thighs firmly with the same restraint as in the closed position — this is the 'pressed' position.
2.6.20. Crossing the thighs — this is the 'entwined' position.
2.6.21. Gripping firmly like a mare — this is the 'mare' position, [acquired] through practice.
2.6.22. That [mare position] is mostly [practiced] among the women of <s>Āndhra</s>. These are the modes of lying down according to <s>Bābhravya</s>.
2.6.23. According to <s>Suvarṇanābha</s>, however:
2.6.24. Both thighs raised upward — this is the 'bent' position (<s>bhugnaka</s>).
2.6.25. The hero holds her feet upward — this is the 'yawning' position (<s>jṛmbhitaka</s>).
2.6.26. When those [feet] are bent — this is the 'pressed up' position (<s>utpīḍitaka</s>).
2.6.27. When one [leg] is extended in that [position] — this is the 'half-pressed' position (<s>ardhapīḍitaka</s>).

body.text: 2.6.28/.nāyakasya^aṃsa eko dvitīyakaḥ prasārita iti punaḥ punar vyatyāsena veṇu^dāritakam//(p.140)
body.translated_text: 2.6.28. One [foot] on the hero's shoulder, the second extended — alternating repeatedly, this is the 'splitting of the bamboo' position (<s>veṇudāritaka</s>).

body.text: 2.6.29/.ekaḥ śirasa upari gacched dvitīyaḥ prasārita iti śūla^citakam ābhyāsikam//(p.140)
body.translated_text: 2.6.29. One [foot] goes above the head, the second is extended — this is the 'impaling' position (<s>śūlacitaka</s>), [acquired] through practice.
2.6.30. Both [legs] contracted, placed on her own abdomen — this is the 'crab' position (<s>kārkaṭaka</s>).
2.6.31. Both thighs raised upward and crossed — this is the 'pressed' position (<s>pīḍitaka</s>).
2.6.32. With legs crossed like the <s>padmāsana</s> (lotus posture).
2.6.33. Embracing her from behind while she faces away — this is the 'turned away' position (<s>parāvṛttaka</s>), [acquired] through practice.

body.text: 2.6.34/.jale ca saṃviṣṭa^upaviṣṭa^sthita^ātmakāṃś citrān yogān upalakṣayet/ tathā sukaratvād iti suvarṇanābhaḥ//(p.141)
body.translated_text: 2.6.34. And in water, one should note various unusual positions — lying down, sitting, and standing — since they are easy to perform. So says <s>Suvarṇanābha</s>.

body.text: 2.6.35/.vārtaṃ tu tat/ śiṣṭair apasmṛtatvād iti vātsyāyanaḥ//(p.141)
body.translated_text: 2.6.35. But that is mere talk, since the cultured disregard it — says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.
2.6.36. Now, unusual positions (<s>citraratāni</s>):
2.6.37. Congress while both young partners stand upright, leaning against each other or against a wall or pillar — this is standing congress.

body.text: 2.6.38/.kuḍya^apāśritasya kaṇṭha^avasakta^bāhu^pāśāyās tad^dhasta^pañjara^upaviṣṭāyā ūrupāśena jaghanam abhiveṣṭayantyā kuḍye caraṇa^krameṇa valantyā avalambitakaṃ ratam//(p.142)
body.translated_text: 2.6.38. Leaning against a wall, her arms clasped around his neck, sitting in the cradle of his hands, encircling his hips with a thigh-clasp, and moving by stepping on the wall — this is the 'suspended' congress (<s>avalambitaka</s>).
2.6.39. Or, when she stands on all fours on the ground, he mounts her in the manner of a bull — this is the 'cow' congress (<s>dhenuka</s>).
2.6.40. There, the back receives the actions [normally applied to] the chest.

body.text: 2.6.41/.etena^eva yogena śauna^maiṇeyaṃ chāgalaṃ gardabha^ākrāntaṃ mārjāra^lalitakaṃ vyāghra^avaskandanaṃ gaja^upamarditaṃ varāha^ghṛṣṭakaṃ turaga^adhirūḍhakam iti yatra yatra viśeṣo yogo +apūrvas tat tad upalakṣayet//(p.143)
body.translated_text: 2.6.41. By this same method [are performed] the 'dog,' the 'he-goat,' the 'donkey-mounting,' the 'cat-play,' the 'tiger-spring,' the 'elephant-pressing,' the 'boar-rubbing,' and the 'horse-mounting' — wherever there is a distinctive, novel technique, one should note it.
2.6.42. Congress with two [women] who have mutual affection — this is the 'united' congress (<s>saṃghāṭaka</s>).
2.6.43. And with many — this is the 'cow-herd' congress (<s>goyūthika</s>).
2.6.44. 'Water-sport' and 'he-goat-play' — these are by imitation of those actions.

body.text: 2.6.45/.grāma^nāri^viṣaye strīrājye ca bāhlīke bahavo yuvāno +antaḥpura^sadharmāṇa ekaikasyāḥ parigraha^bhūtāḥ/
body.translated_text: 2.6.45. In the sphere of village women and in the kingdom of women and in <s>Bāhlīka</s>, many young men, being like those in the harem, belong to a single woman.

body.text: 2.6.46/.teṣām ekaikaśo yugapac ca yathā^sātmyaṃ yathā^yogaṃ ca rañjayeyuḥ//(p.144)
body.translated_text: 2.6.46. They should please her one by one and simultaneously, according to suitability and capacity.

body.text: 2.6.47/.eko dhārayed enām anyo niṣeveta/ anyo *jaghana^mukham[ch:jaghanaṃ mukham] anyo madhyam anya iti vāraṃ vāreṇa vyatikareṇa ca^anutiṣṭheyuḥ//(p.145)
body.translated_text: 2.6.47. One holds her, another penetrates; another [attends to] the lower parts, another the mouth, another the middle — thus they should proceed by turns and by interchange.
2.6.48. By this, [the practices of] group enjoyment with courtesans and royal women are explained.
2.6.49. Among the southerners, even impure congress [is practiced] in the anus. Thus [ends the section on] unusual positions.

body.text:
2.6.50/.puruṣopasṛptakāni puruṣāyite vakṣyāmaḥ//(p.146) bhavataś ca^atra ślokau ---(p.146)
2.6.51ab/.paśūnāṃ mṛgajātīnāṃ pataṅgānāṃ ca vibhramaiḥ/(p.146)
body.translated_text:
2.6.50. We shall discuss woman-on-top approaches in the chapter on woman acting the man's part. And here are two verses:
2.6.51ab. Through the play of animals, deer, and birds,
2.6.51cd. the one skilled in temperament should enhance the techniques of congress through those various means.

body.text: 2.6.52ab/.tat^sātmyād deśa^sātmyāc ca tais tair bhāvaiḥ prayojitaiḥ/(p.146)
body.translated_text: 2.6.52ab. Through the natural temperament and regional custom, when employed with those various dispositions,

body.text: 2.6.52cd/.strīṇāṃ snehaś ca rāgaś ca bahumānaś ca jāyate//(p.146)
body.translated_text: 2.6.52cd. affection, passion, and respect are produced in women.
2.7. (12) Methods of striking and the sequence of accompanying sighs and moans.

body.text: 2.7.1/.kalaha^rūpaṃ suratam ācakṣate/ vivāda^ātmakatvād vāma^śīlatvāc ca kāmasya//(p.147)
body.translated_text: 2.7.1. Sexual congress is described as resembling a quarrel, since <s>kāma</s> (desire) is of a contentious and perverse nature.

body.text: 2.7.2/.tasmāt prahaṇana^sthānam aṅgam/ skandhau śiraḥ stana^antaraṃ pṛṣṭhaṃ jaghanaṃ pārśva iti sthānāni//(p.147)
body.translated_text: 2.7.2. Therefore, the body is the place for striking. The locations are: the shoulders, the head, the space between the breasts, the back, the hips, and the sides.

body.text: 2.7.3/.tac caturvidham --- apahastakaṃ prasṛtakaṃ muṣṭiḥ sama^talakam iti//(p.147)
body.translated_text: 2.7.3. And it is of four kinds: the back of the hand (<s>apahastaka</s>), the open palm (<s>prasṛtaka</s>), the fist (<s>muṣṭi</s>), and the flat palm (<s>samatalaka</s>).

body.text: 2.7.4/.tad udbhavaṃ ca sītkṛtam/ tasya^*atirūpatvāt[ch:ārtirūpatvāt]/ tad aneka^vidham//(p.148)
body.translated_text: 2.7.4. And from that arises sighing and moaning (<s>sītkṛta</s>), because of the pain it produces. It is of many kinds.
2.7.5. And the sounds are eight.

2.7.6. The 'hm' sound (<s>hiṃkāra</s>), the thundering sound (<s>stanita</s>), the cooing (<s>kūjita</s>), the weeping (<s>rudita</s>), the 'sūt' sound (<s>sūtkṛta</s>), the 'dūt' sound (<s>dūtkṛta</s>), and the 'phūt' sound (<s>phūtkṛta</s>).

body.text: 2.7.7/.amvārthāḥ śabdā vāraṇa^arthā mokṣaṇa^arthāś cālam arthās te te ca^artha^yogāt//(p.148)
body.translated_text: 2.7.7. Sounds expressing water-like meanings, sounds for warding off, sounds for release, and sounds meaning 'enough' — these are according to the context.

2.7.8. The sounds of the dove, the cuckoo, the green pigeon, the parrot, the bee, the crane, the goose, the <s>kāraṇḍava</s> duck, and the quail — mostly [accompanied by] sighing — one should employ variedly.
2.7.9. When she sits in his lap, a blow with the fist on the back.

body.text: 2.7.10/.tatra sāsūyāyā iva stanita^rudita^kūjitāni pratīghātaś ca syāt//(p.149)
body.translated_text: 2.7.10. There, as if with jealousy, the thundering, weeping, and cooing sounds should follow, along with a counter-blow.
2.7.11. When she is restrained, one should strike between the breasts with the back of the hand.
2.7.12. Beginning gently and increasing in passion until completion.

body.text: 2.7.13/.tatra hiṃkāra^ādīnām aniyamena^abhyāsena vikalpena ca tatkālam eva prayogaḥ//(p.150)
body.translated_text: 2.7.13. There, the 'hm' and other sounds are employed at that very time — without fixed rules, through practice, and with variation.

body.text: 2.7.14/.śirasi kiṃ cid ākuñcita^aṅgulinā kareṇa vivadantyāḥ phūtkṛtya prahaṇanaṃ tatprasṛtakam//(p.150)
body.translated_text: 2.7.14. On the head, with the hand whose fingers are slightly curved, striking while she protests and blowing 'phūt' — this is the open-palm strike (<s>prasṛtaka</s>).
2.7.15. There, with the mouth turned inward, cooing and blowing 'phūt' [sounds are produced].
2.7.16. And at the end of congress, sighing and weeping.
2.7.17. The imitation of the sound of splitting bamboo is called <s>dūtkṛta</s>.
2.7.18. The imitation of the sound of a berry falling into water is called <s>phūtkṛta</s>.
2.7.19. In all [acts of] kissing and the like, when she has withdrawn, [she makes] a <s>sītkṛta</s> (hissing sound), and [he responds] with that very [sound] in reply.

body.text: 2.7.20/.rāgavaśāt prahaṇana^abhyāse vāraṇa^mokṣaṇālam arthānāṃ śabdānām amba^arthānāṃ ca satānta^śvasita^rudita^stanita^miśrīkṛta^prayogā virutānāṃ ca/ rāga^avasāna^kāle jaghana^pārśvayos tāḍanam ity atitvarayā ca^aparisamāpteḥ//(p.151)
body.translated_text: 2.7.20. Under the influence of passion, when striking is repeated, the sounds of prohibition and release, words of meaningful import and those meaning 'mother,' mingled with sighing, weeping, and thundering, are employed — as well as cries. At the conclusion of passion, striking on the buttocks and sides — and also because of extreme haste, [things remain] incomplete.
2.7.21. In that [context], the cooing of the quail and the goose [are imitated] with haste alone. Thus [are described] the methods of moaning and striking.
2.7.22a. Roughness, impetuosity, and virility are said to be the vigor of a man;
2.7.22b. incapacity, pain, turning away, and weakness [characterize] a woman.

body.text: 2.7.23a/.rāgāt prayoga^sātmyāc ca vyatyayo +api kva cid bhavet/(p.152)
body.translated_text: 2.7.23a. From passion and from habituation to the practice, a reversal [of roles] may sometimes occur;

body.text: 2.7.23b/.na ciraṃ tasya ca^eva^ante prakṛter eva yojanam//(p.152)
body.translated_text: 2.7.23b. but that does not last long, and at the end, the natural [roles] are resumed.

body.text: 2.7.24/.kīlām urasi kartarīṃ śirasi viddhāṃ kapolayoḥ saṃdaṃśikāṃ stanayoḥ pārśvayoś ca^iti pūrvaiḥ saha prahaṇanam aṣṭavidham iti dākṣiṇātyānām/ tad^yuvatīnām urasi kīlāni ca tatkṛtāni dṛṣyante/ deśa^sātmyam etat//(p.153)
body.translated_text: 2.7.24. A wedge (<s>kīlā</s>) on the chest, scissors (<s>kartarī</s>) on the head, a piercing [strike] (<s>viddhā</s>) on the cheeks, pincers (<s>saṃdaṃśikā</s>) on the breasts and sides — these, together with the previous [types], constitute the eightfold striking, according to the Southerners. And the marks of wedge-strikes caused by that [practice] are seen on the chests of their young women. This is a regional custom.
2.7.25. <s>Vātsyāyana</s> [says]: this is painful, ignoble in conduct, and contemptible.

body.text: 2.7.26/.tathā^anyad api deśa^sātmyāt prayuktam anyatra na prayuñjīt//(p.153)checked
body.translated_text: 2.7.26. Likewise, whatever else is practiced through regional custom should not be employed elsewhere.
2.7.27. And even in that [region], one should avoid what is dangerous.

body.text: 2.7.28/.rati^yoge hi kīlayā gaṇikāṃ citraseṇāṃ cola^rājo jaghāna/(p.154)
body.translated_text: 2.7.28. For in the act of love, the king of <s>Cola</s> killed the courtesan <s>Citrasenā</s> with a wedge-strike.
2.7.29. <s>Śātakarṇi Śātavāhana</s>, the <s>Kuntala</s> [king], [killed] his chief queen <s>Malayavatī</s> with a scissors-strike.

body.text: 2.7.30/.nara^devaḥ kupāṇir viddhayā duṣprayuktayā naṭīṃ kāṇāṃ cakāra//(p.154) bhavanti ca^atra ślokāḥ ---(p.154)
body.translated_text: 2.7.30. King <s>Naradeva</s> 'Copper-hand' made an actress one-eyed with a piercing [strike] poorly aimed. And here there are verses:

body.text: 2.7.31ab/.nāsty atra gaṇanā kā cin na ca śāstra^parigrahaḥ/(p.154)
body.translated_text: 2.7.31ab. There is no calculation in this, nor any reliance on the treatise;
2.7.31cd. when the act of love has commenced, passion alone is the cause.

body.text: 2.7.32ab/.svapneṣv api na dṛśyante te bhāvās te ca vibhramāḥ/(p.155)
body.translated_text: 2.7.32ab. Not even in dreams are those emotions and those transports seen
2.7.32cd. that arise, improvised in the moment, in the activities of love-making.

body.text: 2.7.33ab/.yathā hi pañcamīṃ dhārām āsthāya turagaḥ pathi/(p.155)
body.translated_text: 2.7.33ab. Just as a horse on the road, having taken to the fifth speed,

body.text: 2.7.33cd/.sthāṇum śvabhraṃ darīṃ vā^api vega^andho na samīkṣate//(p.155)
body.translated_text: 2.7.33cd. blind with velocity, does not notice a post, a pit, or a ravine,

body.text:
2.7.33c/.evaṃ surata^saṃmarde rāga^andhau kāmināv api/(p.155)
2.7.33d/.caṇḍa^vegau pravartete samīkṣete na ca^atyayam//(p.155)
body.translated_text: 2.7.33c-d. so too, in the press of love-making, the two lovers, blinded by passion, proceeding with fierce impetuosity, do not perceive the danger.

body.text: 2.7.34ab/.tasmān mṛdutvaṃ caṇḍatvaṃ yuvatyā balam eva ca/(p.155)
body.translated_text: 2.7.34ab. Therefore, knowing the softness, the fieriness, and the strength of the woman,

body.text: 2.7.34cd/.ātmanaś ca balaṃ jñātvā tathā yuñjīta śāstravit//(p.155)
body.translated_text: 2.7.34cd. and one's own strength as well, one versed in the treatise should engage accordingly.
2.7.35ab. Not at all times and not with all women are the practices of congress [to be employed];

body.text: 2.7.35cd/.sthāne deśe ca kāle ca yoga eṣāṃ vidhīyate//(p.156)
body.translated_text: 2.7.35cd. their application is prescribed according to the appropriate setting, region, and time.
2.8. (13) The woman's approaches and woman acting the man's part (<s>puruṣāyita</s>).

body.text: 2.8.1/.nāyakasya saṃtata^ābhyāsāt pariśramam upalabhya rāgasya ca^anupaśamam, anumatā tena tam^adho +avapātya puruṣa^āyitena sāhāyyaṃ dadyāt/
body.translated_text: 2.8.1. Perceiving the fatigue of the man from prolonged exertion and the non-subsidence of [her] passion, she, with his consent, should push him down beneath her and provide assistance by acting the man's part.
2.8.2. Or, of her own will, desiring variety;
2.8.3. or to satisfy the man's curiosity.

body.text: 2.8.4/.tatra yukta^yantreṇa^eva^itareṇa^utthāpyamānā tam^adhaḥ pātayet/ evaṃ ca ratam avicchinna^rasaṃ tathā pravṛttam eva syāt/ ity eko +ayaṃ mārgaḥ/
body.translated_text: 2.8.4. There, while being raised up by the other using the fitted instrument itself, she should push him below. And thus the love-making would proceed with uninterrupted pleasure, continuing just so. This is one method.
2.8.5. Or she may begin again from the very start. This is the second [method].

body.text: 2.8.6/.sā prakīryamāṇa^keśa^kusumā śvāsa^vicchinna^hāsinī vaktra^saṃsarga^arthaṃ stanābhyām uraḥ pīḍayantī punaḥ punaḥ śiro nāmayantī yāś ceṣṭāḥ pūrvam *aṃsau[ch:asau] darśitavāṃs tā eva pratikurvīta/ pātitā pratipātayāmi^iti/ hasantī tarjayantī pratighnatī ca brūyāt/ punaś ca vrīḍāṃ darśayet/ śramaṃ virāma^abhīpsāṃ ca/ puruṣopasṛptair eva^upasarpet//(p.158)
body.translated_text: 2.8.6. She, with hair and flowers scattered, laughing with breath interrupted, pressing his chest with her breasts for the sake of face-to-face contact, repeatedly bending her head — she should reciprocate the very same actions that he had previously demonstrated. [She says:] 'Having been thrown down, I shall throw you down!' Laughing, threatening, and striking back, she should say [this]. And again she should display modesty, and fatigue, and desire for a pause. She should approach using the woman's approaches themselves.
2.8.7. Those [approaches] we shall now describe.

body.text: 2.8.8/.puruṣaḥ śayanasthāyā yoṣitas tad vacana^vyākṣipta^cittāyā iva nīvīṃ viśleṣayet/ tatra vivadamānāṃ kapola^cumbanena paryākulayet/
body.translated_text: 2.8.8. When the woman is lying on the bed, as though distracted in mind by his words, the man should loosen her lower garment (<s>nīvī</s>). When she disputes [about it], he should bewilder her with a kiss on the cheek.

body.text: 2.8.13/.svairiṇyāṃ yathā^sātmyaṃ yathā^yogaṃ ca/ alake cumbana^artham enāṃ nirdayam avalambet/ hanu^deśe ca^aṅguli^saṃpuṭena/

body.text: 2.8.17/.gātrāṇāṃ sraṃsanaṃ netra^nimīlanaṃ vrīḍā^nāśaḥ samadhikā ca rati^yojanā^iti strīṇāṃ bhāva^lakṣaṇam//(p.161)

body.text: 2.8.18/.hastau vidhunoti svidyati daśaty utthātuṃ na dadāti pādena^āhanti rata^avamāne ca puruṣa^ativartinī//(p.161)

body.text: 2.8.19/.tasyāḥ prāg^yantra^yogāt kareṇa saṃbādhaṃ gaja eva kṣobhayet/ ā mṛdubhāvāt/ tato yantra^yojanam//(p.161)
body.translated_text: 2.8.19. Before the application of the instrument, he should agitate the narrow [passage] with his hand, like an elephant — until [she becomes] soft. Then the instrument should be applied.

body.text: 2.8.20/.upasṛptakaṃ manthanaṃ hulo +avamardanaṃ pīḍitakaṃ nirghāto varāha^ghāto vṛṣa^āghātaś caṭaka^vilasitaṃ saṃpuṭa iti puruṣopasṛptāni/
body.translated_text: 2.8.20. <s>Upasṛptaka</s> (approach), <s>manthana</s> (churning), <s>hula</s> (swaying), <s>avamardana</s> (pressing down), <s>pīḍitaka</s> (pressing), <s>nirghāta</s> (striking), <s>varāhaghāta</s> (boar's blow), <s>vṛṣāghāta</s> (bull's blow), <s>caṭakavilasita</s> (sparrow's play), and <s>saṃpuṭa</s> (enclosing) — these are the man's approaches.

2.8.23. Lowering the hips and thrusting from above is <s>hula</s> (swaying).

body.text: 2.8.26/.sudūram utkṛṣya vegena svajaghanam avapātayed iti nirghātaḥ/

body.text: 2.8.29/.sakṛn^miśritam aniṣkramayya dvistriś catur iti ghaṭṭayed iti caṭaka^vilasitam/

body.text: 2.8.32/.puruṣāyite tu saṃdaṃśo bhramarakaḥ preṅkholitam ity adhikāni//(p.163)

body.text: 2.8.36/.jaghanam eva dolāyamānaṃ sarvato bhrāmayed iti preṅkholitakam//(p.164)

body.text: 2.9.13/.nimitaṃ pārśvato daṣṭaṃ bahiḥsaṃdaṃśo +antaḥsaṃdaṃśaś cumbitakaṃ parimṛṣṭakam āmracūṣitakaṃ saṃgara iti//(p.167)
body.translated_text: 2.9.13. <s>Nimita</s> (touching), <s>pārśvato daṣṭa</s> (biting on the side), <s>bahiḥsaṃdaṃśa</s> (outer pincers), <s>antaḥsaṃdaṃśa</s> (inner pincers), <s>cumbitaka</s> (kissing), <s>parimṛṣṭaka</s> (licking), <s>āmracūṣitaka</s> (mango-sucking), and <s>saṃgara</s> (swallowing).

body.text: 2.9.16/.kara^avalambitam oṣṭhayor upari vinyastam apavidhya mukhaṃ vidhunuyāt/ tan^nimitam//(p.168)

body.translated_text: 2.9.19. Being entreated for that very [act] somewhat further, she should insert it somewhat more; and she too, pressing the tip with her lips, should spit — this is <s>antaḥsaṃdaṃśa</s> (inner pincers).

body.text: 2.9.21/.tat kṛtvā jihvā^agreṇa sarvato ghaṭṭanam agre ca vyadhanam iti parimṛṣṭakam//(p.169)

body.text: 2.9.22/.tathābhūtam eva rāgavaśād ardha^praviṣṭaṃ nirdayam avapīḍyāv apīḍya muñcet/ iti āmra^cūṣitakam//(p.169)

body.text: 2.9.26/.tad etat tu na kāryam/ samaya^virodhād asabhyatvāc ca/ punar api hy āsāṃ vadana^saṃsarge svayam eva^ārtiṃ prapadyeta/ ity ācāryāḥ//(p.170)

body.text: 2.9.33/.evaṃ hy āhuḥ --- ko hi yoṣitāṃ śīlaṃ śaucam ācāraṃ caritraṃ pratyayaṃ vacanaṃ vā śraddhātum arhati/ nisargād eva hi malina^dṛṣṭayo bhavanty etā na parityājyāḥ/ tasmād āsāṃ smṛtita eva śaucam anveṣṭavyam/ evaṃ hy āhuḥ ---(p.172) vatsaḥ prasravaṇe medhyaḥ śvā mṛga^grahaṇe śuciḥ/(p.172) śakuniḥ phala^pāte tu strī^mukhaṃ rati^saṃgame//(p.172)
body.translated_text: 2.9.33. For thus they say: 'Who indeed is able to trust the character, purity, conduct, behavior, reliability, or word of women? For by their very nature they are of impure disposition — yet they are not to be abandoned. Therefore, one should seek their purity through scriptural authority alone.' body.text: 2.9.34/.śiṣṭa^vipratipatteḥ smṛti^vākyasya ca sāvakāśatvād deśasthiter ātmanaś ca vṛtti^pratyaya^anurūpaṃ pravarteta/ iti vātsyāyanaḥ//(p.173) bhavanti ca^atra ślokāḥ ---(p.173)
body.translated_text: 2.9.34. Since the learned disagree, and since the scriptural text has scope [for interpretation], one should act according to one's own regional custom, personal conduct, and trustworthiness — thus says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>. And here are verses:

body.text: 2.10.1/.nāgarakaḥ saha mitrajanena paricārakaiś ca kṛta^puṣpa^upahāre saṃcārita^surabhi^dhūpe raty^āvāse prasādhite vāsa^gṛhe kṛta^snāna^prasādhanāṃ yuktyā pītāṃ striyaṃ sāntvanaiḥ punaḥ pānena ca^upakramet/

body.text: 2.10.5/.jāta^anurāgāyāṃ kusuma^anulepana^tāmbūla^(177) dānena ca śeṣa^jana^visṛṣṭiḥ/ vijane ca yathā^uktair āliṅgana^ādibhir enām uddharṣayet/ tato nīvī^viśleṣaṇa^ādi yathā^uktam upakrameta/ ity ayaṃ rata^ārambhaḥ//(p.178)

And in private, he should arouse her with embraces and the like as described. Then he should proceed with the loosening of the girdle and the rest as described. This is the commencement of lovemaking.

body.text: 2.10.6/.rata^avasānikaṃ rāgam ativāhya^asaṃstutayor iva savrīḍayoḥ parasparam apaśyatoḥ pṛthak pṛthag ācāra^bhūmi^gamanam/ pratinivṛttya ca^āvrīḍāyamānayor ucita^deśa^upaviṣṭayos tāmbūla^grahaṇam acchīkṛtaṃ candanam anyad vā^anulepanaṃ tasyā gātre svayam eva niveśayet/
body.translated_text: 2.10.6. The conclusion of lovemaking: Having let the passion pass, as if unfamiliar with each other, bashful, not looking at each other, they should go separately to the washing-place. Having returned, no longer bashful, seated in a suitable place, they should take <s>tāmbūla</s> (betel). He should himself apply pure sandalwood or another ointment on her body.

body.text: 2.10.7/.savyena bāhunā ca^enāṃ parirabhya caṣaka^hastaḥ sāntvayan pāyayet/ jala^anupānaṃ vā khaṇḍa^khādyakam anyad vā prakṛti^sātmya^yuktam ubhāv apy upayuñjīyātām/
body.translated_text: 2.10.7. Embracing her with his left arm, holding a cup in his hand, soothing her, he should give her to drink. Or water as a drink, sugar-candy, or other things suited to their natures — both should partake.

body.text: 2.10.8/.accha^rasaka^yūṣam amlayavāgūṃ bhṛṣṭa^māṃsa^upadaṃśāni pānakāni cūta^phalāni śuṣka^māṃsaṃ mātuluṅga^cukrakāṇi saśarkarāṇi ca yathā^deśa^sātmyaṃ ca/ tatra madhuram idaṃ mṛdu viśadam iti ca vidaśya vidaśya tat tad upāharet/
body.translated_text: 2.10.8. Clear fruit-juice, broth, sour rice-gruel with roasted meat as a side-dish, sweet drinks, mango fruits, dried meat, citrus and sour preparations with sugar — according to regional custom. 'This is sweet, this is soft, this is clear' — tasting various things, he should offer them one by one.

body.text: 2.10.9/.harmya^tala^sthitayor vā candrikā^sevana^artham āsanam/ tatra^anukūlābhiḥ kathābhir anuvarteta/ tad^aṅka^saṃlīnāyāś candramasaṃ paśyantyā nakṣatra^paṅkti^vyaktī^karaṇam/ arundhatī^dhruva^saptarṣi^mālā^darśanaṃ ca/ iti rata^avasānikam//(p.179)
body.translated_text: 2.10.9. Or, seated on a terrace for the purpose of enjoying the moonlight, he should engage in pleasing conversation. For her, reclining in his lap and gazing at the moon — pointing out the rows of <s>nakṣatras</s> (constellations), and showing <s>Arundhatī</s>, <s>Dhruva</s> (the Pole Star), and the garland of the Seven Sages (<s>Saptarṣi</s>). This is the conclusion of lovemaking.
2.10.10a. Even at the conclusion, affection enhanced by courteous attentions,
2.10.10b. accompanied by intimate conversations, generates supreme love.
2.10.11a. Through mutually pleasing actions, following each other's nature,
2.10.11b. turning from anger in a moment, exchanging loving glances in a moment,
2.10.12a. through <s>hallīsaka</s> dances and play, through singing and <s>lāṭarāsaka</s> dances,

body.text:
2.10.12b/.rāga^lola^ārdra^nayanaiś candra^maṇḍala^vīkṣaṇaiḥ//(p.181)
2.10.13a/.ādye saṃdarśane jāte pūrvaṃ ye syur manorathāḥ/(p.181)
body.translated_text: 2.10.12b-13a. with eyes moist and rolling with passion, gazing at the disc of the moon — recounting the desires that arose at the first meeting,
2.10.13b. and the suffering of renewed separation —
2.10.13c. at the end of such recounting, with passion, with embraces and kisses,

body.text: 2.10.13d/.tais taiś ca bhāvaiḥ saṃyukto yūno rāgo vivardhate//(p.181)
body.translated_text: 2.10.13d. and with various moods — the passion of the young couple increases.

body.text: 2.10.14/.rāgavad āhāryarāgaṃ kṛtrimarāgaṃ vyavahitarāgaṃ poṭārataṃ khalaratam ayantritaratam iti rataviśeṣāḥ//(p.182)
body.translated_text: 2.10.14. The varieties of love-making are: natural passion (<s>rāgavat</s>), assumed passion (<s>āhāryarāga</s>), artificial passion (<s>kṛtrimarāga</s>), transferred passion (<s>vyavahitarāga</s>), <s>poṭārata</s> (love with a servant), <s>khalarata</s> (rustic love), and unrestrained love (<s>ayantritarata</s>).

body.text: 2.10.15/.saṃdarśanāt prabhṛty ubhayor api pravṛddha^rāgayoḥ prayatna^kṛte samāgame pravāsa^pratyāgamane vā kalaha^viyoga^yoge tad^rāgavat//(p.182)
body.translated_text: 2.10.15. When, from the first meeting onward, both have grown in passion, and their coming together is arranged with effort, or at the return from a journey, or at the union after a quarrel and separation — that is natural passion (<s>rāgavat</s>).
2.10.16. Therein, [one should act] according to one's own desire and as far as appropriate.
2.10.17. When those of moderate passion begin [the act] and become passionate — that is assumed passion (<s>āhāryarāga</s>).

body.text: 2.10.18/.tatra cātuḥṣaṣṭikair yogaiḥ sātmya^anuviddhaiḥ saṃdhukṣya saṃdhukṣya rāgaṃ pravarteta/
body.translated_text: 2.10.18. Therein, one should proceed by kindling passion again and again through the sixty-four techniques, as one has become accustomed to them.
2.10.19. When [the act is performed] for a [specific] purpose, or by those attached elsewhere — that is artificial passion (<s>kṛtrimarāga</s>).
2.10.20. Therein, one should apply the techniques in combination, according to the <s>śāstra</s>.

body.text: 2.10.21/.puruṣas tu hṛdaya^priyām anyāṃ manasi nidhāya vyavaharet/ saṃprayogāt prabhṛti ratiṃ yāvat/ atas tad^vyavahitarāgam//(p.183)
body.translated_text: 2.10.21. When a man, placing in his mind another woman who is dear to his heart, has intercourse [with the present one] — from the beginning of union until the end of the love-act — that is transferred passion (<s>vyavahitarāga</s>).

body.text: 2.10.22/.nyūnāyāṃ kumbha^dāsyāṃ paricārikāyāṃ vā yāvad arthaṃ saṃprayogas tat^poṭāratam//(p.184)
body.translated_text: 2.10.22. Intercourse as far as needed with an inferior woman, a water-carrier, or a maidservant — that is <s>poṭārata</s> (love with a servant).
2.10.23. Therein, one should not care for courtesies.

body.text: 2.10.24/.tathā veśyāyā grāmīṇena saha yāvad arthaṃ khalaratam//(p.184)
body.translated_text: 2.10.24. Likewise, when a courtesan [engages] with a rustic man as far as needed — that is <s>khalarata</s> (rustic love).
2.10.25. And [likewise] for an urbane man with women of villages, pastoral settlements, and frontier regions.
2.10.26. When trust has arisen between the two, and from mutual agreeableness — that is unrestrained love (<s>ayantritarata</s>). Thus are the varieties of love.

body.text: 2.10.27/.vardhamāna^praṇayā tu nāyikā sapatnīnām agrahaṇaṃ tad^āśrayam ālāpaṃ vā gotra^skhalitaṃ vā na marṣayet/ nāyaka^vyalīkaṃ ca//(p.185)
body.translated_text: 2.10.27. But a heroine whose affection is growing should not tolerate the embracing of co-wives, conversation concerning them, a slip of the name [calling her by another's name], or the lover's transgression.

body.text: 2.10.28/.tatra subhṛśaḥ kalaho ruditam āyāsaḥ śiro^ruhāṇām avakṣodanaṃ prahaṇanam āsanāc chayanād vā mahyāṃ patanaṃ mālya^bhūṣaṇa^avamokṣo bhūmau śayyā ca//(p.185)
body.translated_text: 2.10.28. Therein, [there follows] a vehement quarrel — weeping, vexation, tearing of the hair, striking, falling from the seat or bed to the ground, casting off garlands and ornaments, and lying on the ground.

body.text: 2.10.29/.tatra yukta^rūpeṇa sāmnā pāda^patanena vā prasanna^manās tām anunayann upakramya śayanam ārohayet//(p.185)
body.translated_text: 2.10.29. Therein, with suitable conciliation or by falling at her feet, having pleased her mind, approaching her, he should lead her to the bed.

body.text: 2.10.30/.tasya ca vacanam uttareṇa yojayantī vivṛddha^krodhā sakaca^graham asya^āsyam unnamayya pādena bāhau śirosi vakṣasi pṛṣṭhe vā sakṛd dvis trir avahanyāt/ dvāra^deśaṃ gacchet/ tatra^upaviśya^aśrukaraṇam iti/
body.translated_text: 2.10.30. Countering his words with retorts, with increasing anger, seizing him by the hair, raising his face, she should strike him once, twice, or thrice with her foot — on the arm, the head, the chest, or the back. She should go to the doorway and sit there, weeping.

body.text: 2.10.31/.atikruddhā^api tu na dvāra^deśād bhūyo gacchet/ doṣavattvāt/ iti dattakaḥ/ tatra yuktito +anunīyamānā prasādam ākāṅkṣet/ prasannā^api tu sakaṣāyair eva vākyair enaṃ tudatī^iva prasanna^rati^kāṅkṣiṇī nāyakena parirabhyeta//(p.186)
body.translated_text: 2.10.31. But even when very angry, she should not go beyond the doorway — because it is a fault. Thus says <s>Dattaka</s>. Being properly conciliated there, she should seek reconciliation. And even when pleased, she should be embraced by the lover while pricking him with words still tinged with anger, yet desiring the love of reconciliation.

body.text: 2.10.32/.svabhavanasthā tu nimittāt kalahitā tathā^vidha^ceṣṭā^eva nāyakam abhigacchet/ (p.186)
body.translated_text: 2.10.32. But [a woman] in her own house, having quarreled for some reason, should approach the lover with such behavior.

body.text: 2.10.33/.tatra pīṭhamarda^viṭa^vidūṣakair nāyaka^prayuktair upaśamita^roṣā tair eva^anunītā taiḥ saha^eva tad^bhavanam adhigacchet/ tatra ca vaset/ iti praṇayakalahaḥ//(p.187) bhavanti ca^atra ślokāḥ ---(p.187)
body.translated_text: 2.10.33. There, her anger having been calmed by the <s>pīṭhamarda</s> (companion), <s>viṭa</s> (libertine), and <s>vidūṣaka</s> (jester) sent by the lover, and being conciliated by them, she should go with them to his house. And she should stay there. This is the lover's quarrel. And here are verses:
2.10.34ab. Thus, the sixty-four [arts] proclaimed by <s>Bābhravya</s> —
2.10.34cd. a lover who employs them with excellent women achieves success.
2.10.35ab. Even one who speaks of other sciences, but is devoid of the sixty-four,
2.10.35cd. is not greatly honored in the assembly of the learned during conversations.
2.10.36ab. Even one who lacks other knowledge, but is adorned with this [art],
2.10.36cd. takes the foremost place in the conversations of men and women in gatherings.
2.10.37ab. This [art], honored by the learned, well-honored even by the vulgar —
Who would not honor <s>Nandinī</s> (the delightful art), which is honored by the assembly of courtesans?
<s>Nandinī</s> (the delightful), <s>Subhagā</s> (the auspicious), <s>Siddhā</s> (the accomplished), <s>Subhagaṃkaraṇī</s> (the bestower of good fortune),
and <s>Nārīpriyā</s> (beloved of women) — by these names is this [science] designated by the teachers in the treatises.
By maidens, by the wives of others, and by courtesans, with genuine regard,
one who is skilled in the sixty-four [arts] is viewed with great respect.
3. On Virgins (<s>Kanyāsaṃprayuktaka</s>)
3.1. (16) Arrangement of the Selection of a Bride and Determination of the Marriage Alliance

body.text: 3.1.1/.savarṇāyām ananyapūrvāyāṃ śāstrato +adhigatāyāṃ dharmo +arthaḥ putrāḥ saṃbandhaḥ pakṣavṛddhir anupaskṛtā ratiś ca//(p.190)
body.translated_text: From a woman of the same <s>varṇa</s> (social class), one who has not been previously married to another, obtained according to the <s>śāstra</s> (scriptures), come <s>dharma</s> (religious merit), <s>artha</s> (wealth), sons, family alliance, increase of one's party, and unaffected sexual pleasure.

body.text: 3.1.2/.tasmāt kanyām abhijana^upetāṃ mātā^pitṛ^matīṃ tri^varṣāt prabhṛti nyūna^vayasaṃ ślāghya^ācāre dhanavati pakṣavati kule saṃbandhi^priye saṃbandhibhir ākule prasūtāṃ prabhūta^mātṛ^pitṛ^pakṣāṃ rūpa^śīla^lakṣaṇa^saṃpannām anyūna^adhikā^(p.190)vinaṣṭa^danta^nakha^karṇa^keśa^akṣi^stanīm arogi^prakṛti^śarīrāṃ tathā^vidha eva śrutavāñ śīlayet//(p.191)
body.translated_text: Therefore, a man of similar qualities and learning should court a girl who is of good family, whose mother and father are living, who is at least three years younger than himself, born in a family of good conduct and wealth, with a large circle of relations, dear to its relatives, and abounding in them, having ample maternal and paternal kin, endowed with beauty, good character, and auspicious marks, with teeth, nails, ears, hair, eyes, and breasts neither deficient, excessive, nor damaged, and possessing a body of healthy constitution.

body.text: 3.1.3/.yāṃ gṛhītvā kṛtinam ātmānaṃ manyeta na ca samānair nindyeta tasyāṃ pravṛttir iti ghoṭakamukhaḥ//(p.191)
body.translated_text: One should pursue the girl upon marrying whom one would consider oneself accomplished and would not be reproached by one's equals — thus says <s>Ghoṭakamukha</s>.

body.text: 3.1.4/.tasyā varaṇe mātā^pitarau saṃbandhinaś ca prayateran/ mitrāṇi ca gṛhīta^vākyāny ubhaya^saṃbaddhāni//(p.191)
body.translated_text: For her selection, her mother, father, and relatives should make efforts, as well as friends who are trusted intermediaries connected to both sides.

body.text: 3.1.5/.tāny anyeṣāṃ varayitṝṇāṃ doṣān pratyakṣa^anāgamikāṃś ca śrāvayeyuḥ/ kaulān pauruṣeyān abhiprāya^saṃvardhakāṃś ca nāyakaguṇān/ viśeṣataś ca kanyāmātur anukūlāṃs tadātva^āyatiyuktān darśayeyuḥ//(p.192)
body.translated_text: These [friends] should point out the faults of other suitors, both evident and future, and should display the groom's merits — those of his family, his personal qualities, and those that fulfill the bride's family's aspirations — especially those agreeable to the girl's mother, pertaining both to the present and to the future.

body.text: 3.1.6/.daiva^cintaka^rūpaś ca śakuna^nimitta^graha^lagna^bala^lakṣaṇa^darśanena nāyakasya bhaviṣyantam artha^saṃyogaṃ kalyāṇam anuvarṇayet//(p.192)
body.translated_text: And one assuming the role of an astrologer should describe the groom's future prosperity and good fortune by showing favorable omens, signs, planetary positions, the strength of the <s>lagna</s> (ascendant), and auspicious marks.

body.text: 3.1.7/.apare punar asya^anyato viśiṣṭena kanyālābhena kanyāmātaram unmādayeyuḥ//(p.193)
body.translated_text: Others, moreover, should excite the girl's mother by showing that he could obtain a superior girl elsewhere.
One should select a bride and give her in marriage in accordance with favorable divine signs, omens, and overheard words.
Not by chance alone, nor for merely human [considerations] — thus says <s>Ghoṭakamukha</s>.
One who is sleeping, weeping, or has gone out should be avoided during the selection.

body.text: 3.1.11/.apraśasta^nāmadheyāṃ ca guptāṃ dattāṃ ghonāṃ pṛṣatām ṛṣabhāṃ vinatāṃ vikaṭāṃ vimuṇḍāṃ śuci^dūṣitāṃ sāṃkarikīṃ rākāṃ phalīnīṃ mitrāṃ svanujām varṣakarīṃ ca varjayet//(p.193)
body.translated_text: One should also avoid a girl with an inauspicious name, or one who is hidden, already given [to another], flat-nosed, snub-nosed, bull-shaped, stooped, deformed, bald-headed, impure in conduct, born of mixed castes, named <s>Rākā</s>, <s>Phalīnī</s>, <s>Mitrā</s>, or one who is a younger sister [of a girl already considered], or one named <s>Varṣakarī</s>.
A girl named after a <s>nakṣatra</s> (constellation), one named after a river, one named after a tree — these are to be censured;
and one whose name ends in 'la' or 'ra' as the penultimate letter should be avoided in the selection.

body.text: 3.1.13/.yasyāṃ manaś^cakṣuṣor nibandhas tasyām ṛddhiḥ/ na^itarām ādriyeta/ ity eke//(p.194)
body.translated_text: Where the mind and eyes are captivated, therein lies prosperity; one should not regard any other [consideration] — so say some.

body.text: 3.1.14/.tasmāt pradāna^samaye kanyām udāra^veṣāṃ sthāpayeyuḥ/ aparāhṇikaṃ ca nityaṃ prasādhitāyāḥ sakhībhiḥ saha krīḍā/ yajña^vivāha^ādiṣu jana^saṃdrāveṣu prāyatnikaṃ darśanam/ tatha^utsaveṣu ca/ paṇya^sadharmatvāt//(p.195)
body.translated_text: Therefore, at the time of the giving, they should present the girl in splendid attire; and every afternoon, adorned, she should play with her companions; at sacrifices, marriages, and other public gatherings, she should be shown with special effort; and likewise at festivals — since she is like merchandise [to be displayed].

body.text: 3.1.15/.varaṇa^artham upagatāṃś ca bhadra^darśanān pradakṣiṇa^vācaś ca tatsaṃbandhi^saṃgatān puruṣān maṅgalaiḥ pratigṛhṇīyuḥ/
body.translated_text: And men who come for the purpose of selection, who are handsome in appearance and auspicious in speech, and who are accompanied by persons connected with the family, should be received with auspicious rites.
And the girl, adorned, should be shown to them under some other pretext.
They should set a time limit for the examination of divine signs, until the decision of giving is made.

body.text: 3.1.18/.snāna^ādiṣu niyujyamānā varayitāraḥ sarvaṃ bhaviṣyati^ity uktvā na tad^ahar^eva^abhyupagaccheyuḥ//(p.196)
body.translated_text: When the suitors are invited for the bath and other ceremonies, they should say 'everything will come to pass' and not agree on that very day.

body.text: 3.1.19/.deśa^pravṛtti^sātmyād vā brāhma^prājāpatya^ārṣa^daivānām anyatamena vivāhena śāstrataḥ pariṇayet/ iti varaṇa^vidhānam//(p.196) bhavanti ca^atra ślokāḥ ---(p.196)
body.translated_text: According to the customs of the region and what is suitable, one should marry by one of the <s>Brāhma</s>, <s>Prājāpatya</s>, <s>Ārṣa</s>, or <s>Daiva</s> forms of marriage, according to the <s>śāstra</s>. Thus is the procedure for the selection of a bride. And here are verses —
For one of equal status, the first [priorities] are playing together, marriages, and social gatherings;
these should be conducted with equals, not with those above, nor with those below.
Where the groom, having taken the girl, conducts himself like a servant,
that should be known as a marriage with a superior family — it is rejected by the self-respecting.
Where he moves about like a master, honored by his own kinsmen,
that ignoble marriage with an inferior family is also censured by the virtuous.
Where play is engaged in that savors of mutual pleasure,
and that which honors each other — that marriage is recommended.
Even having made an alliance with a superior family, one would afterward have to bow before their relatives;

body.text: 3.1.24cd/.na tv eva hīna^saṃbandhaṃ kuryāt sadbhir vininditam//(p.197)
body.translated_text: but one should never make an alliance with an inferior family, which is condemned by the virtuous.
3.2. Winning the Confidence of the Maiden (<s>Kanyāvisrambhaṇa</s>)

body.text: 3.2.1/.saṃgatayos trirātram adhaḥ śayyā brahma^caryaṃ kṣāra^lavaṇa^varjam āhāras tathā saptāhaṃ satūrya^maṅgala^snānaṃ prasādhanaṃ saha^bhojanaṃ ca prekṣā saṃbandhināṃ ca pūjanam/ iti sārva^varṇikam//(p.198)
body.translated_text: For the newly wed couple, for three nights: sleeping on the floor, <s>brahmacarya</s> (celibacy), food without alkaline substances or salt; likewise for seven days: bathing with music and auspicious rites, adorning, eating together, attending performances, and honoring relatives. This is common to all <s>varṇas</s> (social classes).

body.text: 3.2.2/.tasminn etāṃ niśi vijane mṛdubhir upacārair upakrameta//(p.198)
body.translated_text: During those nights, in a secluded place, he should approach her with gentle attentions.

body.text: 3.2.3/.trirātram avacanaṃ hi stambham iva nāyakaṃ paśyantī kanyā nirvidyeta paribhavec ca tṛtīyām iva prakṛtim/ iti bābhravīyāḥ//(p.199)
body.translated_text: For a maiden who sees the groom silent for three nights like a pillar becomes disenchanted and feels slighted, as if he were a eunuch — thus say the followers of <s>Bābhravya</s>.

body.text: 3.2.4/.upakrameta visrambhayec ca, na tu brahmacaryam ativarteta/ iti vātsyāyanaḥ//(p.199)
body.translated_text: He should approach and win her confidence, but should not transgress the <s>brahmacarya</s> (celibacy) — thus says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.
And in approaching her, he should not do anything by force.

body.text: 3.2.6/.kusuma^sadharmāṇo hi yoṣitaḥ sukumāra^upakramāḥ/ tās tv anadhigata^viśvāsaiḥ prasabham upakramyamāṇāḥ saṃprayoga^dveṣiṇyo bhavanti/ tasmāt sāmnā^eva^upacaret//(p.199)
body.translated_text: For women are like flowers in their nature and require gentle approaches; when approached forcefully by those who have not gained their trust, they develop an aversion to sexual union. Therefore, one should approach only with gentleness.

body.text: 3.2.7/.yuktyā^api tu yataḥ prasaram upalabhet tena^eva^anu praviśet//(p.200)
body.translated_text: And with skill, through whichever avenue he finds an opening, through that very one he should gradually advance.
With an embrace that she finds pleasing and that has been previously practiced, since it does not take too long.
And he should begin with the upper body, since it is more tolerable.
In lamplight for one who is in the bloom of youth and previously acquainted; in darkness for a young girl who is meeting him for the first time.

body.text: 3.2.11/.aṅgīkṛta^pariṣvaṅgāyāś ca vadanena tāmbūla^dānam/ tad^apratipadyamānāṃ ca sāntvanair vākyaiḥ śapathaiḥ pratiyācitaiḥ pāda^patanaiś ca grāhayet/ vrīḍā^yuktā^api yoṣid^atyanta^kruddhā^api na pāda^patanam ativartate iti sārvatrikam//(p.200)
body.translated_text: And when she has accepted the embrace, he should offer <s>tāmbūla</s> (betel) from his mouth; if she does not accept it, he should persuade her with soothing words, oaths, earnest entreaties, and falling at her feet. Even a woman full of modesty, even one extremely angry, does not reject the falling at her feet — this is universal.
On the occasion of giving the betel, a gentle, clear, noiseless kiss on her [lips].
When she is won over in this, he should engage her in conversation.

body.text: 3.2.14/.tac^chravaṇa^arthaṃ yat kiṃ cid alpa^akṣara^abhidheyam ajānann iva pṛcchet/
body.translated_text: In order to hear her speak, he should ask about something that requires only a few words to answer, as if he does not know.

body.text: 3.2.15/.tatra niṣpratipattim anudvejayan sāntvanā yuktaṃ bahuśa eva pṛcchet/
body.translated_text: If she gives no response, without alarming her, he should ask again and again with soothing words.
If she still does not speak, he should press her insistently.

body.text: 3.2.17/.sarvā eva hi kanyāḥ puruṣeṇa prayujyamānaṃ vacanaṃ viṣa^hante/ na tu laghu^miśrām api vācaṃ vadanti/ iti ghoṭakamukhaḥ//(p.201)
body.translated_text: For all maidens endure the words spoken by a man, but they do not themselves utter even a single lighthearted word — thus says <s>Ghoṭakamukha</s>.

body.text: 3.2.18/.nirbadhyamānā tu śiraḥ^kampena prativacanāni yojayet/ kalahe tu na śiraḥ kampayet//(p.202)
body.translated_text: When pressed, she should make her replies by nodding her head; but during a quarrel, she should not nod.

body.text: 3.2.19/.icchasi māṃ na^icchasi vā kiṃ te +ahaṃ rucito na rucito vā^iti pṛṣṭā ciraṃ sthitvā nirbadhyamānā tadā^anukūlyena śiraḥ kampayet/ prapañcyamānā tu vivadet//(p.202)
body.translated_text: When asked 'Do you desire me or not? Am I pleasing to you or not?' — after standing still for a long time and being pressed, she should then nod her head in assent; but if questioned further in detail, she should argue.

body.text:
3.2.20/.saṃstutā cet sakhīm anukūlām ubhayato +api visrabdhāṃ tām antarā kṛtvā kathāṃ yojayet/ tasminn adhomukhī vihaset/ tāṃ ca^ativādinīm adhikṣiped vivadec ca/ sā tu parihāsa^artham idam anayā^uktam iti ca^anuktam (p.202) api brūyāt/ tatra tām apanudya prativacana^artham abhyarthyamānā tūṣṇīm āsīta/ nirbadhyamānā tu na^aham evaṃ bravīmi^ity avyakta^akṣaram
anavasita^arthaṃ vacanaṃ brūyāt/ nāyakaṃ ca vihasantī kadā cit kaṭākṣaiḥ prekṣeta/ ity ālāpa^yojanam//(p.203)
3.2.21/.evaṃ jāta^paricayā ca^anirvadantī tat^samīpe yācitaṃ tāmbūlaṃ vilepanaṃ srajaṃ nidadhyāt/ uttarīye vā^asya nibadhnīyāt/
body.translated_text:
If she is already acquainted, she should place between them a friendly female companion who is agreeable to both and trusted by both, and through her conduct a conversation. She should laugh with downcast face; and she should rebuke that friend for speaking too much and quarrel with her. That friend should then say, for the sake of jest, 'she said this' — even what was not said. Thereupon, pushing away the friend and being entreated for a reply, she should sit in silence; when pressed, she should say 'I did not say so' in indistinct syllables and incomplete meaning; and she should occasionally look at the groom laughingly with sidelong glances. This is the method of engaging in conversation.
3.2.21. Thus, having become familiar and no longer resisting, she should place near him the betel, ointment, and garland that he has asked for, or tie them in his upper garment.
Then, when the moment is right, he should touch the tips of her breasts with a feigned accidental gesture (<s>ācchuritaka</s>).

body.text: 3.2.23/.vāryamāṇaś ca tvam api māṃ pariṣvajasva tato na^evam ācariṣyāmi^iti sthityā pariṣvañjayet/ svaṃ ca hastam ā nābhi^deśāt prasārya nirvartayet/ krameṇa ca^enām utsaṅgam āropya^adhikam adhikam upakramet/ apratipadyamānāṃ ca bhīṣayet//(p.203)
body.translated_text: And when prevented, he should say 'You too embrace me, and then I will not do this again,' and by this stratagem embrace her; and he should extend his own hand down to the region of the navel and then withdraw it; and gradually, placing her on his lap, he should make further and further advances; and if she does not respond, he should frighten her.

body.text: 3.2.24/.ahaṃ khalu tava danta^padāny adhare kariṣyāmi stana^pṛṣṭhe ca nakha^padam/ ātmanaś ca svayaṃ kṛtvā tvayā kṛtam iti te sakhī^janasya purataḥ kathayiṣyāmi/ sā tvaṃ kim atra vakṣyasi^iti bāla^vibhīṣikair bāla^pratyāyanaiś ca śanair enāṃ pratārayet/
body.translated_text: 'I shall make tooth-marks on your lip and nail-marks on your breast, and having made them on myself, I shall tell your friends that you made them. What will you say to that then?' — with such childish threats and childish persuasions, he should gradually win her over.

body.text: 3.2.25/.dvitīyasyāṃ tṛtīyasyāṃ ca rātrau kiṃ cid adhikaṃ visrambhitāṃ hastena yojayet//(p.204)
body.translated_text: On the second and third nights, when she has become somewhat more confident, he should engage her with his hands.
He should begin kissing her on all parts of the body.

body.text: 3.2.27/.ūrvoś ca^upari vinyasta^hastaḥ saṃvāhana^kriyāyāṃ siddhāyāṃ krameṇa^ūru^mūlam api saṃvāhayet/ nivārite saṃvāhane ko doṣa ity ākulayed enām/ tac ca sthirīkuryāt/ tatra siddhāyā guhya^deśa^abhimarśanaṃ
body.translated_text: And with his hands placed upon her thighs, when the practice of massage has been accepted, he should gradually massage even the root of the thighs; if she prevents the massage, he should confuse her by saying 'What fault is there in this?' and should make that [practice] firm. When she is won over in that, the touching of the private parts,

body.text: 3.2.28/.raśanā^viyojanaṃ nīvī^*visraṃsanaṃ[ch:visrasanaṃ] vasana^parivartanam ūru^mūla^saṃvāhanaṃ ca/ ete ca^asya^anya^apadeśāḥ/ yukta^yantrāṃ rañjayet/ na tv akāle vrata^khaṇḍanam
body.translated_text: the loosening of the girdle, the untying of the undergarment, the changing of the clothing, and the massaging of the root of the thighs — these are his pretexts for other things. He should delight her who is restrained by modesty; but there should be no breaking of the vow at an improper time.

body.text: 3.2.29/.anuśiṣyāc ca/ ātma^anurāgaṃ darśayet/ manorathāṃś ca pūrva^kālikān anuvarṇayet/ āyatyāṃ ca tadā^anukūlyena pravṛttiṃ pratijānīyāt/ sapatnībhyaś ca sādhvasam avacchindyāt/ kālena ca krameṇa vimukta^kanyā^bhāvām anudvejayann upakrameta/ iti kanyā^visrambhaṇam//(p.205) bhavanti ca^atra ślokāḥ ---
body.translated_text: He should also instruct her, show his love for her, describe his earlier longings, and promise future conduct agreeable to her; and he should dispel her fear of co-wives. And in due time, gradually, without alarming her who has shed her maiden nature, he should approach her. This is the winning of the maiden's confidence. And here are verses —
Thus, following her heart, one should win over the young girl by skillful means;
in this way, she becomes both enamored of him and fully trusting.
Neither by excessive compliance, nor by too much opposition,
does one succeed with maidens; therefore, one should pursue a middle course.
He who knows how to generate affection for himself and enhance the dignity of women,

body.text: 3.2.32cd/.kanyā^visrambhaṇaṃ vetti yaḥ sa tāsāṃ priyo bhavet//(p.206)
body.translated_text: and who understands the art of winning a maiden's confidence — he becomes dear to them.
3.2.33ab. 'She is excessively bashful' — the man who ignores a girl [with this excuse]
3.2.33cd. is despised as one who does not understand her intentions, [treated] like an animal.
3.2.34ab. Or, a girl who is approached suddenly by one who has not understood her mind

body.text: 3.2.34cd/.bhayaṃ vitrāsam udvegaṃ sadyo dveṣaṃ ca gacchati//(p.207)
body.translated_text: 3.2.34cd. immediately experiences fear, alarm, agitation, and hatred.
3.2.35ab. She, not having attained the union of affection, corrupted by that alarm,
3.2.35cd. may become a man-hater, or, being disgusted, may go to another.
3.3. Approaches to a young girl, and the interpretation of gestures and expressions.

body.text: 3.3.1/.dhana^hīnas tu guṇa^yukto +api, madhyastha^guṇo hīna^apadeśo vā, sadhano vā prātiveśyaḥ, mātṛ^pitṛ^bhrātṛṣu ca paratantraḥ, bāla^vṛttir ucita^praveśo vā kanyām alabhyatvān na varayet/
body.translated_text: 3.3.1. One who is without wealth, though endowed with virtues; or one of middling qualities and low family; or one who is wealthy but a neighbor; or one who is dependent on mother, father, or brothers; or one of childish behavior but of familiar acquaintance — such a one should not seek a girl in formal courtship, since she is unattainable [by that means].
3.3.2. Rather, from childhood itself, he should win her affection personally.

body.text: 3.3.3/.tathā^yuktaś ca mātula^kula^anuvartī dakṣiṇā^pathe bāla eva (p.207) mātrā ca pitrā ca viyuktaḥ paribhūta^kalpo dhana^utkarṣā^dalabhyāṃ mātula^duhitaram anyasmai vā pūrva^dattāṃ sādhayet/
body.translated_text: 3.3.3. And one who is so qualified, following the maternal uncle's family in the southern [Deccan] custom, himself a youth separated from mother and father, of humiliated condition, should win the maternal uncle's daughter who is unattainable due to a difference in wealth, or who has been previously given to another.
3.3.4. He may also desire another, unrelated [girl].

body.text: 3.3.5/.bālāyām evaṃ sati dharma^adhigame saṃvananaṃ ślāghyam iti ghoṭakamukhaḥ//(p.208)
body.translated_text: 3.3.5. When such is the case with a young girl, wooing through the attainment of dharma is praiseworthy — says <s>Ghoṭakamukha</s>.

body.text: 3.3.6/.tayā saha puṣpa^avacayaṃ grathanaṃ gṛhakaṃ duhitṛkā^krīḍā^yojanaṃ bhakta^pāna^karaṇam iti kurvīta/ paricayasya vayasaś ca^anurūpyāt/
body.translated_text: 3.3.6. He should engage in flower-gathering, garland-making, playing house, doll-play, cooking, and drinking with her — according to the familiarity and age [of both].

body.text: 3.3.7/.ākarṣa^krīḍā paṭṭikā^krīḍā muṣṭi^dyūta^kṣullaka^ādi^dyūtāni madhyama^aṅguli^grahaṇaṃ ṣaṭ^pāṣāṇaka^ādīni ca deśyāni tat^sātmyāt tad^āpta^dāsa^ceṭikābhis tayā ca saha^anukrīḍeta/
body.translated_text: 3.3.7. Pulling games, strip games, dice with fists, dice with small [stakes], and other [games] — grasping the middle finger, six-stone game, and other regional games — he should play with her and with her maidservants and companions who are devoted to her, according to their habits.

body.text: 3.3.8/.kṣveḍitakāni sunimīlitakām ārabdhikāṃ lavaṇa^vīthikām anila^tāḍitakāṃ godhūma^puñjikām aṅguli^tāḍitakāṃ sakhībhir anyāni ca deśyāni//(p.209)
body.translated_text: 3.3.8. 'Snapping,' 'blind-folding,' 'beginning,' 'salt-lane,' 'wind-slapping,' 'wheat-piling,' 'finger-tapping,' and other regional games with her friends.

body.text: 3.3.9/.yāṃ ca viśvāsyām asyāṃ manyeta tayā saha nirantarāṃ prītiṃ kuryāt/ paricayāṃś ca budhyeta/
body.translated_text: 3.3.9. And with whichever [friend] he considers trustworthy regarding her, he should cultivate constant friendship and learn about her acquaintances.

body.text: 3.3.10/.dhātreyikāṃ ca^asyāḥ priya^hitābhyām adhikam upagṛhṇīyāt/ sā hi prīyamāṇā vidita^ākārā^apy apratyādiśantī taṃ tāṃ ca yojayituṃ śaknuyāt/ anabhihitā^api pratyācāryakam/
body.translated_text: 3.3.10. And he should especially win over her foster-sister through kindness and favors. For she, when pleased, even knowing his intentions, will not refuse him and will be able to bring them together. Even without being told, she will act as a go-between.

body.text: 3.3.11/.avidita^ākārā^api hi guṇān eva^anurāgāt prakāśayet/ yathā prayojyā^anurajyeta/
body.translated_text: 3.3.11. And even one unaware of his intentions would, out of affection, reveal only his good qualities — so that the girl may fall in love.

body.text: 3.3.12/.yatra yatra ca kautukaṃ prayojyāyās tad anu praviśya sādhayet/
body.translated_text: 3.3.12. And wherever the girl has curiosity, he should enter into that and win her.

body.text: 3.3.13/.krīḍanaka^dravyāṇi yāny apūrvāṇi yāny anyāsāṃ viralaśo vidyeraṃs tāny asyā ayatnena saṃpādayet/
body.translated_text: 3.3.13. He should procure for her playthings and materials that are novel and that others would rarely have — without any apparent effort.

body.text: 3.3.14/.tatra kandukam aneka^bhakti^citram alpa^kāla^antaritam anyad anyac ca saṃdarśayet/ tathā sūtra^dāru^gavala^gaja^danta^mayīr duhitṛkā madhu^ucchiṣṭa^piṣṭa^mṛṇ^mayīś ca/
body.translated_text: 3.3.14. Among these, he should show her balls painted with many colors — different ones at short intervals. Also dolls made of thread, wood, buffalo horn, ivory, wax, flour, and clay.
3.3.15. And [he should display] a great cooking set and [utensils] for her.

body.text:
3.3.16/.kāṣṭha^medhrakayoś ca saṃyuktayoś ca strī^puṃsayor aja^eḍakānāṃ deva^kula^gṛhakānāṃ mṛd^vidala^kāṣṭha^vinirmitānāṃ śuka^parabhṛta^madana^sārikā^lāvaka^kukkuṭa^tittiri^pañjarakāṇāṃ ca vicitra^ākṛti^saṃyuktānāṃ jala^bhājanānāṃ ca yantrikāṇāṃ vīṇikānāṃ paṭolikānām (p.210) alaktaka^manaḥśilā^haritāla^hiṅgulaka^śyāma^varṇaka^ādīnāṃ tathā candana^kuṅkumayoḥ
pūga^phalānāṃ pattrāṇāṃ kāla^yuktānāṃ ca śakti^viṣaye pracchannaṃ dānaṃ prakāśa^dravyāṇāṃ ca prakāśam/ yathā ca sarva^abhiprāya^saṃvardhakam enaṃ manyeta tathā prayatitavyam/
body.translated_text: 3.3.16. And pairs of wooden figures — male and female joined together — [also] pairs of rams and goats; miniature temples and houses made of clay, bamboo-splits, and wood; cages of various shapes for parrots, cuckoos, <s>maina</s> birds, <s>lāvaka</s> quails, roosters, and partridges; water-vessels of curious shapes, mechanical devices, toy lutes, and toy boxes; also [supplies of] lac, red arsite, yellow orpiment, vermilion, lamp-black, and other pigments; also sandalwood and saffron, betel nuts, leaves, and things appropriate to the season — secret gifts of things that can be concealed, and open gifts of things that can be displayed openly. And he should endeavor that she regards him as one who advances all her wishes.
3.3.17. And he should secretly seek [opportunities for] looking at her. Also the arrangement of conversations.

body.text: 3.3.18/.pracchanna^dānasya tu kāraṇam ātmano guru^janād bhayaṃ khyāpayet/ deyasya ca^anyena spṛhaṇīyatvam iti/
body.translated_text: 3.3.18. And regarding the reason for secret gifts, he should intimate his fear of his own elders, and [the fact] that the gift is desired by others.

body.text: 3.3.19/.vardhamāna^anurāgaṃ ca^ākhyānake manaḥ kurvatīm anvarthābhiḥ kathābhiś citta^hāriṇībhiś ca rañjayet/
body.translated_text: 3.3.19. And when she shows interest in a story, her love increasing, he should delight her with appropriate and charming tales.

body.text: 3.3.20/.vismayeṣu prasahyamānām indra^jālaiḥ prayogair vismāpayet/ kalāsu kautukinīṃ tat^kauśalena gīta^priyāṃ śruti^harair gītaiḥ/ āśvayujyām aṣṭamī^candrake kaumudyām utsaveṣu yātrāyāṃ grahaṇe gṛha^ācāre vā vicitrair āpīḍaiḥ *karṇa[ch:karṇaṃ]^pattra^bhaṅgaiḥ sikthaka^pradhānair vastra^aṅgulīyaka^bhūṣaṇa^dānaiś ca/ no ced doṣa^karāṇi manyeta/
body.translated_text: 3.3.20. When she is amazed by wonders, he should astound her with magic tricks and feats. When she is curious about the arts, [he should impress her] with his skill in them. When she loves music, with captivating songs. During the <s>Āśvayujī</s> [festival], the eighth-day moonlight, the <s>Kaumudī</s> [festival], at festivals, processions, eclipses, or domestic ceremonies — with varied flower garlands, ear-ornaments of leaf-cuttings, mainly of wax, and with gifts of garments, rings, and ornaments. Unless she would consider them improper.
3.3.21. Through familiarity with the particular man, the foster-sister should teach her the sixty-four arts of love, [furthering] the man's engagement.
3.3.22. And under the pretext of teaching those [arts], he should display his own skill in lovemaking to the girl.

body.text: 3.3.23/.udāra^veṣaś ca svayam anupahata^darśanaś syāt/ bhāvaṃ ca kurvatīm iṅgita^ākāraiḥ sūcayet/
body.translated_text: 3.3.23. And he himself should appear in fine attire and of unblemished appearance. And when she shows her feelings, he should indicate [them] through gestures and expressions.
