body.translated_text: 5.4.12. 'Listen to this wonderful thing, O fortunate one! Having seen you at such-and-such place, this hero of such-and-such family is experiencing madness of mind. By nature delicate, never before distressed by another, the poor man — from now on, he could even experience death' — thus she should describe.

body.text: 5.4.13/.tatra siddhā dvitīye +ahani vāci vaktre dṛṣṭyāṃ ca prasādam upalakṣya punar api kathāṃ pravartayet/
body.translated_text: 5.4.13. When [the woman] is won there, on the second day, perceiving graciousness in her speech, face, and glance, she should continue the conversation again.

body.text: 5.4.14/.śṛṇvatyāṃ ca^ahalyā^avimāraka^śākuntalā^ādīny anyāny api laukikāni ca kathayet tad^yuktāni/
body.translated_text: 5.4.14. And when she listens, she should tell the stories of <s>Ahalyā</s>, <s>Avimāraka</s>, <s>Śakuntalā</s>, and others — also popular tales relevant to [the situation].

body.text: 5.4.15/.vṛṣatāṃ catuḥṣaṣṭi^vijñatāṃ saubhāgyaṃ ca nāyakasya/ ślāghanīyatāṃ (yā) ca^asya pracchannaṃ saṃprayogaṃ bhūtam abhūta^pūrvaṃ vā varṇayet/
body.translated_text: 5.4.15. She should describe the hero's virility, his mastery of the sixty-four arts, his charm, and his praiseworthiness — and his secret liaisons, whether real or invented.
5.4.16. And she should observe [the woman's] gestures.
5.4.17. [If] she converses having looked with a smile,
5.4.18. and invites [the messenger] to sit,

body.text: 5.4.19/.kvāsitaṃ kva śayitaṃ *kva[ch:omits] bhuktaṃ kva ceṣṭitaṃ kiṃ vā kṛtam iti pṛcchati/
body.translated_text: 5.4.19. and asks 'Where did you sit? Where did you sleep? Where did you eat? What did you do? What was done?'
5.4.20. [if] she shows herself in a private place,
5.4.21. [if] she commissions stories [about him],
5.4.22. [if] she sighs while thinking and yawns,
5.4.23. and gives a gift that produces affection,
5.4.24. and remembers [him] on desired festivals,
5.4.25. [if] she sends [the messenger] away with the promise of another meeting,

body.text: 5.4.26/.sādhuvādinī satī kim idam aśobhanam abhidhatsa iti kathām anubadhnāti/
body.translated_text: 5.4.26. [if] while speaking approvingly, she ties the conversation to 'What is this unseemly thing you are saying?'
5.4.27. [if] she attributes to the hero faults connected with deceit and fickleness,

body.text: 5.4.28/.pūrva^pravṛttaṃ ca tat^saṃdarśanaṃ kathā^abhiyogaṃ ca svayam akathayantī tayā^ucyamānam ākāṅkṣati/
body.translated_text: 5.4.28. and regarding the previously initiated meeting and the approach through conversation — not speaking of it herself, she desires it to be spoken by her [the messenger],

body.text: 5.4.29/.nāyaka^manoratheṣu ca kathyamāneṣu saparibhavaṃ nāma hasati/ na ca nirvadati^iti//(p.279)
body.translated_text: 5.4.29. and when the hero's desires are being described, she laughs as if with contempt, but does not rebuke —
5.4.30. The messenger should reinforce her, who has shown her feelings, with tokens of recognition from the hero.
5.4.31. But one who is unacquainted, she should win over through praise of [the man's] qualities and tales of [his] passion.
5.4.32. There is no role for a go-between (<s>dūtī</s>) between two who are unacquainted and have not seen each other's form — so says <s>Auddālaki</s>.
5.4.33. Even between those who are unacquainted, if they have seen each other's form, there is [a role for a go-between] — so say the followers of <s>Bābhravya</s>.
5.4.34. Even between those who are acquainted, if they have not seen each other's form, there is [a role] — so says <s>Goṇikāputra</s>.
5.4.35. Even between those who are unacquainted and have not seen each other's form, [there can be a meeting] through trust in a go-between — so says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.

body.text: 5.4.36/.tāsāṃ manoharāṇy upāyanāni tāmbūlam anulepanaṃ srajam aṅgulīyakaṃ vāso vā tena prahitaṃ darśayet/
body.translated_text: 5.4.36. She should show [to the woman] charming gifts sent by him: <s>tāmbūla</s> (betel), unguents, garlands, a ring, or a garment.

body.text: 5.4.37/.teṣu nāyakasya yathā^arthaṃ nakha^daśana^padāni tāni tāni ca cihnāni syuḥ/
body.translated_text: 5.4.37. On these, there should be the hero's nail-marks, tooth-marks, and various other signs, [placed] meaningfully.
5.4.38. And on a garment, she should place a saffron-stained handprint in salutation.

body.text: 5.4.39/.pattra^chedyāni nānā^abhiprāya^ākṛtini darśayet/ lekha^patra^garbhāṇi karṇa^pattrāṇy āpīḍāṃś ca
body.translated_text: 5.4.39. She should show leaf-cuttings of various shapes conveying different intentions; and ear-ornaments and headbands containing hidden letters.
5.4.40. On these [should be] the declaration of his desires; and she should induce [the woman] to give a return-gift.
5.4.41. And when the mutual acceptance has been thus established, the meeting [takes place] through trust in the go-between.

body.text: 5.4.42/.sa tu devatā^abhigamane yātrāyām udyāna^krīḍāyāṃ jala^avataraṇe vivāhe yajña^vyasana^utsaveṣv agny^utpāte caura^vibhrame janapadasya cakra^ārohaṇe prekṣā^vyāpāreṣu teṣu teṣu ca kāryeṣv iti bābhravīyāḥ/
body.translated_text: 5.4.42. That [meeting] may occur during a visit to a deity's [temple], during a festival procession, during sport in a garden, during bathing in water, at a wedding, during sacrifices, calamities, celebrations, a fire-outbreak, panic from thieves, the mobilization of the countryside, during spectacles and entertainments, and in various other occasions — so say the followers of <s>Bābhravya</s>.
5.4.43. [The meeting is] easily arranged at the houses of a female friend, a mendicant woman, a female ascetic, or a <s>tāpasī</s> (female renunciant) — so says <s>Goṇikāputra</s>.

body.text: 5.4.44/.tasyā eva tu gehe vidita^niṣkrama^praveśe cintitā^atyaya^pratīkāre praveśanam upapannaṃ niṣkramaṇam avijñāta^kālaṃ ca tan nityaṃ sukha^upāyaṃ ca^iti vātsyāyanaḥ//(p.282)
body.translated_text: 5.4.44. But entry into her own house is appropriate when the comings and goings are known, when the means of averting anticipated dangers have been devised, and the departure is at an undetected time — and that is always easily managed — so says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.

body.text: 5.4.45/.nisṛṣṭa^arthā parimita^arthā patra^hārī svayaṃ^dūtī mūḍha^dūtī bhāryā^dūtī mūka^dūtī vāta^dūtī ca^iti dūtī^viśeṣāḥ//(p.282)
body.translated_text: 5.4.45. The types of go-betweens are: one with full authority (<s>nisṛṣṭārthā</s>), one with limited authority (<s>parimitārthā</s>), a letter-bearer (<s>patrahārī</s>), one acting as her own go-between (<s>svayaṃdūtī</s>), a foolish go-between (<s>mūḍhadūtī</s>), a wife as go-between (<s>bhāryādūtī</s>), a mute go-between (<s>mūkadūtī</s>), and a wind-go-between (<s>vātadūtī</s>).

body.text: 5.4.46/.nāyakasya nāyikāyāś ca yathā^manīṣitam artham upalabhya sva^buddhyā kārya^saṃpādinī nisṛṣṭa^arthā//(p.282)
body.translated_text: 5.4.46. One who, having ascertained the desired object of both the hero and the heroine, accomplishes the task by her own intelligence — she is one with full authority (<s>nisṛṣṭārthā</s>).
5.4.47. She is [employed] mostly between those who are acquainted and have spoken.
5.4.48. When sent by the heroine, [she may act] even between those who are unacquainted and have not spoken.

body.text: 5.4.49/.kautukāc ca^anurūpau yuktāv imau parasparasya^ity asaṃstutayor api//(p.283)
body.translated_text: 5.4.49. And out of curiosity, [thinking] 'These two are suited and fitting for each other' — [she may act] even between those who are unacquainted.
5.4.50. One who, having learned part of the task and part of the approach, accomplishes the rest — she is one with limited authority (<s>parimitārthā</s>).
5.4.51. She [is employed] between those who have seen each other's form but meet rarely.
5.4.52. One who conveys merely the message — she is a letter-bearer (<s>patrahārī</s>).
5.4.53. She [is employed] between those who have deep mutual affection and have been intimate, for the purpose of informing about place and time.

body.text: 5.4.54/.dautyena prahita^anyayā svayam eva nāyakam abhigacched ajānatī nāma tena saha^upabhogaṃ svapne vā kathayet/ gotra^skhalitaṃ bhāryāṃ ca^asya nindet/ tad^vyapadeśena svayam īrṣyāṃ darśayet/ nakha^daśana^cihnitaṃ vā kiṃ cid dadyāt/ bhavate +aham adau dātuṃ saṃkalpitā^iti ca^abhidadhīta/ mama bhāryāyā kā ramanīyā^iti vivikte paryanuyuñjīta sā svayaṃ^dūtī/
body.translated_text: 5.4.54. A woman who, [ostensibly] sent by another on an errand, goes herself to the hero, and pretending ignorance, tells him of her enjoyment with him in a dream; or commits a slip of the tongue [revealing his name]; or criticizes his wife; or under that pretext shows jealousy herself; or gives something marked with nail and tooth impressions; or says 'I was originally intended to be given to you'; or in private asks him 'Which of my co-wives is the most attractive?' — she is one acting as her own go-between (<s>svayaṃdūtī</s>).
5.4.55. Her [approach should include] seeing [the man] in private and accepting [gifts from him].

body.text: 5.4.56/.pratigraha^cchalena^anyām abhisaṃdhāya^asyāḥ saṃdeśa^śrāvaṇa^dvāreṇa nāyakaṃ sādhayet tāṃ ca^upahanyāt sā^api svayaṃ^dūtī/
body.translated_text: 5.4.56. Another [woman] who, under the pretext of accepting [a gift], targets a different [woman], and through the channel of conveying her message, wins over the hero and undermines her [rival] — she too is one acting as her own go-between.
5.4.57. By this, the hero [acting] as his own messenger and a male messenger are also explained.

body.text: 5.4.58/.nāyaka^bhāryāṃ mugdhāṃ viśvāsya^ayantraṇayā^anupraviśya nāyakasya ceṣṭitāni pṛcchet/ yogāñ śikṣayet/ sākāraṃ maṇḍayet/ kopam enāṃ grāhayet/ evaṃ ca pratipadyasva^iti śrāvayet/ svayaṃ ca^asyāṃ nakha^daśana^padāni nirvartayet/ tena dvāreṇa nāyakam ākārayet sā mūḍha^dūtī//(p.285)
body.translated_text: 5.4.58. One who, having gained the trust of the hero's naive wife and having entered [the household] unhindered, asks about the hero's conduct; teaches her love-techniques; decorates her suggestively; makes her angry [at her husband]; tells her 'Respond in this way'; and herself makes nail-marks and tooth-marks on her [to arouse the husband's suspicion] — and through that channel summons the hero — she is a foolish go-between (<s>mūḍhadūtī</s>).
5.4.59. Through her [i.e., the naive wife], he should convey his replies.

body.text: 5.4.60/.sva^bhāryāṃ vā mūḍhāṃ prayojya tayā saha viśvāsena yojayitvā tayā^eva^ākārayet/ ātmanaś ca vaicakṣaṇyaṃ prakāśayet/ sā bhāryā dūtī/ tasyās tayā^eva^ākāra^grahaṇam//(p.285)
body.translated_text: 5.4.60. Or, having employed his own naive wife, having established trust between her and [the target woman], he should summon [the target] through her; and he should display his own expertise — she is a wife-as-go-between (<s>bhāryādūtī</s>). From her, one should receive the signals through her alone.

body.text: 5.4.61/.bālāṃ vā paricārikām adoṣajñām aduṣṭena^upāyena prahiṇuyāt/ tatra sraji karṇa^pattre vā gūḍha^lekha^nidhānaṃ nakha^daśana^padaṃ vā sā mūka^dūtī/ tasyās tayā eva pratyuttara^prārthanam//(p.286)
body.translated_text: 5.4.61. Or one should send a young maid-servant who is innocent of faults, by a blameless method. In that case, concealing a secret letter in a garland or ear-ornament, or [conveying] a nail-mark or tooth-mark — she is a mute go-between (<s>mūkadūtī</s>). From her, one should request a reply through her alone.

body.text: 5.4.62/.pūrva^prastuta^artha^liṅga^saṃbaddham anya^jana^agrahaṇīyaṃ laukika^arthaṃ dvyarthaṃ vā vacanam udāsīnā yā śrāvayet sā vāta^dūtī/ tasyā api tayā^eva pratyuttara^prārthanam iti tāsāṃ viśeṣāḥ//(p.286) bhavanti ca^atra ślokāḥ ---(p.287)
body.translated_text: 5.4.62. One who, appearing indifferent, causes [the target] to hear a speech that is connected with the previously arranged matter through signs, that is not graspable by other people, that has a worldly meaning, or that has a double meaning — she is a wind-go-between (<s>vātadūtī</s>). From her too, a reply should be requested through her alone — these are the distinctions [among go-betweens]. And here are verses:
5.4.63ab. A widow, a fortune-teller, a maid-servant, a mendicant woman, a craftswoman —
5.4.63cd. [such a woman] quickly enters into confidence and accomplishes the work of a go-between.
5.4.64ab. She should create hatred toward the husband and describe the attractions [of the hero];
5.4.64cd. she should describe the wonderful love-making of other [women as well].
5.4.65ab. And the hero's passion, and again his skill in love-making,
5.4.65cd. and the solicitation by many women, and his constancy — she should describe.
5.4.66ab. Even a matter that was not intended, or one that was abandoned because of a fault,
5.4.66cd. a go-between brings back again through skillfulness of speech.
5.5. On the Women of the Royal Harem (<s>Īśvarakāmita</s>)

body.text: 5.5.1/.na rājñāṃ mahāmātrāṇāṃ vā parabhavana^praveśo vidyate/ mahājanena hi caritam eṣāṃ dṛśyate +anuvidhīyate ca//(p.288)
body.translated_text: 5.5.1. There is no entry of kings or high officials into others' houses. For the conduct of the great is seen and imitated by the public.

body.text: 5.5.2/.savitāram udyantaṃ trayo lokāḥ paśyanti anūdyante ca/ gacchantam api paśyanty anupratiṣṭhante ca//(p.288)
body.translated_text: 5.5.2. The three worlds see the rising sun and follow after it; and they see it setting and follow after it [likewise].

body.text: 5.5.3/.tasmād aśakyatvād garhaṇīyatvāc ca^iti na te vṛthā kiṃ cid ācareyuḥ//(p.288)
body.translated_text: 5.5.3. Therefore, because of impossibility and because of censure, they should not engage in any [such conduct] in vain.
5.5.4. But when [the conduct] must necessarily be undertaken, they should employ stratagems.

body.text: 5.5.5/.grāma^adhipater ayuktakasya hala^uttha^vṛtti^putrasya yūno grāmīṇa^yoṣito vacana^mātra^sādhyāḥ/ tāś carṣaṇya ity ācakṣate viṭāḥ//(p.289)
body.translated_text: 5.5.5. The village headman's agent, a young man whose livelihood comes from agriculture — the village women are achievable for him merely by a word. These are called <s>carṣaṇī</s> (peasant women) by the libertines.

body.text: 5.5.6/.tābhiḥ saha viṣṭi^karmasu koṣṭha^āgāra^praveśe dravyāṇāṃ niṣkramaṇa^praveśanayor bhavana^pratisaṃskāre kṣetra^karmaṇi karpāsa^ūrṇa^atasī^śaṇa^valkala^ādāne sūtra^pratigrahe dravyāṇāṃ kraya^vikraya^vinimayeṣu teṣu teṣu ca karmasu saṃprayogaḥ//(p.289)
body.translated_text: 5.5.6. With them, the occasions for union are: in forced labor, in entering the storehouse, in the exit and entry of goods, in the maintenance of houses, in field-work, in the collection of cotton, wool, flax, hemp, and bark, in the receipt of thread, in the buying, selling, and exchange of goods, and in various other tasks.
5.5.7. Likewise, for the superintendent of cattle with the women of the cow-herding [settlement].
5.5.8. For the superintendent of spinning, with widows, the destitute, and female renunciants.
5.5.9. For the city-officer, with women who roam about at night, because he knows their secrets.
5.5.10. For the superintendent of trade, [the opportunities arise] in buying and selling.

5.5.11. On the occasions of the <s>Aṣṭamī</s> (eighth-day festival), <s>Candrakaumudī</s> (Moonlight Festival), <s>Suvasantaka</s> (Spring Festival), and the like, the women of towns, cities, and market-towns generally sport in the lord's palace together with the women of the inner apartments.

body.text: 5.5.12/.tatra ca^apānaka^ante nagara^striyo yathā^paricayam antaḥpurikāṇāṃ pṛthak pṛthag bhoga^avāsakān praviśya kathābhir āsitvā pūjitāḥ prapītāś ca^upapradoṣaṃ niṣkrāmayeyuḥ//(p.290)
body.translated_text: 5.5.12. And there, at the conclusion of the drinking-party, the city women, according to their acquaintance, should enter the individual pleasure-chambers of the harem women one by one, and having sat conversing, honored and given drinks, they should be sent away toward dusk.

body.text: 5.5.13/.tatra praṇihitā rāja^dāsī prayojyāyāḥ pūrva^saṃsṛṣṭā tāṃ tatra (p.290) saṃbhāṣeta/
body.translated_text: 5.5.13. There, a female servant of the king, previously intimate with the target woman and appointed [for this purpose], should engage her in conversation.
5.5.14. She should attract her by showing her beautiful things.

body.text: 5.5.15/.prāg eva svabhavanasthāṃ brūyāt/ amuṣyāṃ krīḍāyāṃ tava rāja^bhavana^sthānāni rāmanīyakāni darśayiṣyāmi^iti kāle ca yojayet/ bahiḥ pravāla^kuṭṭimaṃ te darśayiṣyāmi/
body.translated_text: 5.5.15. Even beforehand, while [the woman is] still in her own home, she should say: 'At such-and-such a festival, I will show you the beautiful sights of the royal palace' — and at the [appropriate] time she should arrange [the meeting]. 'I will show you the coral-floor outside.'

body.text: 5.5.16/.maṇi^bhūmikāṃ vṛkṣa^vāṭikāṃ mṛdvīkā^maṇḍapaṃ samudra^gṛha^prāsādān gūḍha^bhitti^saṃcārāṃś citra^karmāṇi krīḍā^mṛgān yantrāṇi śakunān vyāghra^siṃha^pañjara^ādīni ca yāni purastād varṇitāni syuḥ/
body.translated_text: 5.5.16. [She should mention] the jeweled floor, the tree-garden, the grape-arbor, the ocean-house, the palace, the secret passages in the walls, the paintings, the pet animals, the mechanical devices, the birds, and the tiger and lion cages and the like — whatever has been previously described.
5.5.17. And in private, she should inform her of the lord's passion directed toward her.
5.5.18. And she should describe [his] skill in love-making.
5.5.19. And she should arrange [a meeting] with one who has consented, ensuring no one else overhears.

body.text: 5.5.20/.apratipadyamānāṃ svayam eva^īśvara āgatya^upacāraiḥ sānvitāṃ rañjayitvā saṃbhūya ca sa^anurāgaṃ visṛjet/
body.translated_text: 5.5.20. If she does not consent, the lord himself should come, and having pleased her with courteous attentions and having been intimate with her, he should send her away with affection.

body.text: 5.5.21/.prayojyāyāś ca patyur anugraha^ucitasya dārān nityam antaḥpuram aucityāt praveśayet/ tatra praṇihitā (p.291) rāja^dāsī^iti samānaṃ pūrveṇa/
body.translated_text: 5.5.21. And he should regularly admit into the inner apartments the wife of the target woman's husband, to whom a favor is owed — due to propriety [she has cause to enter]. There, 'a female servant of the king appointed [for this purpose]' — the same as before.

body.text: 5.5.22/.antaḥpurikā vā prayojyayā saha svaceṭikā saṃpreṣaṇena prītiṃ kuryāt/ prasṛta^prītiṃ ca sa^apadeśaṃ darśane niyojayet/ praviṣṭāṃ pūjitāṃ pīta^vartīm praṇihitā rāja^dāsī^iti samānaṃ pūrveṇa/
body.translated_text: 5.5.22. Or a harem woman, having made friends with the target woman through the sending of her own maid-servant, and having extended that friendship, should contrive to show her [the palace] with a pretext. When she has entered and been honored and given drink — 'a female servant of the king appointed [for this purpose]' — the same as before.

body.text: 5.5.23/.yasmin vā vijñāne prayojyā vikhyātā syāt tad darśana^artham antaḥpurikā sa^upacāraṃ tām āhvayet/ praviṣṭāṃ praṇihitā rāja^dāsī^iti samānaṃ pūrveṇa/
body.translated_text: 5.5.23. Or, whatever art the target woman is famous for, the harem woman should invite her with courteous attentions for the purpose of seeing that [art]. When she has entered — 'a female servant of the king appointed [for this purpose]' — the same as before.

body.text:
5.5.24/.udbhūtān arthasya bhītasya vā bhāryāṃ bhikṣukī brūyāt asāv antaḥpurikā rājani siddhā gṛhīta^vākyā mama vacanaṃ śṛṇoti/ svabhāvataś ca kṛpā^śīlā tām anena^upāyena^adhigamiṣyāmi/ aham eva te praveśaṃ kārayiṣyāmi/ sā ca te bhartur mahā^antam anarthaṃ nivartayiṣyati^iti pratipannāṃ dvis trir iti praveśayet/ antaḥpurikā ca^asyā abhayaṃ dadyāt/ abhaya^śravaṇāc
ca saṃprahṛṣṭāṃ praṇihitā rāja^dāsī^iti samānaṃ pūrveṇa/
body.translated_text: 5.5.24. Or, a mendicant woman should tell the wife of a prominent man or one who is frightened: 'Such-and-such a harem woman is influential with the king and her word is heeded; she is by nature compassionate — she listens to what I say. I will approach her by this means. I will arrange your admission. And she will avert the great catastrophe threatening your husband.' When [the woman] consents, she should be admitted a second or third time. And the harem woman should give her assurance of safety. And upon hearing the assurance of safety, when [the woman] is delighted — 'a female servant of the king appointed [for this purpose]' — the same as before.

body.text: 5.5.25/.etayā vṛtty^arthināṃ mahāmātra^abhitaptānāṃ balād vigṛhītānāṃ vyavahāre durbalānāṃ sva^bhogena^asaṃtuṣṭānāṃ rājani prīti^kāmānāṃ rājya^janeṣu paṅkti(vyakti)m icchatāṃ sajātair bādhyamānānāṃ sajātān bādhitukāmānāṃ sūcakānām anyeṣāṃ kārya^vaśināṃ jāyā vyākhyātāḥ//(p.292)
body.translated_text: 5.5.25. By this [method], the wives of the following are explained: those seeking employment, those harassed by high officials, those overpowered by force, those weak in legal disputes, those unsatisfied with their own possessions, those desiring favor with the king, those seeking rank among the royal retinue, those oppressed by their kinsmen, those wishing to oppress their kinsmen, informers, and others subject to the compulsion of [pending] matters.

body.text: 5.5.26/.anyena vā prayojyāṃ saha saṃsṛṣṭāṃ saṃgrāhya dāsyam upanītāṃ krameṇa^antaḥpuraṃ praveśayet/
body.translated_text: 5.5.26. Or, having attached the target woman through intimacy with another [already associated with the harem], and having brought her as a servant, he should gradually admit her into the inner apartments.

body.text: 5.5.27/.praṇidhinā ca^āyatim asyāḥ saṃdūṣya rājani vidviṣṭa iti kalatra^avagraha^upāyena^enām antaḥpuraṃ praveśayed iti pracchanna^yogāḥ/ ete rāja^putreṣu prāyeṇa//(p.293)
body.translated_text: 5.5.27. Or, having compromised her future through an agent, [and making it appear that] her husband is hostile to the king, he should admit her into the inner apartments by the device of detaining her husband — these are the secret stratagems. These [apply] mostly to princes.
5.5.28. But the lord should not in this manner enter another's house.

body.text: 5.5.29/.ābhīraṃ hi koṭṭa^rājaṃ para^bhavana^gataṃ bhrātṛ^prayukto rajako jaghāna/ kāśirājaṃ jayasenam aśva^adhyakṣa iti//(p.294)
body.translated_text: 5.5.29. For the <s>Ābhīra</s> king <s>Koṭṭa</s>, having gone to another's house, was killed by a washerman sent by [the king's] brother. And the king of <s>Kāśī</s>, <s>Jayasena</s>, [was killed] by his horse-superintendent.
5.5.30. But open [expressions of] desire [are permissible] in accordance with regional customs.

body.text: 5.5.31/.prattā janapada^kanyā daśame +ahani kiṃcid aupāyanikam upagṛhya praviśanty antaḥpuram upabhuktā eva visṛjyanta ity āndhrāṇām/
body.translated_text: 5.5.31. Married girls from the countryside, on the tenth day, bringing some gift, enter the harem; having been enjoyed, they are sent away — this is the practice of the <s>Āndhra</s> people.

body.text: 5.5.32/.mahāmātra^iṣvarāṇām antaḥpurāṇi niśi sevā^arthaṃ rājānam upagacchanti vātsagulmakānām/
body.translated_text: 5.5.32. The harems of the great ministers and lords visit the king at night for the purpose of service — this is the practice of the <s>Vātsagulma</s> people.

body.text: 5.5.33/.rūpavatīr janapada^yoṣitaḥ prīty^apadeśena māsaṃ māsā^ardhaṃ vā^ativāsayanty antaḥpurikā vaidarbhāṇām/
body.translated_text: 5.5.33. The harem women detain beautiful women of the countryside for a month or half a month under the pretext of affection — this is the practice of the <s>Vaidarbha</s> people.

body.text: 5.5.34/.darśanīyāḥ svabhāryāḥ prīti^dāyām eva mahāmātra^rājabhyo dadaty aparāntakānām/
body.translated_text: 5.5.34. They give their own beautiful wives to the great ministers and kings solely as a love-gift — this is the practice of the <s>Aparāntaka</s> people.

body.text: 5.5.35/.rāja^krīḍā^arthaṃ (p.294) nagara^striyo janapada^striyaś ca saṅghaśa ekaśaś ca rāja^kulaṃ praviśanti saurāṣṭrakāṇām iti//(p.295) ślokāv atra bhavataḥ(p.295)
body.translated_text: 5.5.35. Women of the city and women of the countryside, in groups or singly, enter the royal household for the king's amusement — this is the practice of the <s>Saurāṣṭra</s> people. Here are two verses:
5.5.36ab. These and many other practices of seduction of others' wives
5.5.36cd. prevail in various regions, being established by kings.

body.text: 5.5.37ab/.na tv eva^etān prayuñjīta rājā lokahite rataḥ/(p.295)
body.translated_text: 5.5.37ab. But a king devoted to the welfare of the people should never employ them;
5.5.37cd. having subdued the six internal enemies, he thus conquers the earth.
5.6. [Chapter on] the conduct of harem women and the guarding of wives.

body.text: 5.6.1/.na^antaḥpurāṇāṃ rakṣaṇa^yogāt puruṣa^saṃdarśanaṃ vidyate patyuś ca^ekatvād aneka^sādhāraṇatvāc ca^atṛptiḥ/ tasmāt tāni prayogata eva parasparaṃ rañjayeyuḥ//(p.296)
body.translated_text: 5.6.1. Since there is no opportunity for seeing men due to the guarding of the harem, and since the husband is one but [the women are] shared among many, there is dissatisfaction. Therefore they should satisfy each other through various devices.

body.text: 5.6.2/.dhātreyikāṃ sakhīṃ dāsīṃ vā puruṣavad alaṃkṛtya^ākṛtisaṃyuktaiḥ kanda^mūla^phala^avayavair apadravyair vā^ātma^abhiprāyāṃ nirvartayeyuḥ//(p.296)
body.translated_text: 5.6.2. They should gratify their desire using a foster-sister, companion, or maid-servant adorned like a man, with roots, bulbs, fruits, or other artificial objects of suitable shape.
5.6.3. They should lie with male statues or those of ambiguous gender.

body.text: 5.6.4/.rājānaś ca kṛpā^śīlā vinā^api bhāva^yogād āyojita^apadravyā yāvad artham ekayā rātryā bahvībhir api gacchanti/ yasyāṃ tu prītir vāsaka ṛtuv vā tatra^abhiprāyataḥ pravartanta iti prācya^upacārāḥ//(p.297)
body.translated_text: 5.6.4. And kings, being compassionate by nature, even without the union of passion, equipped with artificial devices, suffice for many [women] in one night; but where there is affection, a designated visit, or the season [is right], they proceed according to their preference — these are the customs of the eastern regions.

body.text: 5.6.5/.strī^yogeṇa^eva puruṣāṇām apy alabdha^vṛttīnāṃ viyoniṣu vijātiṣu strī^pratimāsu kevala^upamardanāc ca^abhiprāya^nivṛttir vyākhyātā//(p.297)
body.translated_text: 5.6.5. By the same method as women, men too who have not obtained [natural] satisfaction can relieve their desire through [use of] non-natural orifices, different species, female statues, or mere rubbing — this has been explained.

body.text: 5.6.6/.yoṣav eṣāṃś ca nāgarakān prayeṇa antaḥpurikāḥ paricārikābhiḥ saha praveśayanti/
body.translated_text: 5.6.6. These harem women generally bring in such urbane men through their attendants.

body.text: 5.6.7/.teṣām upāvartane dhātreyikāś ca abhyantara^saṃsṛṣṭā āyatiṃ darśayantyaḥ prayateran/
body.translated_text: 5.6.7. For their introduction, foster-sisters who are intimate within [the harem], showing future [rewards], should make efforts.

body.text: 5.6.8/.sukha^praveśitām apasāra^bhūmiṃ viśālatāṃ veśmanaḥ pramādaṃ rakṣiṇām anityatāṃ parijanasya varṇayeyuḥ/
body.translated_text: 5.6.8. They should describe the easy access, the place of escape, the spaciousness of the dwelling, the negligence of the guards, and the instability of the retinue.
5.6.9. But they should not introduce a person by means of a false pretext, because of the danger [involved].

body.text: 5.6.10/.nāgārakas tu suprāpam apy antaḥpuram apāya^bhūyiṣṭhatvān na praviśed iti vātsyāyanaḥ//(p.298)
body.translated_text: 5.6.10. However, the urbane man (<s>nāgaraka</s>) should not enter the harem, even if easily accessible, because it is mostly fraught with danger — thus says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.

body.text: 5.6.11/.sa^apasāraṃ tu pramadavana^avagāḍhaṃ vibhakta^dīrgha^kakṣyam alpa^pramatta^rakṣakaṃ proṣitā^rājakaṃ kāraṇāni samīkṣya bahuśa āhūyamāno +artha^buddhyā kakṣyā^praveśaṃ ca dṛṣṭvā tābhir eva vihita^upāyaḥ praviśet/
body.translated_text: 5.6.11. But [if it is] a harem with escape routes, situated deep within a pleasure garden, with separate long enclosures, with few and careless guards, and with the king away — having examined the circumstances, being repeatedly invited, with a view to gain, and seeing the access to the enclosures, provided with means arranged by those [women], he may enter.
5.6.12. And if within his capacity, he should exit every day.

body.text: 5.6.13/.bahiś ca rakṣibhir anyad eva kāraṇam apadiśya saṃsṛjyeta/
body.translated_text: 5.6.13. And outside, he should have contact with the guards by giving some other pretext.

body.text: 5.6.14/.antaś^cāriṇyāṃ ca paricārikāyāṃ vidita^arthāyāṃ saktam ātmānaṃ rūpayet/ tad alābhāc ca śokam antaḥpraveśinībhiś ca dūtī^kalpaṃ sakalam ācaret/ (p.298)
body.translated_text: 5.6.14. And he should display his attachment to an attendant woman who moves within [the harem] and who knows his purpose; and [simulate] grief at not obtaining her; and through women who have access inside, he should carry out the entire role of a messenger.
5.6.15. And he should be aware of the king's spies.

body.text:
5.6.16/.dūtyās tv asaṃcāre yatra gṛhīta^ākārāyāḥ prayojyāyā darśana^yogas tatra^avasthānam/
5.6.17/.tasminn api tu rakṣiṣu paricārikā^vyapadeśaḥ/
body.translated_text: 5.6.16. When the messenger cannot move about, wherever there is possibility of seeing the employed woman whose gestures have been grasped, there he should station himself. 5.6.17. And even there, among guards, the pretext of [visiting] an attendant [should be used].
5.6.18. When she follows with her eyes, communication through hints and gestures [should be made].

body.text: 5.6.19/.yatra saṃpāto +asyās tatra citra^karmaṇas tad yuktasya vyarthānāṃ gīta^vastukānāṃ krīḍanakānāṃ kṛta^cihnānām āpīnakānā(kasya)m aṅgulīyakasya ca nidhānam/
body.translated_text: 5.6.19. Wherever her meeting-place is, there he should deposit paintings suitable to the purpose, meaningless song-objects, playthings with marks made on them, oil-cakes, and a ring.

body.text: 5.6.20/.pratyuttaraṃ tayā dattaṃ prapaśyet/ tataḥ praveśane yateta//(p.299)
body.translated_text: 5.6.20. He should watch for the reply given by her. Then he should endeavor to enter.

body.text: 5.6.21/.yatra ca^asyā niyataṃ gamanam iti vidyāt tatra pracchannasya prāg eva^avasthānam/
body.translated_text: 5.6.21. And wherever he knows she certainly goes, there he should station himself in concealment beforehand.
5.6.22. Or he may enter in the guise of a guard at the time permitted by them.
5.6.23. Or entrance and exit [may be effected while] wrapped in bedding and coverings.
5.6.24. Or by the application of open and closed [techniques], [becoming] of invisible shadow-form.

body.text: 5.6.25/.tatra^ayaṃ prayogaḥ --- nakula^hṛdayaṃ coraka^tumbī^phalāni sarpākṣīṇi ca^antardhūmena pacet/ tato +añjanena samabhāgena peṣayet/ anena^abhyakta^nayano naṣṭa^cchāyā^rūpaś carati/ (anyaiś ca jala^brahma^kṣema^śiraḥ^praṇītair bāhya^pānakair vā)
body.translated_text: 5.6.25. Here is the procedure: one should cook mongoose-heart, the fruits of <s>coraka</s>-gourd, and serpent's eyes over hidden smoke; then grind [them] with equal quantity of collyrium. Anointing the eyes with this, one moves about with invisible shadow-form. (Or with external potions prepared with water, <s>brahma</s>, and <s>kṣema</s> herbs.)

body.text: 5.6.26/.rātri^kaumudīṣu ca dīpikā^saṃbādhe suraṅgayā vā//(p.300) tatra^etad bhavati ---(p.300)
body.translated_text: 5.6.26. And on moonlit nights, in the crowding of lamps, or through a tunnel. Here it is said:
5.6.27a. During the carrying out of goods, during the bringing in of drinks,
5.6.27b. during a drinking festival, and during the bustle of maid-servants,
5.6.27c. during the exchange of dwellings and the change of guards,
5.6.27d. during departures for garden-excursions, and entering from such excursions,
5.6.27e. during a long-awaited festival, and also when the king is away —
5.6.27f. entrance is generally [possible] for young men, and exit likewise.
5.6.28a. And having learned each other's affairs, the harem-dwellers,
5.6.28b. being of one purpose, should then bring about the corruption of the rest.
5.6.28c. Having corrupted [the others], being firm in the commitment to a single purpose,
5.6.28d. having become impenetrable, one quickly enjoys the desired fruit.

body.text: 5.6.29/.tatra rāja^kula^cāriṇya eva lakṣaṇyān puruṣān antaḥpuraṃ praveśayanti na^atisurakṣatvād āparāntikānām/
body.translated_text: 5.6.29. There, the women who move about the royal household bring in handsome men into the harem, since [the harem] of the <s>Aparāntika</s> people is not very well-guarded.
5.6.30. The women of the <s>Ābhīra</s> people accomplish their purpose with the very harem guards known as <s>Kṣatriyas</s>.
5.6.31. They bring in sons of urbane men disguised in the clothes of female servants — this is the practice of the <s>Vātsagulma</s> people.

body.text: 5.6.32/.svair eva putrair antaḥpurāṇi kāmacārair jananī^varjam upayujyante vaidarbhakāṇām/
body.translated_text: 5.6.32. The harems are used by their own freely-moving sons, excepting the mother — this is the practice of the <s>Vaidarbha</s> people.

body.text: 5.6.33/.tathā praveśibhir eva jñātisaṃbandhibhir na^anyair upayujyante strairājakānām/
body.translated_text: 5.6.33. Similarly, they are used only by relatives and kinsmen who have access, not by others — this is the practice of the <s>Strairājaka</s> people.
5.6.34. By brāhmaṇas, friends, servants, and slaves — this is the practice of the <s>Gauḍa</s> people.

body.text: 5.6.35/.parispandāḥ karma^karāś ca^antaḥpureṣv aniṣiddhā anye +api tad^rūpāś ca saindhavānām/
body.translated_text: 5.6.35. Attendants and workers are not prohibited in the harems; and others of similar appearance — this is the practice of the <s>Saindhava</s> people.

body.text: 5.6.36/.arthena rakṣiṇam upagṛhya sāhasikāḥ saṃhatāḥ praviśanti haimavatānām/
body.translated_text: 5.6.36. Bold men, having bribed the guard with money, enter together — this is the practice of the <s>Haimavata</s> people.

body.text: 5.6.37/.puṣpa^dāna^niyogān nagara^brāhmaṇā rāja^viditam antaḥpurāṇi gacchanti/ paṭa^antaritaiś ca^eṣām ālāpaḥ/ tena prasaṅgena vyatikaro bhavati vaṅga^aṅga^kaliṅgakānām/
body.translated_text: 5.6.37. City brāhmaṇas, under the pretext of the duty of offering flowers, go to the harems with the king's knowledge; their conversation [takes place] behind a curtain; by that opportunity, intercourse occurs — this is the practice of the <s>Vaṅga</s>, <s>Aṅga</s>, and <s>Kaliṅga</s> people.

body.text: 5.6.38/.saṃhatya nava^daśa^ity ekaikaṃ (p.301)yuvānaṃ pracchādayanti prācyānām iti/ evaṃ para^striyaḥ prakurvīta/ ity antaḥpurikā^vṛttam//(p.302)
body.translated_text: 5.6.38. Nine or ten together conceal one young man — this is the practice of the eastern people. Thus one should deal with others' wives. This is the conduct regarding harem women.
5.6.39. And for these very reasons, one should guard one's own wives.
5.6.40. One should station guards in the harem who are proven pure with respect to the test of lust — say the teachers.

body.text: 5.6.41/.te hi bhayena ca^arthena ca^anyaṃ prayojayeyus tasmāt kāma^bhaya^artha^upadhā^śuddhān iti goṇikāputraḥ/
body.translated_text: 5.6.41. For they might employ another through fear or money; therefore [guards should be] proven pure with respect to the tests of lust, fear, and money — says <s>Goṇikāputra</s>.

body.text: 5.6.42/.adroho dharmas tam api bhayāj jahyād ato dharma^bhaya^upadhā^śuddhān iti vātsyāyanaḥ//(p.303)
body.translated_text: 5.6.42. Non-treachery is <s>dharma</s>; one might abandon even that through fear; therefore [guards should be] proven pure with respect to the tests of <s>dharma</s>, fear, and money — says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.

body.text: 5.6.43/.para^vākya^abhidhāyinībhiś ca gūḍha^ākārābhiḥ pramadābhir ātmadārān upadadhyāc chauca^aśauca^parijñāna^artham iti bābhravīyāḥ/
body.translated_text: 5.6.43. And one should set women of concealed appearance who report others' words upon one's own wives, for the purpose of ascertaining their purity or impurity — say the followers of <s>Bābhravya</s>.

body.text: 5.6.44/.duṣṭānāṃ yuvatiṣu siddhatvān na^akasmād aduṣṭa^dūṣaṇam ācared iti vātsyāyanaḥ//(p.303)
body.translated_text: 5.6.44. Since the wicked succeed with young women, one should not groundlessly corrupt the uncorrupted — says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.

body.text: 5.6.45/.atigoṣṭhī niraṅkuśatvaṃ bhartuḥ svairatā puruṣaiḥ saha^aniyantraṇatā/ pravāse +avasthānaṃ videśe nivāsaḥ svavṛtty^upaghātaḥ svairiṇī^saṃsargaḥ patyur īrṣyālutā ca^iti strīṇāṃ vināśa^kāraṇāni//(p.304)
body.translated_text: 5.6.45. Excessive socializing, lack of restraint, the husband's absence, unrestricted contact with men, dwelling abroad, residence in a foreign place, destruction of one's livelihood, association with wanton women, and jealousy of the husband — these are the causes of women's ruin.
5.6.46a. Having observed from the <s>śāstra</s> the methods marked as seduction of others' wives,

body.text: 5.6.46b/.na yāti cchalanāṃ kaścit svadārān prati śāstravit//(p.304)
body.translated_text: 5.6.46b. no one who knows the <s>śāstra</s> is deceived regarding his own wives.
5.6.47a. Because the methods are one-sided, and from seeing the dangers,
5.6.47b. and because of the opposition to <s>dharma</s> and <s>artha</s>, one should not practice seduction of others' wives.
5.6.48a. This [discussion] was undertaken for the purpose of guarding wives, for the welfare of men;
5.6.48b. its method should not be understood as for the corruption of people.
6. [Book on] Courtesans (<s>Vaiśika</s>).
6.1. [Chapter on] Consideration of allies, those approachable and not approachable, reasons for approaching, and the winning over of an approachable one.
6.1.1. For courtesans (<s>veśyās</s>), the approach of men [brings] pleasure and livelihood by nature.
6.1.2. The initiative arising from desire is natural; the artificial is for the sake of gain.
6.1.3. Even that [artificial initiative] should be made to appear as if natural,
6.1.4. because men have trust in women who are devoted to passion.
6.1.5. And she should display non-greediness for the purpose of demonstrating that.
6.1.6. And she should not pursue gain by improper means, for the sake of preserving the future [relationship].

body.text: 6.1.7/.nityam alaṃkāra^yoginī rāja^mārga^avalokinī dṛśyamānā na ca^ativivṛtā tiṣṭhet/ paṇya^sadharmatvāt//(p.306)
body.translated_text: 6.1.7. Always adorned, looking at the royal road, visible yet not too exposed, she should stand — because she is of the nature of merchandise.

body.text: 6.1.8/.yair nāyakam āvarjayed anyābhyaś ca^avacchindyād ātmanaś ca^anarthaṃ pratikuryād arthaṃ ca sādhayen na ca gamyaiḥ paribhūyeta tān sahāyān kuryāt/
body.translated_text: 6.1.8. She should make [as] allies those by whom she might attract a patron, and separate [him] from others, and counteract her own misfortune, and accomplish her gain, and not be scorned by those who are approachable.

body.text: 6.1.9/.te tv ārakṣaka^puruṣā dharma^adhikaraṇasthā daivajñā vikrāntāḥ śūrāḥ samāna^vidyāḥ kalā^grāhiṇaḥ pīṭhamarda^viṭa^vidūṣaka^mālākāra^gandhika^śauṇḍika^rajaka^nāpita^bhikṣuk ās te ca te ca kārya^yogāt//(p.307)
body.translated_text: 6.1.9. These are: protector-men, those established in the courts of law, astrologers, the bold, heroes, those of equal learning, connoisseurs of arts, the <s>pīṭhamarda</s> (libertine's attendant), <s>viṭa</s> (parasite), <s>vidūṣaka</s> (jester), garland-makers, perfumers, liquor-sellers, washermen, barbers, and mendicants — and such others as are useful according to the task.

body.text:
6.1.10/.kevala^arthās tv amī gamyāḥ --- svatantraḥ pūrve vayasi vartamāno vittavān aparokṣavṛttir adhikaraṇavān akṛcchra^adhigata^vittaḥ/ saṃgharṣavān saṃtatāyaḥ subhaga^mānī ślāghanakaḥ ṣaṇḍakaś ca puṃ^śabda^arthī/ samāna^spardhī svabhāvatas tyāgī/ rājani mahāmātre vā siddho daiva^pramāṇo vitta^(p.307)avamānī gurūṇāṃ śāsana^atigaḥ sajātānāṃ lakṣya^bhūtaḥ
savitta eka^putro liṅgī pracchanna^kāmaḥ śūro vaidyaś ca^iti//(p.308)
6.1.11/.prīti^yaśo^arthās tu guṇato +adhigamyāḥ//(p.308)
body.translated_text: 6.1.10. But these are approachable solely for gain: one who is independent, in the prime of youth, wealthy, of evident livelihood, possessed of legal authority, one whose wealth is easily obtained; one who is competitive, of sustained income, considers himself fortunate, boastful, a eunuch desirous of the name 'man'; a rival of equals, naturally generous; one who has succeeded with a king or minister, who takes fate as authority, who despises wealth, who transgresses the orders of elders, who is a target among his peers; a wealthy only-son, a religious mendicant of secret passions, a hero, and a physician. 6.1.11. But those to be approached for affection, fame, and gain are those obtained on account of [their] qualities.

body.text:
6.1.12/.mahākulīno viddhān sarva^samayajñaḥ kavir ākhyāna^kuśalo vāggmī (p.308)pragalbho vividha^śilpajño vṛddha^darśī sthūla^lakṣo mahā^utsāho dṛḍha^bhaktir anasūyakas tyāgī mitra^vatsalo ghaṭā^goṣṭhī^prekṣaṇaka^samāja^samasyā^krīḍana^śīlo nīrujo +avyaṅga^śarīraḥ prāṇa^vāna^madyapo vṛṣo maitraḥ strīṇāṃ praṇetā lālayitā ca/ na ca^āsāṃ vaśagaḥ svatantra^vṛttir
aniṣṭhuro +anīrṣyālur anavaśaṅkī ca^iti nāyaka^guṇāḥ//(p.309)
body.translated_text: 6.1.12. [The ideal lover is:] born of a great family, learned, knowledgeable of all conventions, a poet, skilled in narration, eloquent, bold, proficient in various arts, one who has seen elders [i.e., experienced], broad-minded, greatly enthusiastic, firmly devoted, free from envy, generous, affectionate toward friends, fond of assemblies, gatherings, spectacles, festivals, riddle-games, and pastimes, healthy, with an unblemished body, vigorous, not addicted to liquor, virile, friendly, a leader of women and one who pampers them; yet not subservient to them, independent in conduct, not cruel, not jealous, and not suspicious — these are the qualities of the hero (<s>nāyaka</s>).

body.text: 6.1.13/.nāyikāyāḥ punā rūpa^yauvana^lakṣaṇa^mādhurya yoginī guṇeṣv anuraktā na tathā^artheṣu prīti^saṃyoga^śīlā sthiram atireka^jātīyā viśeṣa^arthinī nityam akadarya^vṛttir goṣṭhī^kalā^priyā ca^iti [nāyikā^guṇāḥ]//(p.309)
body.translated_text: 6.1.13. The qualities of the heroine (<s>nāyikā</s>) are: beauty, youth, auspicious marks, sweetness, being a <s>yoginī</s> (skilled woman), attached to virtues rather than to wealth, disposed to love and union, constant, of a nature surpassing [others], desirous of distinction, never miserly in conduct, and fond of assemblies and arts.

body.text: 6.1.14/.nāyikā punar^buddhi^śīla^ācāra ārjavaṃ kṛtajñatā dīrgha^dūra^darśitvaṃ avisaṃvāditā deśa^kāla^jñatā nāgarakatā dainya^atihāsa^paiśunya^parivāda^krodha^lobha^stambha^cāpala^varjanaṃ pūrva^abhibhāṣitā kāmasūtra^kauśalaṃ tad^aṅga^vidyāsu ca^iti sādhāraṇa^guṇāḥ/
body.translated_text: 6.1.14. The general qualities [shared by both hero and heroine] are: intellect, good character, proper conduct, straightforwardness, gratitude, far-sightedness, trustworthiness, knowledge of place and time, urbanity (<s>nāgarakatā</s>), avoidance of meanness, mockery, slander, reproach, anger, greed, obstinacy, and fickleness, speaking first [in greeting], skill in the <s>Kāmasūtra</s>, and [proficiency] in the arts ancillary to it.
6.1.15. The opposite of these qualities constitutes faults.

body.text: 6.1.16/.kṣayī rogī kṛmi^śakṛd^vāyasāsyaḥ priya^kalatraḥ paruṣa^vāk^kadaryo nirghṛṇo gurujana^parityaktaḥ steno dambha^śīlo mūla^karmaṇi prasakto māna^apamānayor anapekṣī dveṣyair apy artha^hāryo vilajja ity agamyāḥ//(p.310)
body.translated_text: 6.1.16. Those who should not be resorted to (<s>agamya</s>) are: one who is consumptive, diseased, one whose mouth smells of worms or excrement [lit. worm-excrement-crow-mouth], one who is attached to his own wife, one who is harsh in speech, miserly, merciless, abandoned by elders, a thief, deceitful by nature, one addicted to sorcery (<s>mūlakarman</s>), indifferent to honor and dishonor, one who can be won over even by enemies for money, and one who is shameless.

body.text: 6.1.17/.rāgo bhayam arthaḥ saṃgharṣo vaira^niryātanaṃ jijñāsā pakṣaḥ khedo gharmo yaśo +anukampā suhṛd^vākyaṃ hrīḥ priya^sādṛśyaṃ dhanyatā rāga^apanayaḥ sājātyaṃ sāhaveśyaṃ sātatyam āyatiś ca gamana^kāraṇāni bhavanti^ity^ācāryāḥ/
body.translated_text: 6.1.17. The reasons for going [to a lover], according to the teachers (<s>ācāryas</s>), are: passion, fear, profit, rivalry, revenge, curiosity, partisanship, sorrow, heat [of passion], fame, compassion, a friend's words, shame, resemblance to a beloved, prosperity, removal of passion, common origin, being fellow-courtesans, habituation, and future prospects.
6.1.18. <s>Vātsyāyana</s> [says the reasons are]: profit, prevention of loss, and affection.

body.text: 6.1.19/.arthas tu prītyā na bādhitaḥ/ asya prādhānyāt/
body.translated_text: 6.1.19. But profit is not overridden by affection, because of its primacy.

6.1.20. However, in matters of fear and the like, one should weigh the relative importance — thus is the consideration regarding companions and the reasons for going or not going to the accessible and inaccessible.

body.text: 6.1.21/.upamantritā^api gamyena sahasā na pratijānīyāt/ puruṣāṇāṃ sulabha^avamānitvāt/
body.translated_text: 6.1.21. Even when invited by a desirable man (<s>gamya</s>), she should not agree hastily, for men despise what is easily obtained.

body.text: 6.1.22/.bhāva^jijñāsā^arthaṃ praicāraka^mukhān saṃvāhaka^gāyana^vaihāsikān gamye tadbhaktān vā praṇidadhyāt/
body.translated_text: 6.1.22. For the purpose of ascertaining his feelings, she should send out agents — masseuses, singers, jesters, or devotees of that [man] — to investigate.

body.text: 6.1.23/.tad^abhāve pīṭhamarda^ādīn/ tebhyo nāyakasya śauca^aśaucaṃ rāga^aparāgau sakta^asaktāṃ dāna^adāne ca vidyāt/
body.translated_text: 6.1.23. In the absence of these, [she should use] the <s>pīṭhamarda</s> (male companion) and others. From them she should learn of the hero's purity or impurity, his passion or indifference, his attachment or detachment, and his generosity or lack thereof.
6.1.24. And with one who has been assessed favorably, she should establish affection, with the <s>viṭa</s> (libertine) as intermediary.

body.text: 6.1.25/.lāvaka^kukkuṭa^meṣa^yuddha^śuka^śārikā^pralāpana^prekṣaṇaka^kalā^ vyapadeśena pīṭhamardo nāyakaṃ tasyā udavasitam ānayet/
body.translated_text: 6.1.25. Under the pretext of [watching] quail-fights, cock-fights, ram-fights, parrot and mynah recitations, spectacles, and arts, the <s>pīṭhamarda</s> should bring the hero to her dwelling.
6.1.26. Or [bring] her to his.

body.text: 6.1.27/.āgatasya prīti^kautuka^jananaṃ kiṃ cid dravya^jātaṃ svayam idam asādhāraṇa^upabhogyam iti prīti^dāyaṃ dadyāt/
body.translated_text: 6.1.27. When he arrives, she should give him some pleasing gift, saying 'This is for your exclusive enjoyment and is not shared with others,' thus generating affection and curiosity.

body.text: 6.1.28/.yatra ca ramate tayā goṣṭhya^enam upacāraiś ca rañjayet//(p.313)
body.translated_text: 6.1.28. And wherever he takes pleasure, she should delight him with conversation and courtesies.

body.text: 6.1.29/.gate ca saparihāsa^pralāpāṃ sa^upāyanāṃ paricārikām abhikṣṇaṃ preṣayet/
body.translated_text: 6.1.29. When he has departed, she should frequently send an attendant with playful talk and gifts.

body.text: 6.1.30/.sapīṭhamardāyāś ca kāraṇa^apadeśena svayaṃ gamanam iti gamya^upāvartanam//(p.313) bhavanti ca^atra ślokāḥ ---(p.314)
body.translated_text: 6.1.30. And she herself, accompanied by the <s>pīṭhamarda</s>, should visit [him] under some pretext — thus is the method of attracting a desirable man. And here are verses:
6.1.31ab. Betel-leaves, garlands, and refined ointments —
6.1.31cd. she should bring [these] to the one who has arrived, with affection, and arrange conversations about the arts.
6.1.32ab. She should give gifts to inspire love and arrange reciprocal exchanges;
6.1.32cd. and the intent of union she should convey through her own [hints].
6.1.33ab. Through love-gifts, offerings, and courtesies alone,

body.text: 6.1.33cd/.gamyena saha saṃsṛṣṭā rañjayet taṃ tataḥ param//(p.314)
body.translated_text: 6.1.33cd. having become intimate with the desirable man, she should then delight him further.
6.2. Compliance with the beloved (<s>kāntānuvṛtta</s>)
6.2.1. Having united with the hero, she should follow the conduct of the sole wife (<s>ekacāriṇī</s>) for the purpose of pleasing him.

body.text: 6.2.2/.rañjayen na tu sajjeta saktavac ca viceṣṭeta^iti saṃkṣepa^uktiḥ/
body.translated_text: 6.2.2. She should delight [him] but not become attached; yet she should behave as though attached — this is the summary statement.
6.2.3. If her mother is cruel-natured and money-minded, she should be dependent on her.
6.2.4. In the absence of the mother, on a surrogate mother (<s>mātṛkā</s>).
6.2.5. But she [the mother/surrogate] should not be overly fond of the desirable man.
6.2.6. And she should forcibly bring her daughter away [from him when needed].

body.text: 6.2.7/.tatra tu nāyikāyāḥ saṃtatam aratir nirvedo vrīḍā^bhayaṃ ca/
body.translated_text: 6.2.7. In that case, the heroine should show constant displeasure, weariness, shame, and fear.
6.2.8. But she should never actually transgress [the mother's] command.

body.text: 6.2.9/.vyādhiṃ ca^ekam animittam ajugupsitam acakṣurgrāhyam anityaṃ ca khyāpayet/
body.translated_text: 6.2.9. She should announce an illness — one that has no apparent cause, is not repulsive, is not visible to the eye, and is impermanent.
6.2.10. And when there is a [real] reason, [she should make] that the pretext for visiting the hero.

body.text: 6.2.11/.nirmālyasya tu nāyikā ceṭikāṃ preṣayet tāmbūlasya ca//(p.315)
body.translated_text: 6.2.11. The heroine should send an attendant with the remnants of [ritual] offerings and with betel.
6.2.12. [She should show] wonder at his lovemaking and his courtesies,
6.2.13. pupilship in the sixty-four arts,
6.2.14. and diligent practice of the techniques taught by him,
6.2.15. adaptation to his habits in private conduct,
6.2.16. revealing her desires,
6.2.17. concealing her physical defects in intimate matters,
6.2.18. not disregarding him when he turns away in bed,
6.2.19. compliance when he touches her private parts,
6.2.20. kissing and embracing him while he sleeps.

body.text: 6.2.21/.prekṣaṇam anya^manaskasya/ rāja^mārge ca prāsādasthāyās tatra viditāyā vrīḍā^śāṭhya^nāśaḥ/
body.translated_text: 6.2.21. Gazing at him when he is absent-minded; and when she, standing on a balcony, is recognized [by him] on the royal highway — the abandonment of bashfulness and pretense.

body.text: 6.2.22/.tad^dveṣye dveṣyatā/ tat^priye priyatā/ tad^ramye (p.316)ratiḥ/ tam anu harṣa^śokau/ strīṣu jijñāsā/ kopaś ca^adīrghaḥ/
body.translated_text: 6.2.22. Hostility toward what he hates; affection for what he loves; delight in what pleases him; sharing his joy and sorrow; curiosity about [rival] women; and anger that is not prolonged.
6.2.23. Even regarding nail and bite marks made by herself, [she should show] suspicion of another woman.
6.2.24. Not speaking of her love [directly],
6.2.25. but showing it through gestures.
6.2.26-27. But expressing it openly during intoxication, sleep, or illness; and likewise regarding the praiseworthy deeds of the hero.

body.text: 6.2.28/.tasmin bruvāṇe vākya^artha^grahaṇam/ tad^avadhārya praśaṃsā^viṣaye bhāṣaṇam/ tad^vākyasya ca^uttareṇa yojanam/ bhaktimāṃś cet/
body.translated_text: 6.2.28. When he speaks, grasping the meaning of his words; having understood, speaking on topics worthy of praise; and connecting his statements with [appropriate] responses — if he is devoted.
6.2.29. Following along in conversations, except regarding a co-wife.

body.text: 6.2.30/.niḥśvāse jṛmbhite skhalite patite vā tasya ca^ārtim āśaṃsīta/
body.translated_text: 6.2.30. At his sighing, yawning, stumbling, or falling, she should express concern for his well-being.
6.2.31. At sneezing, exclaiming, or expressions of wonder, saying 'Live long!'
6.2.32. In his despondency, [she should give] the pretext of illness or pregnancy cravings.
6.2.33. Not praising another for his qualities.
6.2.34. Not criticizing one who has the same faults [as himself].
6.2.35. Wearing what has been given [by him].
6.2.36. In the case of a groundless offense by him, or during his misfortune — not wearing ornaments and not eating.
6.2.37. And lamentations befitting the occasion.

body.text: 6.2.38/.tena saha deśa^mokṣaṃ rocayed rājani niṣkrayaṃ ca/(p.317)
body.translated_text: 6.2.38. She should express desire to leave the country with him, and [offer to pay] ransom to the king.
6.2.39. [She should say:] 'My life's purpose is fulfilled in obtaining him.'
6.2.40. When he acquires wealth, when a cherished wish is fulfilled, or when his body recovers [from illness] — offerings to the deity previously invoked [in prayer].
6.2.41. Constant adornment; moderate eating.

body.text: 6.2.42/.gīte ca nāma^gotrayor grahaṇam/ glānyām urasi lalāṭe ca karaṃ kurvīta/ tat^sukham upalabhya nidrā^lābhaḥ/
body.translated_text: 6.2.42. In singing, mentioning his name and family name. In languor, placing a hand on his chest and forehead; and having experienced that pleasure, falling asleep.
6.2.43. Sitting in his lap and sleeping [there]; going [to him] during separation.
6.2.44. From him she should desire a son; she should not wish for a longer life [than his].
6.2.45. She should not reveal to others any secret matter unknown [to the public] about him.

body.text: 6.2.46/.vratam upavāsaṃ ca^asya nirvartayet mayi doṣa iti/ aśakye svayam api tad^rūpā syāt/
body.translated_text: 6.2.46. She should carry out his vows and fasts [saying] 'The fault is mine'; and if unable, she should herself observe similar ones.
6.2.47. In a dispute, [she should say] 'Even for him it is impossible' — this is the indication of [her commitment to his] interests.
6.2.48. She should look upon his property and her own without distinction.
6.2.49. Without him, not going to assemblies and the like.
6.2.50. Taking pride in wearing his flower-remnants and in eating his leftovers.
6.2.51. Honoring his family, character, craft, caste, learning, complexion, wealth, country, friends, qualities, age, and sweetness.
6.2.52. Urging him [to perform] in singing and other [arts] when he is skilled.
6.2.53. Going to him regardless of fear, cold, heat, or rain.

body.text: 6.2.54/.sa eva ca me syād ity aurdhva^dehikeṣu vacanam/
body.translated_text: 6.2.54. And saying regarding matters after death: 'May he alone be mine [in the next life].'
6.2.55. Conforming to his preferred tastes, sentiments, temperament, and conduct.
6.2.56. Suspicion of [his practicing] sorcery (<s>mūlakarman</s>).
6.2.57. And constant quarreling with her mother regarding going to him.

body.text: 6.2.58/.balāt kāreṇa ca yady anyatra tayā nīyeta tadā viṣama^naśanaṃ śastraṃ rajjum iti kāmayeta/
body.translated_text: 6.2.58. If she is forcibly taken elsewhere by her [mother], she should express desire for poison, weapons, or a rope [i.e., threaten suicide].

body.text: 6.2.59/.pratyāyanaṃ ca praṇidhibhir nāyakasya/ svayaṃ vā^ātmano vṛtti^grahaṇam/
body.translated_text: 6.2.59. And reassuring the hero through agents; or herself adopting a [desperate] demeanor.
6.2.60. But never a dispute about money.
6.2.61. She should do nothing without [consulting] her mother.
6.2.62. During [his] travel, making him swear to return quickly.

body.text: 6.2.63/.proṣite mṛjā^niyamaś ca^alaṃkārasya pratiṣedhaḥ/ maṅgalaṃ tv apekṣyam/ ekaṃ śaṅkha^valayaṃ vā dhārayet/
body.translated_text: 6.2.63. When he is away — cleanliness, religious observance, and abstaining from ornaments; but auspicious tokens should be maintained; she should wear a single conch-shell bracelet.
6.2.64. Remembering past [moments together]; visiting fortune-tellers and those who interpret omens; longing for the moon, sun, and stars.
6.2.65. Upon seeing a pleasant dream, saying 'May I be united with him.'
6.2.66. Anxiety upon an inauspicious [dream], and performing a pacification rite.
6.2.67. When he has returned — worship of <s>Kāma</s> (the god of love).
6.2.68. Making offerings to the deities.
6.2.69. Having friends bring a full vessel [as an auspicious offering].
6.2.70. And worship of crows.
6.2.71. And this same [set of observances applies] after the first union, except for the worship of crows.
6.2.72. She should speak of dying with him [after death], if he is attached.

body.text: 6.2.73/.nisṛṣṭa^bhāvaḥ samāna^vṛttiḥ prayojana^kārī nirāśaṅko nirapekṣo +artheṣv iti sakta^lakṣaṇāni//(p.322)
body.translated_text: 6.2.73. The signs of an attached [lover] are: open-heartedness, similar habits, acting purposefully [for her benefit], freedom from suspicion, and indifference to money.

body.text: 6.2.74/.tad etan nirdarśana^arthaṃ dattaka^śāsanād uktam/ anuktaṃ ca lokataḥ śīlayet puruṣa^prakṛtitaś ca//(p.322) bhavataś ca^atra ślokau ---(p.323)
body.translated_text: 6.2.74. This has been stated for the purpose of illustration, from the teaching of <s>Dattaka</s>. And what has not been stated, one should learn from common practice and from the nature of men.
6.2.75ab. Due to subtlety, excessive greed, and natural ignorance,
6.2.75cd. the signs of love in women are hard to know, even by those experienced [in such matters].
6.2.76ab. They desire, they become detached, they enchant, they abandon,
6.2.76cd. and even while extracting all wealth, women are never truly understood.
6.3. Methods of acquiring wealth, signs of detachment, understanding of the detached, and the procedure of dismissal.
6.3.1. The acquisition of wealth from the attached and other [types of lovers] is natural or through stratagems.

body.text: 6.3.2/.tatra svābhāvikaṃ saṃkalpāt samadhikaṃ vā labhamānā na^upāyān prayuñjīta^ity ācāryāḥ/
body.translated_text: 6.3.2. In the case of natural [acquisition], the teachers (<s>ācāryas</s>) say: if she obtains equal or more than expected through [the lover's] own volition, she should not employ stratagems.

body.text: 6.3.3/.viditam apy upāyaiḥ pariṣkṛtaṃ dviguṇaṃ dāsyati^iti vātsyāyanaḥ//(p.324)
body.translated_text: 6.3.3. <s>Vātsyāyana</s> [says]: even if it is known [that she uses stratagems], when refined by [skillful] means, he will give double.

6.3.4. Through arrangements with merchants dealing in ornaments, food, drink, beverages, garlands, garments, and fragrant substances — [she obtains money] by deducting a commission through the return of goods on account.
6.3.5. Praising his wealth in his presence.
6.3.6. Making pretexts of vows, tree-gardens, temples, ponds, garden-festivals, and love-gifts.
6.3.7. The theft of ornaments by guards or thieves, occasioned by [the courtesan's] visiting [the lover].
6.3.8. And the destruction of property in her house by fire, wall-breaching, or negligence.

body.text: 6.3.9/.tathā yācita^alaṃkārāṇāṃ nāyaka^alaṃkārāṇāṃ ca tad^abhigamana^arthasya vyayasya praṇidhibhir nivedanam/
body.translated_text: 6.3.9. Likewise, informing through spies about borrowed ornaments, the hero's ornaments, and the expenditure incurred for visiting him.

body.text: 6.3.10/.tad^artham ṛṇa^grahaṇam/ jananyā saha tad^udbhavasya vyayasya vivādaḥ/
body.translated_text: 6.3.10. Incurring debts for that purpose. Quarreling with her mother about the expenses arising from that.
6.3.11. Not going to a friend's affairs, because of not bringing gifts.

body.text: 6.3.12/.taiś ca pūrvam āhṛtā guravo +abhihārāḥ pūrvam (p.324)upanītāḥ pūrvaṃ śrāvitāḥ syuḥ/
body.translated_text: 6.3.12. Not attending the festivals and gatherings of friends and acquaintances, due to lack of means.
6.3.13. Among these, whichever cause suits the occasion should be employed.
6.3.14. Not having performed the promised rites of former lovers, she declares: 'Not having fulfilled my obligation, I am disreputable.'
6.3.15. [She says:] 'The servants of a powerful man who desires me have carried away my property.'
6.3.16. Such are the means of obtaining money.

body.text: 6.3.17/.gṛha^karma/ sakhyāḥ putrasya^utsañjanam dohado vyādhir mitrasya duḥkha^apanayanam iti/
body.translated_text: 6.3.17-18. She should also demonstrate to him the expenditures required, make them visible, and gradually increase her demands while maintaining his affection.
6.3.19-20. Signs that a lover's passion is waning: he gives less, visits less, makes excuses, and shows interest in others.

body.text: 6.3.19/.tayā śīlitasya ca^alaṃkārasya bhāṇḍa^upaskarasya vā vaṇijo vikraya^arthaṃ darśanam/
body.translated_text: 6.3.21-22. When these signs appear, she should attempt to revive his interest through various means.

body.text: 6.3.20/.pratigaṇikānāṃ ca sadṛśasya bhāṇḍasya vyatikare prativiśiṣṭasya grahaṇam/
body.translated_text: 6.3.23-24. If that fails, she should proceed to extract maximum resources before the final separation.
6.3.25. Thus ends the section on obtaining money.
6.3.26-28. Signs that a lover's attachment has ended: indifference, coldness, breaking promises, and avoidance.

body.text: 6.3.23/.tāsu nāyaka^samakṣam ātmano +abhyadhikaṃ lābhaṃ bhūtam abhūtaṃ vā vrīḍitā nāma varṇayet/
body.translated_text: 6.3.29-30. Recognizing these signs, the courtesan should plan her next course of action.

body.text: 6.3.24/.pūrva^yogināṃ ca lābha^atiśayena punaḥ saṃdhāne yatamānānām aviṣkṛtaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ/
body.translated_text: 6.3.31-32. Methods of getting rid of an unwanted lover — she should make him disgusted through deliberate rudeness, or through revealing his secrets.
6.3.33-34. Or she should provoke a quarrel by praising his rivals, or embarrass him in public.
6.3.35-37. [Further methods:] Ignoring his wishes, expressing contempt for his gifts, yawning during conversation, casting eyes on other men, and refusing intimacy.

body.text: 6.3.27/.viraktaṃ ca nityam eva prakṛti^vikriyāto vidyāt mukha^varṇāc ca//(p.328)
body.translated_text: 6.3.38-39. She should show contempt for his abilities, speak of his faults before others, and associate with his enemies.
6.3.40-42. When he is finally disgusted and leaves, she should express indifference. But if he is still useful, she should maintain a thread of connection.
6.3.43-45. [Concluding verses on dismissal methods.] Thus ends the section on getting rid of a lover.
6.4. On reunion with a former lover:
6.4.1. A courtesan who has been abandoned, or who has herself abandoned a lover, may wish to return to him. She should consider whether it is profitable.
6.4.2-3. If the former lover has grown wealthy, if he still has affection, if her current situation is poor — these are reasons for reunion.
6.4.4-5. She should send intermediaries, remind him of past pleasures, and express regret for the separation.
6.4.6-7. Through a messenger, she should convey: 'I was compelled by circumstances, not by my own wish.'
6.4.8-10. If he agrees to reunion, she should show genuine change and devotion. But she should be wary of former grievances.

body.text: 6.3.36/.tasya sāra^dravyāṇi prāg avabodhād anya^apadeśena haste kurvīta/
body.translated_text: 6.4.11-13. [Verses on reunions:] 'A fire covered with ashes may burn again' — so too a former attachment. The wise courtesan acts accordingly.
6.4.14-16. She should evaluate what went wrong before and ensure the same mistakes are not repeated.
6.4.17-18. [Concluding guidance on managing reunions.] Thus ends the section on reunion with former lovers.
6.5. Types of gain:
6.5.1. Gain, loss, associated gain, associated loss, doubt about gain, doubt about loss — these are to be considered.

body.text: 6.3.41/.tad^aniṣṭha^sevā/ nindita^abhyāsaḥ/ oṣṭha^nirbhogaḥ/ pādena bhūmer abhighātaḥ/ avijñāta^viṣayasya saṃkathā/ tad^vijñāteṣv avismayaḥ *kutsā ca/ darpa^vighātaḥ/ adhikaiḥ saha saṃvāsaḥ/ *anapekṣaṇam/[ch:omits] samāna^doṣāṇāṃ nindā/ rahasi ca^avasthānam//(p.330)
body.translated_text: 6.5.2. Having considered the place, time, situation, her own qualities, good fortune, and whether she is inferior or superior to other [courtesans] — she should set the price for the night.

body.text: 6.3.42/.rata^upacāreṣu^udvegaḥ/ mukhasya^ādānam/ jaghanasya rakṣaṇam/ nakha^daśana^kṣatebhyo jugupsā/ parisvaṅge bhujamayyā sūcyā vyavadhānam/ stabdhatā gātrāṇām/ sakthnor vyatyāsaḥ/ nidrā^aparatvaṃ ca/ śrāntam (p.330)upalabhya codanā/ aśaktau hāsaḥ/ śaktāv anabhinandanam/ divā^api/ bhāvam upalabhya mahājana^abhigamanam//(p.331)
body.translated_text: 6.5.3. She should employ messengers for those who are approachable, and should herself send away those who are attached to her.

body.text: 6.3.43/.vākyeṣu cchala^grahaṇam/ anarmaṇi hāsaḥ/ narmaṇi ca^anyam apadiśya hasati vadati tasmin kaṭākṣeṇa parijanasya prekṣaṇaṃ tāḍanaṃ ca/ āhatya ca^asya kathām anyāḥ kathāḥ/ tad^vyalīkānāṃ vyasanānāṃ ca^aparihāryāṇām anukīrtanam/ marmaṇāṃ ca ceṭikayā^upakṣepaṇam/
body.translated_text: 6.5.4. For an excess of gain, she may visit even a single man twice, thrice, or four times; and she should maintain the relationship.

body.text: 6.3.44/.āgate ca^adarśanam/ ayācya^yācanam/ ante svayaṃ mokṣaś ca^iti parigrahakasya^iti dattakasya//(p.331) bhavataś ca^atra ślokau ---(p.332)
body.translated_text: 6.5.5-6. When two suitors appear simultaneously, she should choose the one who offers more. But she must also consider future prospects and reputation.
6.5.7-8. Among suitors, a generous man of steady nature is preferable to a wealthy but fickle one.

body.text: 6.3.45cd/.raktād arthasya ca^ādānam ante mokṣaś ca vaiśikam//(p.332)
body.translated_text: 6.5.9-11. She should also consider: who will give ornaments, who will give money, who will remove difficulties, who will provide protection.
6.5.12-13. Between a generous poor man and a stingy rich man — the generous poor man may be preferable for long-term advantage.
6.5.14-16. [Verses comparing types of lovers and their relative worth to the courtesan.]
6.5.17-18. Thus the courtesan should always calculate advantage, using the methods described.
6.5.19-20. A courtesan should also keep accounts and records of her transactions to manage her affairs efficiently.

body.text: 6.4.2/.sa ced avasita^artho vittavān sānu^rāgaś ca tataḥ saṃdheyaḥ//(p.333)
body.translated_text: 6.6. Gains and losses — detailed calculations:
6.6.1-2. The consideration of gain (<s>artha</s>), loss (<s>anartha</s>), their attendant consequences, and doubt — this is the courtesan's constant duty.
6.6.3-5. Gain is of three kinds: gain leading to future gain, gain leading to future loss, and gain with uncertain future.
6.6.6-8. Similarly, loss is threefold, and doubt is sixfold.
6.6.9-11. When gain from one side is matched with loss from another, the courtesan must weigh the balance carefully.
6.6.12-14. Future prospects, reputation, and safety should all be considered alongside immediate monetary gain.
6.6.15-17. [Verses on calculating compound gains and losses across multiple scenarios.]
6.6.18-20. A gain that secures future prosperity is better than a larger gain that leads to future loss.

body.text: 6.4.10/.itas tataś ca svayam eva^apasṛtya^upajapati ced ubhayor guṇān apekṣī cala^buddhir asaṃdheyaḥ//(p.334)
body.translated_text: 6.6.21-23. She should also consider: 'Will this gain attract other wealthy suitors? Or will it drive them away?'

body.text: 6.4.11/.itas tataś ca niṣkāsita^apasṛtaḥ sthira^buddhiḥ/ sa ced anyato bahu^labhamānayā niṣkāsitaḥ syāt sasāro +api tayā roṣito mama^amarṣād bahu dāsyati^iti saṃdheyaḥ//(p.335)
body.translated_text: 6.6.24-26. [Further analysis of compound gains, losses, and doubts.]
6.6.27-29. Among multiple suitors of different qualities, she should prefer the one who maximizes long-term gain while minimizing risk.

body.text: 6.4.13/.itaḥ svayam apasṛtas tato niṣkāsita^apasṛto yady atiriktam ādau ca dadyāt tataḥ pratigrāhyaḥ//(p.335)
body.translated_text: 6.6.30-32. [Detailed examples of how to evaluate multiple simultaneous proposals.]

body.text: 6.4.14/.itaḥ svayam apasṛtya tatra sthita upajapaṃs tarkayitavyaḥ//(p.335)
body.translated_text: 6.6.33-34. The courtesan who masters this calculus of gain and loss will always prosper.

body.text: 6.4.15/.viśeṣa^arthī ca^āgatas tato viśeṣam apaśyann āgantukāmo [mayi] māṃ jijñāsitukāmaḥ sa āgatya sa^anurāgatvād dāsyati/ tasyāṃ vā doṣān dṛṣṭvā mayi bhūyiṣṭhān guṇān adhunā paśyati sa guṇa^darśī bhūyiṣṭhaṃ dāsyati//(p.335)
body.translated_text: 6.6.35. Where approaching a new [suitor] involves expense, and a former attached [lover] in anger may cause harm or may not, or the attached [lover] in resentment may demand back what was given or may not — this is doubt on both sides.

body.text: 6.4.16/.bālo vā na^ekatra^dṛṣṭir atisaṃdhāna^pradhāno vā haridrā^rāgo vā yat kiṃcana^kārī vā ity avetya saṃdadhyān na vā//(p.336)
body.translated_text: 6.6.36. The <s>Bābhravīyas</s> say:

body.text:
6.4.17/.ito niṣkāsita^apasṛtas tataḥ svayam apasṛta upajapaṃs tarkayitavyaḥ/
6.4.18/.anurāgād āgantukāmaḥ sa bahu dāsyati/ mama gunair bhāvito yo +anyasyāṃ na ramate//(p.336)
body.translated_text: 6.6.37. Where approaching [a suitor] yields gain, and not approaching yields gain from the attached [lover] — that is gain on both sides.

body.text: 6.4.19/.pūrvam ayogena vā mayā niṣkāsitaḥ sa māṃ śīlayitvā vairaṃ niryātayitukāmo dhanam abhiyogād vā mayā^asya^apahṛtaṃ tad^viśvāsya pratīpam ādātukāmo nirveṣṭukāmo vā māṃ vartamāna^udbhedayitvā tyaktukāma ity akalyāṇa^buddhir asaṃdheyaḥ//(p.336)
body.translated_text: 6.6.38. Where approaching yields fruitless expense, and not approaching yields irremediable loss — that is loss on both sides.
6.6.39. Where approaching involves no expense, and [the suitor] may or may not give, and not approaching [means] the attached [lover] may or may not give — that is doubt of gain on both sides.

body.text: 6.4.21/.ito niṣkāsitas tatra sthita upajapann etena vyākhyātaḥ//(p.337)
body.translated_text: 6.6.40. Where approaching involves expense, and the former powerful [lover] who is offended may or may not obtain [what he wants], and not approaching may or may not cause him to inflict harm in anger — that is doubt of loss on both sides.

6.6.41. In the combination of these: gain on one side and loss on the other; gain on one side and doubt of gain on the other; gain on one side and doubt of loss on the other — thus six mixed combinations.

body.text: 6.4.23/.vyalīka^arthaṃ niṣkāsito mayāsāvan yatra gato yatnād ānetavyaḥ/
body.translated_text: 6.6.42. Among these, having deliberated with companions, she should proceed where gain is greatest, where doubt of gain is weightier, or where loss is most mitigated.
6.6.43. Thus, <s>dharma</s> and <s>kāma</s> too should be exemplified by this same reasoning; and mixed together and interlinked — these are the combinations on both sides.
6.6.44. And <s>viṭas</s> (boon companions), together taking up one [courtesan] — that is the assembly's patronage.

body.text: 6.4.26/.artha^āgama^kālo vā^asya/ sthāna^vṛddhir asya jātā/ labdham anena^adhikaraṇam/ dārair viyuktaḥ/ pāra^tantryād vyāvṛttaḥ/ pitrā bhrātrā vā vibhaktaḥ/
body.translated_text: 6.6.45. She, being involved with them here and there, should extract wealth from each through their mutual rivalry.

body.text: 6.4.27/.anena vā pratibaddham anena saṃdhiṃ kṛtvā nāyakaṃ dhaninam avāpsyāmi/
body.translated_text: 6.6.46. And at the <s>Suvasantaka</s> festival and the like, she should have her mother announce: 'Whoever provides this and that for her, to him my daughter will go tonight.'

body.text: 6.4.28/.vimānito vā bhāryayā tam eva tasyāṃ vikramayiṣyāmi/
body.translated_text: 6.6.47. And in their rivalry-driven visits, she should observe the business purposes.

body.text: 6.4.29/.asya vā mitraṃ mad^dveṣiṇīṃ sapatnīṃ kāmayate tad amunā bhedayiṣyāmi/
body.translated_text: 6.6.48. Gain from one is gain from all; loss from one is loss from all; gain from half is gain from all; loss from half is loss from all — these are the all-sided combinations.

6.6.49. Doubt of gain and doubt of loss should be combined as before; and likewise <s>dharma</s> and <s>kāma</s> should be mixed. Thus the consideration of gains, losses, consequences, and doubts [is completed].

body.text: 6.4.31/.tasya pīṭhamarda^ādayo mātur dauḥśīlyena nāyikāyāḥ saty apy anurāge (p.338)vivaśāyāḥ pūrvaṃ niṣkāsanaṃ varṇayeyuḥ/
body.translated_text: 6.6.50. A water-carrier servant, an attendant, a loose woman, a woman of free conduct, an actress, an artisan woman, an openly ruined woman, a woman living by her beauty, and a <s>gaṇikā</s> (courtesan) — these are the types of courtesans.

6.6.51. And for all of them — suitable clients, companions, how to please them, means of obtaining wealth, dismissal, re-engagement, distinctions of gain, and considerations of gain, loss, consequences, and doubts — [all should be understood] correspondingly.
6.6.52ab. Men seek pleasure, and women too seek pleasure.
6.6.52cd. Since the <s>śāstra</s> is primarily concerned with <s>artha</s>, therefore the science here is applied to women [courtesans].

body.text: 6.4.35/.apūrva^pūrva^saṃsṛṣṭayoḥ pūrva^saṃsṛṣṭaḥ śreyān/ sa hi vidita^śīlo dṛṣṭa^rāgaś ca sūpacāro bhavati^ity ācāryāḥ/
body.translated_text: 6.6.53ab. Some women are devoted to passion, and some are devoted to wealth.

body.text: 6.4.36/.pūrva^saṃsṛṣṭaḥ sarvato niṣpīḍita^arthatvān na^atyartham arthado duḥkhaṃ ca punar^viśvāsayitum/ apūrvas tu sukhena^anurajyata iti vātsyāyanaḥ/
body.translated_text: 6.6.53cd. Earlier, passion was described; the practices of courtesans are [described] in this book on courtesans.
7. The secret section (<s>aupaniṣadika</s>):

body.text: 6.4.38ab/.anyāṃ bhedayituṃ gamyād anyato gamyam eva vā/(p.340)
body.translated_text: 7.1. Making oneself attractive (<s>subhagaṃkaraṇa</s>), subjugation (<s>vaśīkaraṇa</s>), and aphrodisiac preparations (<s>vṛṣya</s>):
7.1.1. The <s>Kāmasūtra</s> has been expounded.
7.1.2. When one does not achieve the desired object by the methods stated therein, one should resort to the secret [arts].

body.text: 6.4.39cd/.atisaktaḥ pumān yatra bhayād bahu dadāti ca//(p.340)
body.translated_text: 7.1.3. Beauty, good qualities, youth, and liberality — these make one attractive.
7.1.4. An ointment of <s>tagara</s>, <s>kuṣṭha</s>, and <s>tālīsapatra</s> makes one attractive.
7.1.5. With these very [ingredients], finely ground, making a collyrium stick and applying it with castor oil — and eye-salve prepared in a skull —
7.1.6. An anointing oil prepared with leaves of <s>punarnavā</s>, <s>sahadevī</s>, <s>sārivā</s>, <s>kuraṇṭaka</s>, and blue lotus.
7.1.7. And garlands mixed with these same [substances].

body.text: 6.4.42ab/.saktaṃ tu vaśinaṃ nārī saṃbhāṣya^apy anyato vrajet/(p.340)
body.translated_text: 7.1.8. Having licked a powder of dried lotus, blue lotus, and <s>nāgakesara</s> with honey and ghee, one becomes attractive.
7.1.9. These same, mixed with <s>tagara</s>, <s>tālīsa</s>, and <s>tamālapatra</s>, make an ointment.
7.1.10. Coating the eye of a peacock or a <s>tarakṣu</s> (hyena) with gold and wearing it on the right hand — this is a charm for attractiveness.
7.1.11. Likewise, a <s>bādara</s> gem and a conch-gem — and the <s>Ātharvaṇa</s> rites [should be performed] for them.

7.1.12. From the tantric science, through the practice of secret knowledge, the master should keep a maidservant who has reached puberty away [from others] for one year; then considering her restrained, [he should marry her] —

body.text: 6.5.1/.gamya^bāhulye bahu pratidinaṃ ca labhamānā na^ekaṃ pratigṛhṇīyāt//(p.342)
body.translated_text: 7.1.13. A courtesan should have her daughter who has reached puberty [married] by inviting [suitors] appropriate to her knowledge, character, and beauty, [saying]: 'Whoever gives her this and that shall take her hand.'

body.text: 6.5.2/.deśaṃ kālaṃ sthitim ātmano guṇān saubhāgyaṃ ca^anyābhyo nyūna^atiriktatāṃ ca^avekṣya rajanyām arthaṃ sthāpayet//(p.342)
body.translated_text: 7.1.14. And she, unknown to her mother, should greatly endear herself to sons of wealthy men-about-town.

body.text: 6.5.3/.gamye dūtāṃś ca prayojayet/ tat^pratibaddhāṃś ca svayaṃ prahiṇuyāt//(p.342)
body.translated_text: 7.1.15. Their opportunities for meeting [are] at learning sessions for the arts, at the <s>Gandharva</s>-hall, and at the abode of female mendicants.

body.text: 6.5.4/.dvis triś catur iti lābhā^atiśaya^graha^artham ekasya^api gacchet/ parigrahaṃ ca caret//(p.342)
body.translated_text: 7.1.16. The mother should give her hand [in marriage] to one who gives as promised.

body.text: 6.5.5/.gamya^yaugapadye tu lābha^sāmye yad dravya^arthinī syāt tad dāyini viśeṣaḥ pratyakṣa ity ācāryāḥ//(p.343)
body.translated_text: 6.5.5. When two eligible [clients] present themselves simultaneously and the gains are equal, the one who gives what she desires in kind has the advantage — this is evident, say the teachers.
6.5.6. Since [gold] cannot be returned [i.e., is non-refundable] and all transactions are rooted in it, the one who gives gold [has the advantage] — thus says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.

6.5.7. Among gold, silver, copper, bronze, iron, vessels, furnishings, bedding, coverlets, special garments, fragrant substances, pungent preparations, ghee, oil, grains, and cattle — each preceding [item] has the advantage over the following.

body.text: 6.5.8/.yat tatra sāmyād vā dravya^sāmye mitra^vākyād atipātitvād āyatito gamya^guṇataḥ prītitaś ca viśeṣaḥ//(p.343)
body.translated_text: 6.5.8. Where there is equality even in that, distinction [is made] on the basis of equality of goods, the word of a friend, urgency, future prospects, the qualities of the [potential] client, and personal affection.
6.5.9. Between one who is passionate and one who is generous, the generous one has the evident advantage — say the teachers.
6.5.10. For generosity can be cultivated in a passionate one.

body.text: 6.5.11/.lubdho +api hi raktas tyajati na tu tyāgī nirbandhād rajyata iti vātsyāyanaḥ//(p.344)
body.translated_text: 6.5.11. Even a miser, when in love, gives; but a generous one does not, through compulsion, fall in love — thus says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.

body.text: 6.5.12/.tatra^api dhanavad^adhanavator dhanavati viśeṣaḥ/ tyāgi^prayojana^kartroḥ prayojana^kartari viśeṣaḥ pratyakṣa ity ācāryāḥ//(p.344)
body.translated_text: 6.5.12. Even there, between a wealthy and a non-wealthy [generous person], the wealthy one has the advantage. Between one who is generous and one who accomplishes purposes, the one who accomplishes purposes has the evident advantage — say the teachers.

body.text: 6.5.13/.prayojana^kartā sakṛt kṛtvā kṛtinam ātmānaṃ manyate tyāgī punar atītaṃ na^apekṣata iti vātsyāyanaḥ//(p.344)
body.translated_text: 6.5.13. One who accomplishes purposes, having done [the task] once, considers himself to have discharged his duty; but a generous one does not regard what has passed [as sufficient reason to stop giving] — thus says <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.
6.5.14. Even there, distinction [is made] on the basis of urgency.
6.5.15. Between one who is grateful and one who is generous, the generous one has the evident advantage — say the teachers.

body.text: 6.5.16/.ciram ārādhito +api tyāgī vyalīkam ekam upalabhya pratigaṇikayā vā mithyā^dūṣitaḥ śramam atītaṃ na^apekṣate/
body.translated_text: 6.5.16. A generous one, even if served for a long time, upon perceiving a single offense, or being falsely defamed by a rival courtesan, does not regard the past effort [as worthy of consideration].

body.text: 6.5.17/.prāyeṇa hi tejasvina ṛjavo +anādṛtāś ca tyāgino bhavanti/
body.translated_text: 6.5.17. For generous ones are generally spirited, straightforward, and [easily] offended.
